title: skyscapeR technical manual
text:
About this edition
This is the technical manual for skyscapeR 2.0, with methods anchored to 2.0.9004 and versioned validation through 2.0.9011. The function catalogue and vignette guide were checked against 2.0.9012. It documents how the package calculates its results, which assumptions affect their interpretation and which comparisons have been made against independent observations. Each study names the build tested.
The measurement-model guide compares six ways to represent uncertainty and gives the assumptions behind each. In build 2.0.9012 the uniform opening convolved with Gaussian survey error defaults to a survey-error standard deviation of 0.5°.
For a first analysis, follow the worked vignette. The package README covers installation and migration to version 2.0.

title: skyscapeR technical manual
text:
Finding a method
Use the function index to find a help page or an implementation note by name. The methods guide groups the calculations by research question. The vignette guide connects each step in the worked analysis to its technical explanation.

title: skyscapeR technical manual
text:
Finding the evidence
A01, D01 and S03 report calendar, density and significance checks on build 2.0.9005 and the D01 and S03 corrections verified on 2.0.9006. S01 evaluates false positives and power for the uniform-orientation test in 2.0.9007. S02 covers specified models, H07 covers partial photographs, and W01 compares drawn coordinates with numerical results. A05, A08 and W02 cover solar limits, target selection and the field-to-sky replay. For astronomical positions and prehistoric lunar bearings, A02 compares skyscapeR with the parent JPL ephemerides and JPL Horizons. For terrain horizons, H01 measures field accuracy and H02 compares numerical skylines at matched viewpoints. For sky reconstruction, consult the Milky Way tracing and calibration and the sky-rendering studies. The heliacal-rising study evaluates event timing. The ephemeris chapter distinguishes upstream precision claims from independent tests of this package.

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.1 Time, coordinates and ephemerides
Use this guide to move from a research question to its methods chapter, principal functions and validation evidence. Open question identifies a comparison that remains to be carried out. For alphabetical lookup and individual help pages, use the function index.
The astronomical conventions chapter traces a BCE date across two calendars, compares lunar positions from two origins and follows the fixed-star calculation across epochs.
Existing evidence. The ephemeris chapter identifies the inspected data generation and the supplier’s precision claim.
Open question. What positional differences remain against the matching JPL solution when epoch, time scale, origin and reference frame are held fixed?
Entry points. BC.AD(), astroYear(), jd2time(), time2jd(), long.date(), timestring(), ten(), skyscapeR.vars(), obliquity(), parallax.corr(), body.position().
Ephemeris background.

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.2 Reducing field observations
The field reduction chapter follows a compass reading and a timed solar sight from instrument readings to true bearing, including a circle reading that crosses north.
Existing evidence. The horizon studies use published survey bearings. Their residuals do not isolate the reduction step.
Open question. Can an independently oriented baseline be recovered from repeat compass and solar-reference observations, including the transition across north?
Entry points. mag.dec(), reduct.compass(), reduct.theodolite(), sunAz().

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.3 Terrain horizons and panoramas
The terrain methods explain how measured profiles, DEM skylines and reconstructed features enter a horizon object. The photographic calibration and interchange chapter traces a mask through control-point fitting, angular sampling and landscape export.
Existing evidence. The international H01 study reports field agreement for DEM-derived skyline altitudes by observing setup and terrain product, including the effect of search distance. H02 compares independently computed skylines at matched viewpoints.
Open question. How well are narrow features recovered between sampled bearings? How closely does a calibrated photographic skyline match surveyed points from the same viewpoint?
Entry points. createHor(), horFeature(), hor2alt(), importPanorama(), importPeakFinder(), createHWT(), downloadHWT(), exportHor(), exportStellarium(), exportPanorama(), demPalettes(), relinkHor(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.4 From bearings to celestial targets
The candidate-screening chapter takes a measured bearing and skyline altitude through the declination calculation to candidate targets. It explains how the spatial equinox convention and the search dates affect the candidates returned.
Existing evidence. The horizon comparisons constrain one input. The worked stellar study checks a different output, a seasonal date.
Open question. Where do high or asymmetric skylines change candidate membership, and how closely do the declination limits agree with independently calculated sightlines?
Entry points. az2dec(), hor2max.dec(), hor2min.dec(), findTargets(), skyObject(), sky.objects(), zenith(), antizenith(), orbit(), spatial.equinox().

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.5 Solar, lunar and planetary events
The event-search chapter distinguishes the first and last crossing of an irregular skyline. The lunar crossover chapter explains how the observing calendar and event definition determine which lunation is selected.
Existing evidence. The EFM and CC help pages record comparisons with published simulations and remaining discrepancies. The ephemeris chapter identifies the upstream assumptions.
Open question. Which discrepancies survive matching observing geometry, event definition and calendar? Can a reference calculation recover brief or repeated crossings of an uneven skyline?
Entry points. riseset(), dS(), jS(), eq(), nMjLX(), nmnLX(), sMjLX(), smnLX(), solar.date(), moonphase(), planet.extremes(), EFM(), CC().

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.6 Stellar positions and seasonal visibility
The stellar-phases chapter follows a catalogue position through the epoch calculation, extinction and visibility tests. It distinguishes the phase on the schematic seasonal axis from the Julian date used for a sky reconstruction.
Existing evidence. The worked heliacal-rising chapter compares two visibility models over seven stars with comparable dates. The models share ephemeris and site inputs.
Open question. How well do first and last visibility dates agree with dated sightings under documented observing conditions? Which phase transitions are still untested?
Entry points. star(), star.phases(), plot.skyscapeR.starphases().

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.7 Sky brightness and visualisation
The sky reconstruction chapter follows the direct, diffuse and atmospheric light components from skyRadiance() to the display. Its Milky Way comparison shows which structures the adopted boundary and brightness classes retain.
Existing evidence. The register distinguishes outline derivation, held-out twilight measurements, conservation of flux across zoom levels and an extinction implementation check.
Open question. Which independent observations constrain the outer Milky Way boundary and low-altitude surface brightness? How does performance change outside the twilight geometries already tested?
Entry points. sketchSky(), skyRadiance(), planisphere(), importConstellations(), stellariumSky(), skyStep().
Sky-rendering evidence.

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.8 Uncertainty and orientation distributions
The orientation-density chapter shows how a measured opening becomes a bearing distribution, how the local skyline changes its declination distribution, and what is lost when disjoint highest-density intervals are reduced to a single range.
Existing evidence. The doorway example records the transformed densities for the same measured opening against a level skyline and a notch.
Open question. Does the transformation preserve probability mass at north and near declination limits? Can multimodal examples recover the expected disjoint intervals?
Entry points. az.pdf(), dec.pdf(), coordtrans(), spd(), hpdi(), subset.skyscapeR.pdf(), plot.skyscapeR.pdf(), plot.skyscapeR.spd(), plotAzimuth(), plotBars().

title: 1  Methods by research question
text:
1.9 Null models and significance
The significance chapter documents the scientific hypothesis represented by each null, what counts as a trial, the handling of repeated sites, simulation size, and how global and local results should be read.
Existing evidence. Existing package checks include stored significance outputs. Those checks address numerical reproducibility; calibration of false-positive rates is a separate question.
Open question. Under data generated by each specified null, how often does the test reject at its stated threshold? How does that rate change with sample size and repeated measurements?
Entry points. randomTest(), modelTest(), bernoulli.trial(), pval2stars(), plot.skyscapeR.sigTest(), print.skyscapeR.sigTest().

title: 2  swephR and the Swiss Ephemeris
text:
2.1 Which layer supplies the result?
Scope. This page records the astronomical dependency, the manufacturer’s accuracy claim and the A02 comparisons for build 2.0.9004. The documented visibility and terrain studies address different quantities from the planetary and lunar position errors discussed here.
The environment inspected for the 7 November pilot had swephR 0.3.2, Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03 and swephRdata 0.0.1. The headers of the planetary and lunar files inspected for the modern and prehistoric blocks (sepl_18.se1, semo_18.se1, seplm36.se1, semom36.se1) identify DE431. Astrodienst reports a transition to DE441 in May 2026. An installation can continue to use older files. The four headers establish the provenance of these files only. They do not establish the data used for a different run (Astrodienst, n.d.b).
The event-search examples were subsequently run with modern planetary and lunar files whose headers identify DE441. The accompanying example archive records both hashes. These runs illustrate event selection and do not test compression accuracy.

title: 2  swephR and the Swiss Ephemeris
text:
Layer
Role in an analysis




skyscapeR
Chooses the body, date, site and calculation settings. In 2.0.9004 its file-backed planetary position routine checks for paired planetary and lunar file coverage at the epoch, requests Swiss files and checks the returned ephemeris flag and messages. A missing file can therefore stop a calculation.


swephR
Provides R bindings to the Swiss Ephemeris routines. The R package and the underlying engine have separate versions. The wrapper documentation describes the file-free Moshier option and the optional swephRdata distribution (swephR maintainers, n.d.).


Swiss Ephemeris and its data files
The engine reads the available numerical ephemeris and applies the requested transformations. The compressed planetary and lunar files identify their parent JPL solution. File generation and temporal coverage must be recorded for the position being compared (Astrodienst, n.d.b, n.d.a).
crumbs: 2  swephR and the Swiss Ephemeris

title: 2  swephR and the Swiss Ephemeris
text:
2.2 What the quoted accuracy measures
Astrodienst reports 0.001 arcsecond precision for its compressed ephemeris in reproducing the parent JPL data (Astrodienst, n.d.b). This specifies agreement between two numerical representations of the same underlying lunar and planetary trajectories. A comparison against another release also includes differences between the two JPL solutions. JPL makes a corresponding distinction between the precision of its numerical representation and the uncertainty in the trajectory itself (Jet Propulsion Laboratory, n.d.).
For an archaeological horizon event, another question is where the body would have appeared to a person at a particular place and time. The answer also depends on the observer’s position, the skyline, atmospheric refraction and Earth rotation. For ancient epochs, the conversion between dynamical time and Earth-rotation time involves an uncertain ΔT (Espenak, n.d.). A fixed star brings in its catalogue position and motion as well. The quoted planetary and lunar figure therefore supplies no general error bound for stellar phase dates or horizon bearings.

title: 2  swephR and the Swiss Ephemeris
text:
2.3 Validation status



Question
Evidence in this edition




How closely did the file-backed calculations reproduce JPL?
A02 checked 1,080 geocentric directions against DE431 and DE441 using matching file generations. Maximum separation was 0.0065″.


How did local lunar bearings compare with Horizons?
Across 177 prehistoric crossings, the median default azimuth difference was 0.059° and the maximum was 0.322°. Matching ΔT alone reduced the maximum to 0.027°. Crossing protocol and results.


Which comparisons still require separate evidence?
The heliacal-rising study concerns visibility models, H01 concerns terrain altitude, and A03 covers stellar catalogue positions.

title: 3  Astronomical conventions and stellar positions
text:
3.1 From a year label to an instant
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/dates.R, R/mechanics.R, R/stars.R, R/ephemeris.R and R/misc.R. To reproduce a position, specify the instant, the origin of the coordinate frame, the axes and the observer. A calendar agreement does not guarantee that two programs return the same coordinate. This chapter follows those choices from a dated record to a local sightline. The ephemeris chapter covers file selection and the supplier’s accuracy claim.
See the independent checks on build 2.0.9005 for results and limitations.
astroYear() and BC.AD() translate between historical labels and astronomical year numbers. Astronomical year 0 is 1 BCE, −1 is 2 BCE and −3499 is 3500 BCE. This conversion addresses the year numbering only. The Gregorian and Julian calendars in time2jd() are proleptic: the analyst selects a rule for the whole calculation, without an automatic reform date. A Julian day number can represent an instant specified in either calendar.
With a fixed civil offset zz hours east of UTC, the conversion is JDUT=JDcivil−z/24JD_{\mathrm{UT}}=JD_{\mathrm{civil}}-z/24. The input is checked for a valid calendar date; a date alone starts at local midnight. A Julian day rolls over at noon. In the reverse direction, jd2time() rounds to the nearest second, applies the offset at that rounded instant and handles day rollover. The output string does not retain its offset. Keep the numeric JD, calendar and timezone with a published result.
The +02:00 offset is a declared convention for this example. Longitude alone does not assign an ancient civil timezone. Current code accepts fixed offsets between −14 and +14 hours; UTC, GMT and an empty string all mean zero. Named zones use the installed IANA rules for the Gregorian date and are supported for 1900–9999. Ambiguous or nonexistent local times at a clock transition are rejected. Two distinct JDs can format to the same repeated wall time, so reversing a zone-free output string may be ambiguous (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, n.d.). The helpers do not apply leap-second, UT1 or TT corrections. Earth-rotation uncertainty and the dynamical ephemeris enter downstream (Espenak, n.d.; Astrodienst, n.d.).
timestring() formats components and defaults an omitted time to noon; a date passed alone to time2jd() defaults to midnight. long.date() formats a month/day label without resolving its year. ten() converts angular fields to decimal degrees, with a sign applied to the entire angle. These helpers address representation; none resolves an unknown epoch, timezone or angular reference.

title: 3  Astronomical conventions and stellar positions
text:
3.2 Origin, axes and apparent altitude
body.position() accepts numeric UT Julian dates or civil timestamps. Without a site it forces geocentric equatorial output. With a site it can calculate topocentric coordinates, applying the observer’s longitude, latitude and elevation before the horizontal conversion. In this build the geocentric branch requests equatorial Swiss coordinates, while the topocentric branch also requests the true-position flag; a numerical difference between those outputs therefore need not be pure parallax. Right ascension and declination are returned in degrees. Azimuth increases clockwise from true north, with altitude above the local astronomical horizontal. A horizon object contributes its georeference, not a terrain clearance test (Astrodienst, n.d.).
The Moon makes the distinction measurable. At 06:30 UTC on 20 March 2026, at 51° N, 0° longitude and 100 m elevation, the following three calls refer to one instant:

When comparing software, match the origin, date, frame, parallax, refraction and positional corrections before interpreting a residual as an ephemeris error. A printed equality in RA and declination in this example should not be used to infer a choice of horizontal altitude.

title: 3  Astronomical conventions and stellar positions
text:
3.3 Catalogue positions across epochs
star() resolves a Western name through star.names or accepts a catalogue identifier. It evaluates Swiss fixed-star coordinates at noon UT on Gregorian 1 January of each requested astronomical year. In this build the explicit flag combination requests the file-backed Swiss backend, equatorial axes, barycentric origin and true positions. The calculation checks the returned backend; the fixed catalogue magnitude is read separately. Use the identifier, epochs, catalogue revision and ephemeris files when reproducing a result (Astrodienst, n.d.).
For Aldebaran (α Tau), the 3500 BCE annual position was RA 356.67231°, declination −7.85151°; a century later it was 357.91715°, −7.29134°. The target-screening chapter shows the consequences for a narrow declination band. These are annual catalogue positions. For a rise time or the appearance of the star on a particular morning, use the appropriate local event and visibility calculations. A star object prepared for one year must be recomputed for another when the receiving function uses the supplied coordinates as given.
obliquity() supplies an annual true-obliquity reference; parallax.corr() supplies the approximate latitude- and altitude-dependent correction used by the limiting declination helpers. Neither substitutes for an instantaneous topocentric ephemeris of the Moon. Record skyscapeR.vars() settings along with the calls: the same script can otherwise inherit a different atmosphere, timezone, calendar or frame. A02 compares planetary and lunar positions against JPL. Stellar propagation and reference frames are the subject of the planned A03 check.
Reproduce the time, frame and stellar calculations.
For astronomy results carrying a provenance attribute, inspect attr(result, "provenance")$packages. It records skyscapeR and swephR namespace versions. It does not identify the fixed-star catalogue, ephemeris files, development commit or session settings. Save these alongside the original result before subsetting.

title: 4  Reducing compass and theodolite observations
text:
4.1 Magnetic reference and observation date
Build 2.0.9009 accepts a single site or a site per theodolite observation and reduces the final bearing modulo 360°. The earlier −558.77° control returns 161.23°. W02 field controls.
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/data-reduction.R, R/misc.R and R/mechanics.R. A compass gives a direction relative to magnetic north. A theodolite gives an angle on an instrument circle whose zero may be arbitrary. Reduction places each observation on a true-bearing scale before the skyline or celestial declination is evaluated. Retain the original readings; two corrected numbers alone cannot reveal an erroneous correction sign, solar limb or time convention (Ruggles 1999).
mag.dec() evaluates IGRF-14 through oce::magneticField() at sea level for the survey latitude, longitude and date. The date is converted to a decimal year by dividing elapsed days since 1 January by the actual number of days in the year. This implementation accepts 1 January 1900 through 1 January 2030 inclusive. Supply one site and many dates, one date and several sites, or matched rows. The date is that of the instrument reading, even for a monument built millennia earlier (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, n.d.; Kelley and Richards, n.d.).
With east-positive magnetic declination DD, reduct.compass() computes AT=AM+DA_T=A_M+D. An explicit magdec takes precedence if a date is also supplied. A bearing and correction shared across measurements or paired corrections should retain their row identities. The routine rounds using the numeric representation of the input bearings. It does not reduce the reported sum modulo 360°. Where altitude is provided, it also calculates celestial declination. An explicit altitude takes precedence over a supplied horizon; otherwise the corrected true bearing is used to look up the horizon altitude.
At 35.84° N, 14.57° E on 20 February 2026 the model returned +3.827142°. The input and altitude columns below are illustrative readings.
In particular, subtracting the positive correction would rotate the sightline in the wrong direction. IGRF models the main geomagnetic field. Local disturbance, instrument bias, a grid bearing mistaken for a magnetic bearing, or movement between observing positions require separate evidence. Numerical agreement with another IGRF implementation cannot test these field effects.

title: 4  Reducing compass and theodolite observations
text:
4.2 Solar-reference reduction
Let rTr_T and rSr_S be instrument-circle readings to the target and the observed solar point. If AS(t)A_S(t) is the predicted true bearing of that same solar point, the reduced bearing modulo one turn is
AT=[AS(t)+rT−rS]mod360°. A_T = [ A_S(t) + r_T-r_S ]\bmod 360°.
sunAz() parses the survey clock with R’s civil-time machinery, converts it to UTC, forms a Gregorian Julian date and calculates a topocentric solar direction. Its horizontal calculation uses 1013.25 mbar and 15 °C. The centre is used if no limb is given. Left and right limbs subtract or add a fixed 16 arcminutes in azimuth. Optional altitude is the geometric centre altitude. The fixed limb offset is an approximation; it does not vary with the apparent solar diameter or project a changing semidiameter onto azimuth at each altitude. This timestamp route is distinct from the proleptic ancient-date conversion in the conventions chapter.
reduct.theodolite() adds the observed circle difference to the computed solar reference, rounded according to the input readings. For |rT−rS|>180°|r_T-r_S|>180° this build subtracts a full turn from the difference, including when it is already negative. It does not wrap the final sum. The resulting number represents the correct direction modulo 360° but can be far outside the normal horizon lookup range. For a crossing of north, retain the raw result and compute True.Azimuth %% 360 before matching a profile; for that case one can reduce the bearing first and then pass the wrapped value and measured altitude to az2dec(). With one observation, a one-row, three-column location matrix works in this build; a plain three-element vector can fail in the internal matrix indexing.
The optional name, ID and HWT.ID fields identify output records. Supplying a HeyWhatsThat ID in these reduction functions records it in the table. To use the external skyline, retrieve the horizon with downloadHWT() and supply the resulting object as the location; an explicit measured altitude takes precedence.
crumbs: 4  Reducing compass and theodolite observations

title: 4  Reducing compass and theodolite observations
text:
4.3 Worked circle reading
At the same site on 20 February 2026 at 11:07:17 Europe/Malta, the calculated solar bearings were 157.4611° for the left limb, 157.7278° for the centre and 157.9944° for the right limb. A clock one minute later changed the centre bearing by +0.30759° in this example. That is a local time sensitivity, not a universal correction.
site <- matrix(c(35.84, 14.57, 100), nrow = 1)
r <- reduct.theodolite(site, az = 2.25, az.sun = 358.75,
    date = "2026/02/20", time = "11:07:17", tz = "Europe/Malta", alt = 2)
r$True.Azimuth
r$True.Azimuth %% 360
The instrument crossed north by +3.50° between the solar and target readings. The rounded solar reference is 157.73°. The routine returns −558.77°, equivalent to 161.23°, the direction obtained by adding 3.50° to the solar reference. The companion script also includes a non-wrapping reading and a compass reduction. These examples show why retaining the solar reading, limb, timestamp, timezone and original circle values matters when recovering a field result.



A clockwise turn from 358.75° to 2.25° adds 3.50° to the solar reference. The two scales show the same turn in instrument and true coordinates.


The international H01 field comparison evaluates DEM skylines against already reduced bearings. Independent validation of the two reduction functions requires a different reference. The relevant future check is a repeat solar or magnetic orientation of a baseline with independently established endpoints, accompanied by instrument readings, timestamps, atmospheric conditions and positional uncertainties. Download the synthetic field records and reduction scripts.

title: 5  Constructing a site horizon
text:
5.1 From field measurements
Function createHor() · Package skyscapeR 2.0.9004
A skyline is the altitude of the obstruction at each bearing from a particular viewpoint. createHor() builds this profile from observations or predicts it from a digital elevation model (DEM). Both routes return the same kind of horizon object. The evidence between adjacent bearings is quite different.
Supply the measured bearings and altitudes in degrees, with the observer’s latitude, longitude and elevation. The constructor repeats the measurements on either side of north, removes duplicate bearings and linearly interpolates both altitude and the supplied altitude uncertainty. This gives a continuous profile across north on a 0.01° grid. The grid is convenient for evaluating a sightline at any bearing. A narrow notch between two measurements can still be absent from the result.
For example, two measured points of equal altitude on opposite sides of a notch produce a level interpolated skyline between them. Record a foresight at the bottom of the notch if that feature matters to the interpretation. Repeated readings at the same bearing should be reduced to an estimate and uncertainty before calling the constructor. Optional smoothing averages over neighbouring samples and can lower a peak or fill a notch. With the default smoothing width of 1,000 samples, the window spans about 10°. Smoothing is off by default.

title: 5  Constructing a site horizon
text:
5.2 From an elevation model

Place the observer. The function samples the ground height at the site unless an elevation is supplied explicitly, then adds eye.height. Supply numeric latitude and longitude in that order for the default WGS84 route. When loc.crs is explicit, coordinates are in x, y order. A point object with its own coordinate reference system removes that ordering ambiguity. Ground height and DEM elevations must use compatible vertical datums.
Trace rays. A local azimuthal equidistant projection supplies distances and bearings clockwise from true north. Along each ray the function samples the source raster by bilinear interpolation, calculates the elevation angle to each terrain sample and keeps the maximum. A more distant ridge may set the horizon even if the near terrain rises steeply.
Correct the terrain angle. The default combines Earth curvature and terrestrial refraction using the pressure, temperature and vertical temperature gradient in Patat’s approximation (Patat 2011, eqs. 1–2). With an explicit refraction.k, the calculation uses an effective Earth radius. Zero retains geometric curvature. With curvature = FALSE, it uses the uncorrected height difference and distance. Refraction along a terrain sightline is a separate choice from astronomical refraction applied later to a star or the Sun.
Retain the profile and its provenance. Record the elevation product and date, horizontal and vertical reference systems, observer position and height, sampling settings, coverage and any reconstructed features. The optional panorama has its own sampling and lighting. Changing its pixel width cannot recover a ridge missed by the numerical rays.


5.2.1 Which point supplies the skyline?
For an observer at elevation zoz_o (including eye height), the solver maximises the apparent terrain angle over finite samples along each ray. In the default Patat branch, with ground elevation ziz_i, horizontal distance did_i, and local Earth radius RR, the candidate angle in radians is
hi=arctan(zi−zodi−di2R)+CdiR,C=0.252P(34.2+g)(T+273.15)2.
h_i=\arctan\!\left(\frac{z_i-z_o}{d_i}-\frac{d_i}{2R}\right)+C\frac{d_i}{R},
\qquad C=\frac{0.252\,P\,(34.2+g)}{(T+273.15)^2}.

Here PP is pressure in mbar, TT is temperature in °C, and gg is the vertical temperature gradient in °C/km. The retained altitude is maxihi\max_i h_i. A lower but nearer ridge can therefore conceal higher ground beyond it. This is the terrestrial light path from terrain to observer. Atmospheric refraction applied subsequently to a celestial position is a separate calculation (Patat 2011). With a supplied constant refraction coefficient kk, the code instead uses the spherical geometry of an effective radius 6371008.8/(1−k)6\,371\,008.8/(1-k) metres. With curvature disabled it uses atan2(zi−zo,di)\operatorname{atan2}(z_i-z_o,d_i).



The two-ridge example viewed due east. For this geometric illustration, the maximum viewing angle occurs on the near face of the farther ridge. The production calculation also applies the selected curvature and refraction model.


For search distance DD and requested radial step ss, the ordinary numerical rays use n=max(2,⌈D/s⌉)n=\max(2,\lceil D/s\rceil) samples at di=iD/nd_i=iD/n. The default ss is half the smaller local raster-cell dimension. The base bearing grid similarly uses ⌈360/𝚊𝚣.𝚜𝚝𝚎𝚙⌉\lceil 360/\texttt{az.step}\rceil equally spaced rays, supplemented for reconstructed features. Bilinear sampling can smooth a narrow crest. A denser output grid cannot recover a crest absent from the terrain data. If the ray has missing coverage, its largest available angle can underestimate the skyline. The source metadata records incomplete bearings. When examining a disputed foresight, inspect that bearing and the winning ridge distance before pooling errors across a station. H01 gives per-station errors and compares DEMs over common bearings in Ireland.

title: 5  Constructing a site horizon
text:
5.3 Generating a terrain panorama
The DEM route through createHor() produces two outputs: the numerical skyline in h$data and a shaded image of the terrain visible below it. A measured series of azimuths and altitudes supplies no distances, slopes or intervening surfaces from which to render that foreground. To make a panorama, supply a single-band DEM with elevations in metres, observer coordinates in the specified reference system, and an output directory. The R packages terra and png are required for this example.
library(skyscapeR)
library(terra)

dem <- rast(xmin=499450, xmax=500550, ymin=5699450, ymax=5700550,
            resolution=5, crs="EPSG:32630")
xy <- xyFromCell(dem, seq_len(ncell(dem)))
east <- xy[, 1] - 500000
north <- xy[, 2] - 5700000
values(dem) <- 100 + 15 * exp(-((east-80)/35)^2 - ((north+30)/90)^2) +
    88 * exp(-((east-270)/70)^2 - ((north-40)/200)^2)

h <- createHor(dem=dem, loc=c(500000, 5700000), loc.crs="EPSG:32630",
               name="Two ridges", eye.height=1.6, max.distance=500,
               az.step=1, distance.step=2.5, panorama=TRUE, width=1024,
               image.dir="terrain-images", ncores=1)
stopifnot(file.exists(h$metadata$image$path))
plot(h, xrange=c(35,145), yrange=c(-3,21), use.image=TRUE)
For a survey, replace the synthetic surface with rast("survey-dtm.tif"), enter the actual observer coordinates and choose a search radius that includes any distant ridge liable to form the skyline. The DEM should cover that search area. Supply the dataset credit and terms using attribution and license. If working from a photograph with a sky mask, use the photographic calibration chapter.



Eastern sector of the generated DEM panorama. The darker foreground rise obscures the lower part of the taller ridge. Only the upper terrain edge enters the skyline.



5.3.1 From terrain rays to image pixels
The output is a 2:1 equirectangular RGBA PNG covering 0–360° clockwise from north and −90° to +90° altitude. Column centres are displaced half a pixel from the north seam. The renderer interpolates the numerical skyline to each column to fix the upper edge and leaves sky pixels transparent. Along each column it traces near to far, tracking the greatest elevation angle encountered. For a row below the skyline, the first terrain segment that reaches its viewing angle supplies the visible surface. More distant terrain below that line is hidden. The renderer interpolates surface properties between samples. A reconstructed horFeature() can change the foreground colours or relief even when a distant ridge still determines the upper edge.



Setting
What changes




az.step, distance.step, max.distance
The bearings, radial sampling and outer limit used to calculate the numerical skyline. The outer limit also bounds the rendered terrain.


width
The number of panorama columns. Height is half the width. The default 4096 × 2048 has an angular pixel width of about 5.27 arcminutes.


panorama.distance.step, panorama.acuity
The radial spacing for the image. With the default adaptive rule, the effective angle is the larger of one PNG pixel and the requested acuity (default one arcminute). At distance dd, the proposed step is the larger of the near step (normally one local DEM cell) and dtanθd\tan\theta, with θ\theta the effective angle. A narrow ridge can fall between samples. Supply a fixed step in metres to check a critical feature, or NULL to reuse the numerical ray spacing.


terrain.palette, land_cols, sea_cols, sea_level
Colour the surface by elevation. Inspect the available ramps with demPalettes(). A sea-level threshold can colour low-lying dry ground as water. Use sea_level=NULL where that interpretation is inappropriate.


lighting, light.azimuth, light.altitude, ambient, haze
Relief mode blends observer-facing and directional illumination. Directional mode uses the selected light direction. The hillshade has no cast shadows. For an inspection of the palette alone, set ambient=1, haze=0. The default illumination is illustrative and does not reconstruct illumination at a dated solar event.



The example wrote a 1024 × 512 PNG. Its adaptive grid used 100 radial samples, with an effective angular target of 21.09 arcminutes. Inspect h$metadata$image$sampling for the values used on another DEM. Increasing image width alone leaves the numerical bearing grid unchanged. When a narrow bank or notch matters, check both grids.


5.3.2 Keeping and reusing the image
panorama=TRUE is the DEM default. image.dir defaults to the working directory, and h$metadata$image$path identifies the actual file. An image-rendering failure can return a valid numerical horizon with a warning and no image metadata. Save the PNG alongside saveRDS(h, "two-ridges.rds"); the RDS stores its path and checksum. After moving the files, assign the result of relinkHor(). plot.skyscapeR.horizon() displays the terrain, sketchSky() places a sky above it, and exportStellarium() packages it for Stellarium. The interchange section describes that export.
Download the runnable example, full-sphere PNG, eastern view and run log. The terrain is synthetic and illustrates rendering and occlusion. The field comparisons in the study register evaluate skyline altitudes.

title: 5  Constructing a site horizon
text:
5.4 Reconstructing features on a DEM
A bank can be visible from a monument without forming its skyline. To distinguish those possibilities, pass a horFeature() object, or an ordered list of them, in the features argument to createHor(). This route requires a DEM. A profile supplied as measured bearing–altitude pairs contains no terrain distances at which to place the earthwork.

5.4.1 Footprint, height and viewpoint
Supply vector geometry with a known coordinate reference system. Dimensions are in metres. A point stone or pole uses a circular footprint of the given diameter. A line becomes a strip of the specified total width, centred on the line. For a polygon, banks, ditches and walls follow the boundary by default; stones, poles, mounds and platforms occupy the area. Use use = "area" or "boundary" explicitly when the distinction matters. Interior rings are respected, including their edges in boundary mode.
At each sample the reconstruction modifies the local DEM elevation. A bank adds height, a ditch subtracts depth, and a zero-height feature can colour a visible surface without raising it. If the DEM already contains 0.6 m of surviving bank and the hypothesis is a 1.5 m crest above the adjacent ground, the additional height at that crest is 0.9 m. Adding the full 1.5 m there would count the surviving relief twice. The viewpoint stays at its original elevation. To place the observer on a reconstructed platform, supply its hypothesised top elevation as the observer’s ground elevation, then add eye height.
Banks, ditches and mounds default to a rounded profile. The displacement rises from zero at the edge according to sin2(πt/2)\sin^2(\pi t/2), where tt is the inward distance expressed as a fraction of the profile radius. For a line this radius is half its width. Stones, poles, platforms and walls default to a flat profile that follows the underlying terrain. Where features overlap, the greatest positive displacement and the deepest negative displacement are added. Two overlapping banks therefore contribute the taller bank at each sample. Later layers, and later rows within a layer, take colour precedence. This representation supports terrain-attached relief; a doorway through a bank requires a gap in its footprint.


5.4.2 From feature to skyline
The numerical calculation adds bearings at the edges and centre of raised or cut features and samples where rays intersect their footprints. It evaluates the modified surface against all other terrain along the same ray. A bank changes the skyline only where it exceeds the previous maximum elevation angle. A ditch can lower the skyline only where it cuts the terrain that previously set that maximum. A foreground feature below a distant ridge can therefore alter the panorama while leaving the skyline altitude effectively unchanged.
Panorama columns trace the reconstructed surface independently. Colour is subject to visibility, shading and haze. A narrow feature can fall between columns even when the numerical rays detect it. Refine az.step and distance.step for a critical bearing and increase PNG width to check the depiction. The returned numerical profile is interpolated to the usual 0.01° grid.


5.4.3 Example: a 1.5 m bank across a sightline
This illustrative terrain is level at 100 m. A bank 100 m east of the observer crosses the due-east ray. The crest is 1.5 m above ground and the eye is 1 m above ground. With curvature disabled, the line to the crest has an altitude of approximately arctan(0.5/100)=0.29°\arctan(0.5/100)=0.29°. The returned skyline uses the maximum along the rounded bank, which can occur slightly nearer than its centre.
dem <- terra::rast(xmin = 499500, xmax = 500500, ymin = 5699500,
                   ymax = 5700500, resolution = 5, crs = "EPSG:32630")
terra::values(dem) <- 100
axis <- terra::vect("LINESTRING (500100 5699950, 500100 5700050)",
                    crs = "EPSG:32630")
bank <- horFeature(axis, "bank", width = 6, height = 1.5, colour = "ivory")

settings <- list(dem = dem, loc = c(500000, 5700000), loc.crs = "EPSG:32630",
                 eye.height = 1, max.distance = 400, curvature = FALSE,
                 panorama = FALSE, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE)
bare <- do.call(createHor, settings)
raised <- do.call(createHor, c(settings, list(features = bank)))
vapply(list(bare = bare, raised = raised), function(h) {
  approx(h$data$az, h$data$alt, xout = 90)$y
}, numeric(1))
To model a chalk-coloured cursus enclosure, a zero-height polygon in area mode can supply the interior colour, with a raised boundary bank later in the list. This lets the interior and bank have different colours while only the bank adds relief. Save the feature objects with the DEM provenance, viewpoint and settings. The returned metadata$features summarises the layers and records checksums; rebuilding the geometry requires the saved features. Save the external PNG as well when a panorama was requested.
The rules above follow the 2.0.9004 implementation in R/horizon-features.R and R/dem-horizon.R. The example illustrates the geometry of an assumed bank. H01 tests terrain skylines. Reconstructed earthworks need independent measurements of their geometry.

title: 5  Constructing a site horizon
text:
5.5 Choices that affect a sightline







Choice
Practical consequence




Viewpoint and terrain source
A small shift on a barrow can change the nearest obstruction. A bare-earth DTM omits trees and buildings that may appear in a survey. An assumed instrument height introduces a station-specific uncertainty.


Search radius and coverage
The default radius is 10 km. Terrain beyond it cannot contribute. Missing raster samples can leave a ray incomplete. Inspect incomplete.bearings and repeat with a wider radius where distant ground is plausible.


Angular and radial sampling
The default angular interval is 0.25°, about 22 m between adjacent rays at 5 km. Along a ray, the default step is half the smaller estimated local cell dimension. Refine the two independently when a narrow feature determines a result.


Altitude uncertainty
alt.unc carries the uncertainty supplied by the analyst. The default 0.5° is an input assumption. Assign a value appropriate to the survey or error evidence available for the site.

title: 5  Constructing a site horizon
text:
5.6 Changes and evidence
The 2.0 development documentation records the DEM construction route, terrestrial refraction and external terrain panorama. An existing horizon interpolated from a survey and a new one derived from a DTM can differ even at the same nominal location. Record which route supplied the profile in a published analysis.

The H01 field comparison quantifies error at surveyed bearings. H02 compares independently computed profiles at matched viewpoints. The English controls hold the terrain product, observer setup and search radius fixed. Delivered online profiles can also differ in their input terrain and effective observer height.

title: 5  Constructing a site horizon
text:
5.7 Full package help


Read the complete createHor() help page

Construct a site horizon from measurements or an elevation model

Description

Build a continuous horizon profile from measurements of horizon altitude at known
bearings around a site, or predict the horizon and visible terrain from a DEM.



Usage

createHor(
  az,
  alt,
  loc,
  dem = NULL,
  loc.crs = NULL,
  name = "",
  alt.unc = 0.5,
  smooth = F,
  .scale = 1000,
  eye.height = 1.6,
  max.distance = 10000,
  az.step = 0.25,
  distance.step = NULL,
  features = NULL,
  curvature = TRUE,
  refraction.k = NULL,
  atm = skyscapeR.env$atm,
  temp = skyscapeR.env$temp,
  tempgrad = -10,
  panorama = TRUE,
  width = 4096,
  panorama.distance.step = "adaptive",
  panorama.acuity = 1,
  terrain.palette = "temperate",
  land_cols = NULL,
  sea_cols = NULL,
  sea_level = 0,
  n_sea = 3L,
  palette_n = 256L,
  lighting = c("relief", "directional"),
  light.azimuth = 315,
  light.altitude = 45,
  ambient = 0.38,
  haze = 0.65,
  image.dir = getwd(),
  attribution = "User-supplied DEM",
  license = "See source DEM terms",
  ncores = NULL,
  verbose = TRUE,
  progress = interactive() && verbose
)



Arguments





az
Array of azimuth values


alt
Array of altitude values.


loc
Observer location. For DEMs, pass a single CRS-bearing terra SpatVector point directly as loc, or a numeric latitude and longitude. Ground elevation is read from the DEM unless supplied as a third numeric value. Measured horizons take latitude, longitude and elevation.


dem
Optional single-band terra SpatRaster or local raster filename. Supply dem in place of az and alt. Requires the optional terra package.


loc.crs
CRS for numeric DEM observer coordinates in x,y order (easting, northing or longitude, latitude). Without it, numeric loc uses latitude, longitude in WGS84. A single terra SpatVector point carries its own CRS. An optional third numeric coordinate is ground elevation in metres.


name
Name of site.


alt.unc
Either a single value or an array of altitude uncertainty.


smooth
Logical to control whether to smooth horizon profile using rolling mean. Defaults to FALSE


.scale
Number of samples in the rolling mean when smooth = TRUE. The grid spacing is 0.01 degrees, so 1000 samples span approximately 10 degrees.


eye.height
Observer height above the selected ground elevation in metres.


max.distance
DEM search radius in metres, default 10000. Include any distant terrain that could form the horizon within the DEM coverage.


az.step
Maximum spacing of numerical DEM rays in degrees. The default is 0.25. An equal number of steps fills the circle.


distance.step
Maximum spacing of samples along each ray in metres. By default use half the smaller native cell dimension estimated at the site.


features
Optional horFeature object or list of such objects describing reconstructed or highlighted structures. Requires dem. Elevations are additive, with the largest positive and deepest negative contributions combined at overlaps. Later footprints take colour precedence. Features affect both numerical horizon and visible terrain. Their geometry is kept out of the returned horizon; save the feature objects separately.


curvature
Apply Earth curvature to DEM sightlines. Default TRUE.


refraction.k
Default NULL applies Patat when curvature is enabled. Set zero for geometric curvature without terrestrial refraction, or supply a coefficient below one for the effective-radius model.


atm
Ground atmospheric pressure in millibars for Patat terrestrial refraction.


temp
Ground air temperature in degrees Celsius.


tempgrad
Vertical temperature gradient in kelvins per kilometre (default -10).


panorama
Render an external terrain PNG for a DEM. Default TRUE. Set FALSE for the numerical horizon alone.


width
DEM panorama width in pixels, an even integer from 32 to 81920. Default 4096 by 2048 pixels. Height is half the width. Widths above 8192 are assembled from temporary image tiles. Both dimensions grow with width, so a tenfold increase generates 100 times as many pixels.


panorama.distance.step
The default, "adaptive", starts at one local DEM cell and increases radial spacing with distance using the larger of the requested angular acuity and one horizontal PNG pixel. This transverse footprint is a proxy for radial detail. A narrow ridge may fall between samples. Use a positive number for fixed spacing in metres or NULL to reuse distance.step. The numerical horizon uses distance.step independently. Inspect metadata$image$sampling for the effective angle, sample count and actual step range. On large DEM-only panoramas, the renderer checks near terrain against a conservative upper bound for the remaining terrain on each ray. It skips distant samples only where all remaining elevations are hidden and keeps neighbours for surface shading. Terrain with added archaeological features uses the full sampling path.


panorama.acuity
Angular detail target in arcminutes for adaptive PNG sampling. Defaults to 1 (nominal 20/20 acuity). Larger values coarsen distant terrain.


terrain.palette
Named land/water pair from demPalettes. Options are temperate (default), standalone, arid, alpine, coastal and relief.


land_cols, sea_cols
Opaque R colour names or hex colours in increasing elevation order. NULL inherits the respective ramp from terrain.palette. Supply either vector to override just that ramp. One colour gives a uniform base. Colours interpolate in Lab space.


sea_level
DEM elevation in metres at or below which the sea colour ramp is used. Default 0. A level water surface uses the shallow colour. This is an elevation threshold. Use NULL to apply the land palette over the whole visible elevation range, including depressions. The temperate land ramp starts at the lowest visible land level or sea threshold, whichever is higher. Other palettes with a threshold start at sea_level. The ramp ends at the highest visible elevation. The sea ramp starts at the lowest visible elevation.


n_sea
Number of entries reserved for the sea ramp, leaving at least two land colours. Default 3.


palette_n
Total number of palette entries, from 4 to 65536. Default 256.


lighting
Relief lighting (default) blends a light at the observer (75 percent) with the directional source (25 percent). It shades both sides of a slope and lifts deep shadows. Choose "directional" for one-sided hillshade. Lighting affects the PNG only.


light.azimuth, light.altitude
Direction towards the illustrative light source in degrees clockwise from true north and above the horizon. Defaults are 315 and 45 degrees. Hillshading uses upward surface normals in metric east, north and vertical coordinates. This is local illumination without cast shadows from other terrain.


ambient
Fraction of illumination retained on slopes facing away from the light (0 to 1). Default 0.38. Use 1 for unshaded palette colours.


haze
Maximum fraction of distance haze (0 to 1). Default 0.65. Set haze=0 and ambient=1 to inspect the colour mapping alone.


image.dir
Directory for the DEM PNG. Defaults to the working directory. Site names form the filename; different images with the same name receive a checksum suffix.


attribution
Credit for the DEM, included in plots and exports. The generic default credit is omitted from plots.


license
Source licence or terms for the DEM, included in exports.


ncores
Maximum DEM tracing workers. Defaults to half the available logical cores, rounded down with a minimum of one. The startup message reports used and available cores. Workers share file-backed DEM data and process separate bearings.


verbose
Announce the DEM radius, sampling and rendering stages.


progress
Show a progress bar for each tracing stage. Default on in interactive verbose sessions.






Details

Measured bearings. To evaluate sightlines between measured bearings, the constructor repeats the azimuths
one turn in each direction, removes duplicate azimuth entries and linearly interpolates
altitude and altitude uncertainty onto a 0.01-degree grid from -90 to 450 degrees.
Scalar uncertainty is repeated. Optional smoothing applies a running mean over the
specified number of grid samples to both series, with zero fill at the outer ends.
Latitude, longitude and elevation identify the observer; omitted elevation defaults to
zero. Interpolation cannot recover narrow features between measurements.

Observer and DEM coverage. For a DEM, supply a point with a CRS, projected x and y with loc.crs, or WGS84 latitude and longitude.
The optional third coordinate is ground elevation in metres in the DEM's vertical
datum. Otherwise ground elevation is bilinearly sampled at the site. Observer
elevation in the returned georeference is ground elevation plus eye.height.
A terrain model represents bare earth. A surface model includes the objects
represented in its elevations. Use a single continuous band in metres with a
defined horizontal CRS. Missing samples and terrain beyond the raster edge are skipped. A warning and the incomplete.bearings metadata identify incomplete coverage. Each bearing needs at least one usable sample.

Sampling narrow ridges. Terrain is sampled along true bearings from north, clockwise. A WGS84 local
azimuthal equidistant projection sets the distances and bearings. Sample coordinates
are transformed to the source grid for bilinear elevation extraction in batches.
Each horizon angle is the maximum sampled elevation angle along its ray. The
requested radius is included wherever covered. A missing observer ground elevation without an override or an observer outside the
DEM cause an error. Rays and distance samples are discrete. A finer constructor
output grid cannot recover a ridge between rays, steps or DEM cells. Increase
the radius and refine both sampling intervals to check convergence for a site.
At 5 km the default 0.25-degree rays are approximately 22 metres apart.
The supplied altitude uncertainty is an assumption in degrees.

Curvature and terrestrial refraction. By default the apparent altitude at each sampled distance d (metres) follows
Patat (2011), equations 1 and 2. The geometric angle is atan((z-observer)/d - d/(2R)).
Add (d/R) times 0.252 P (34.2 + tempgrad) / T squared in radians, using
temperature T in kelvins and the latitude-dependent radius R from Appendix A1.
The same corrected angles determine the numerical horizon and the visible terrain in the PNG.
An explicit numeric refraction.k selects a spherical vertical section of effective radius
6371008.8 / (1 - refraction.k) metres. At ground distance d and elevation z,
the forward component is (R + z) sin(d/R) and the vertical component is
z minus observer elevation minus 2 (R + z) sin(d/(2R)) squared, where the
square applies to the sine. The angle is obtained with atan2. With curvature
disabled, use the height difference and horizontal distance directly.
Terrestrial refraction applies to the terrain
sightline. Atmospheric refraction is controlled separately in astronomical calls.

Panorama and reconstructed features. By default a second set of rays paints the first visible terrain at each
azimuth and elevation, using local surface normals, elevation colours and
distance haze. The transparent sky edge follows the numerical horizon.
With features, each PNG column is traced directly through the reconstructed
terrain; its edge can differ from the interpolated numerical horizon between
rays. Refine az.step and width when examining narrow structures.
The panorama spans the full 360 degrees from nadir to zenith. The horizon object
stores its bounds, checksum, attribution and licence in metadata$image.
Save the external PNG alongside the RDS. If you move them, use relinkHor
to reconnect the image. A rendering failure returns the numerical horizon with a warning.
Plotting also falls back to the numerical horizon if the image is missing or has changed.



Value

A skyscapeR.horizon list with metadata (site name and georeference) and a data frame named data. Its az, alt and alt.unc columns contain azimuth, horizon altitude and altitude uncertainty, all in degrees.



Accuracy, uncertainty and reproducibility

H01 compared 334 bearings at 31 observing setups.
At the surveyed bearings, createHor() reproduced the observed terrain skyline to within half a degree in 91.9% of cases.
See the H01 field validation in the skyscapeR technical manual for the survey protocol, station results and limitations.

With the same 1 m terrain, createHor() reproduced Horizon’s skylines to a mean absolute difference of 0.004 degrees at each of two English sites. Against field measurements at 344 Irish bearings, createHor() using SRTM had a mean absolute error of 0.328 degrees, lower than either HeyWhatsThat or PeakFinder on that sample. Field accuracy varied by site. See the H02 comparison in the skyscapeR technical manual.

The numerical skyline is a maximum over sampled terrain, not an accuracy
certificate for the DEM. Horizontal and vertical datum differences, observer
height, missing raster values, vegetation and buildings can exceed the sampling
error. DEM elevations and a supplied observer ground elevation must use a
compatible vertical datum. No geoid conversion or vertical-datum correction is
performed automatically. Refine the angular and distance sampling and expand
the radius until the relevant sightlines are stable. Compare with surveyed
bearings and altitudes where available.

alt.unc is supplied by the user and is not estimated from DEM resolution,
control residuals or atmospheric variability. Smoothing a measured profile can
remove narrow notches or peaks. Adaptive panorama sampling and illustrative
lighting concern the image; they do not increase numerical horizon precision.
The terrestrial refraction approximation assumes the supplied atmosphere and
cannot reproduce all near-ground gradients or mirage conditions.

Save the DEM provenance, observer location and datum, constructor arguments,
feature objects, returned horizon and external PNG. Rebuilding from the same
source is distinct from merely replotting the saved horizon.



References

Patat, F. (2011). Horizon synthesis for archaeo-astronomical purposes. Astronomische Nachrichten 332, 743-749. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1002/asna.201111570")}.



See Also

importPeakFinder, plot.skyscapeR.horizon

createHWT, downloadHWT



Examples

## Not run: 
observer <- terra::vect("observer.gpkg") # one point with a CRS
h <- createHor(dem="terrain.tif", loc=observer, eye.height=1.6)

## End(Not run)
# Create a skyscapeR.horizon from 5 measurements:
az <- c(0,90,180,270,360)
alt <- c(0,5,5,0,0)
hor <- createHor(az, alt, alt.unc=0.1, loc=c(40.1,-8), name='Test')
plot(hor)
## Not run: 
# loc is latitude, longitude. Distances and elevations are metres.
terrain <- createHor(dem="site-dtm.tif", loc=c(51.19,-1.75),
  name="Survey site", max.distance=5000, eye.height=1.6,
  image.dir="horizons", attribution="Survey DTM", license="Survey terms")
plot(terrain)
exportStellarium(terrain, name="Survey site")

## End(Not run)


Related function entries
createHor(), hor2alt(), horFeature(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon(), relinkHor().
For control-point fitting, mask sampling and landscape export, see photographic horizons.




Patat, Ferdinando. 2011. ‘Horizon Synthesis for Archaeo-Astronomical Purposes’. Astronomische Nachrichten 332: 743–49. https://doi.org/10.1002/asna.201111570.

title: 6  Calibrating photographic skylines and exchanging horizons
text:
6.1 From a masked panorama to angular samples
Using a partial photographic skyline.
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/importPanorama.R, R/peakfinder.R, R/exportPanorama.R, R/horizon.R and R/relinkHor.R. A horizon object can carry both a numerical altitude profile and an image. A terrain crossing uses the former. Reproducing the drawn landscape can also require the latter. The terrain chapter describes the alternative construction of a profile from elevations and reconstructed features.
importPanorama() expects an equirectangular PNG with transparent sky above terrain in every column. A stitched photograph must already have this projection and a sky mask. Supply the observer location, clockwise bearing limits and bottom and top altitude limits. For width WW, column jj samples Aj=AL+(j−1/2)(AR−AL)/WA_j=A_L+(j-1/2)(A_R-A_L)/W. If the first pixel meeting the opacity threshold is row rr from the top of an image of height HH, the altitude is hT−(r−1)(hT−hB)/Hh_T-(r-1)(h_T-h_B)/H. This places the skyline at the upper edge of the terrain pixel. The default threshold is 0.5. A bird, mast or isolated opaque mask artefact above the ridge can therefore select the wrong edge. A column with no qualifying terrain or no sky above it stops the import.
Controls may constrain azimuth, altitude or both. Their pixel coordinates are measured from the upper left. For bearing controls, residuals are reduced to the shortest angular difference across north. A single control or a full turn fixes the angular offset while preserving the supplied span. On a partial panorama, distinct horizontal control coordinates also allow a least-squares adjustment of angular scale. In a sector crossing north, 330° to 30° describes a clockwise 60° sector.
Altitude controls at distinct horizontal coordinates can estimate tilt. With u=(x/W−1/2)(AR−AL)u=(x/W-1/2)(A_R-A_L) in radians, the correction consists of a common offset plus centred sinu\sin u and cosu\cos u terms. The implementation estimates only singular directions whose singular values exceed the greater of 10−810^{-8} and 1% of the largest singular value. Closely grouped controls can leave a tilt direction undetermined. Where a tilt can be estimated, columns are resampled at native vertical resolution with transparent padding and clipping at the poles. Otherwise a single vertical control shifts the altitude limits, and observations at distinct vertical positions can fit a vertical scale. This near-horizon model cannot correct arbitrary stitch distortion. Independent controls withheld from the fit are needed to measure that error.
The default alt.unc=0.5 assigns 0.5° to each skyline sample. It is supplied uncertainty, not a standard error from the control residuals. A partial profile preserves sampled limits and can be used within its observed sector. Sampling, alpha-mask preparation and control geometry all affect what comparison with a survey can establish.

6.2 A skyline with a known answer
The example creates a 360 × 100 pixel masked skyline with a vertical pixel size of 0.1°. Its prescribed profile is 2+1.4sinA+0.6cos(2A)2+1.4\sin A+0.6\cos(2A) degrees, with trigonometric arguments converted to radians. The image is given nominal limits of 0–360° and −4° to +6°. A single control at (90,30)(90,30) corresponds to bearing 92° and altitude 3.5°. The fitted bounds are 2–362° and −3.5° to +6.5°. The comparison evaluates both profiles at the same 360 true bearings.

The worked mask and its angular control, followed by errors at the same true bearings under nominal and fitted limits. The remaining steps reflect the 0.1° pixel height.


The remaining error is consistent with rounding the generated edge to the nearest pixel boundary. This exercise checks the sign and placement of angular corrections on an ideal mask. title: 6  Calibrating photographic skylines and exchanging horizons
section: 6.3 PeakFinder, Stellarium and moving an observation
text:
6.3 PeakFinder, Stellarium and moving an observation
importPeakFinder() takes the numerical horizon from the Stellarium export and, where available, calibrates the companion vector drawing against it. The vertical calibration fits image ordinate as an affine function of tanh\tan h. The ordinary fit requires at least 20 matches covering at least 180° in bearing and 0.5° in relief. The allowed RMS and maximum angular residuals are 0.05° and 0.2° respectively, with a further holdout check. For low-relief, clipped profiles, the importer can use the alpha edges of eight north-first textures with coverage and agreement checks. An unusable drawing can leave a usable numerical horizon. These tolerances measure correspondence between export components from the same source. They cannot establish the accuracy of PeakFinder terrain against survey. Verify observer elevation separately when the export reports zero ground elevation plus eye height.
exportPanorama() maps the calibrated image or numerical silhouette onto a north-first, 2:1 spherical PNG. Unobserved sectors remain transparent. Increasing output dimensions changes sampling of the texture without adding measured directions. exportHor() and its alias exportStellarium() create a Stellarium landscape for a closed 360° profile. The landscape configuration controls texture bounds and rotation, which must agree with the bearing convention of the numerical horizon (Stellarium contributors, n.d.). In the example a 720 × 360 PNG is exported. The landscape ZIP contains the image, horizon.txt and landscape.ini. Its angle_rotatez=-88 registers the 2° origin and the vertical bounds are −3.5° and +6.5°. The sector from 330° to 30° is rejected for landscape export. A useful interoperability check is to inspect named skyline bearings, especially at north, after loading the landscape in the receiving application. This example verifies the written files only.
relinkHor() matches a moved PNG by its saved checksum. Save the displayed or levelled PNG alongside the RDS horizon object, assign the returned horizon after relinking, and save it again. The original PeakFinder export is a separate dependency for native-layout export. Keep the original controls and source image alongside the derived numerical profile so that changes in mask, projection or control values can be traced.
Download the example scripts, input mask, 360-profile comparison and exported landscape.

title: 6  Calibrating photographic skylines and exchanging horizons
section: 6.4 Looking up a bearing and choosing an export layout
text:
6.4 Looking up a bearing and choosing an export layout
hor2alt() takes two routes in 2.0.9004. For an imported photograph it wraps the requested bearing relative to the start of the clockwise sector, linearly interpolates the per-column skyline and returns NA outside the observed sector. For other horizons it evaluates a spline through the stored altitude samples and, when requested, a separate spline through their uncertainty values. These can extrapolate. With return.unc=TRUE a single bearing returns an unnamed pair; several bearings return a two-column matrix in input order. The visible precision of a rounded altitude is distinct from survey resolution. coordtrans() has its own linear horizon interpolation.
exportPanorama() samples a verified source image by nearest neighbour in its angular bounds. use.image=FALSE instead fills the numerical silhouette below the profile. An unavailable or modified image can also trigger the silhouette fallback. For a partial photograph the unobserved sector stays transparent. exportHor() and exportStellarium() offer a separate choice for PeakFinder landscapes. The default single texture is portable. The native layout needs the original archive with the recorded checksum and supported calibrated tile geometry. When those assets cannot be verified, inspect the exported configuration to determine which layout was written. A closed landscape retains the numerical profile in its archive; the altitude-uncertainty series belongs to the R horizon. Both exporters protect existing destination files.

title: 6  Calibrating photographic skylines and exchanging horizons
section: 6.5 When a partial panorama is passed to another calculation
text:
6.5 When a partial panorama is passed to another calculation
In builds through 2.0.9007, an imported photograph recorded its angular coverage separately from the numerical profile, whose rows are repeated across turns to make lookup across north possible. hor2alt() checks that coverage. coordtrans() interpolates the profile rows directly. Likewise, riseset() can accept those rows as a closed horizon and interpolate across the unphotographed gap. The profile solver used by star.phases() also works from the rows. A finite result does not establish that the relevant terrain was observed.
In the archived example, the photographed sector covers 330° through north to 30°. At 180°, the direct altitude lookup returns NA, yet transforming a uniform bearing of 180° ± 1° produces a finite declination curve. On 20 March 2026 the same partial profile produces a sunrise bearing of 92.48°, outside the photograph. There is no field evidence for the terrain at that bearing in this example. Before transforming an orientation, check the entire support of its azimuth PDF against the photographed sector. For a daily or seasonal crossing search, supply a full skyline or complete the missing sector from an independently identified source. The script object-coverage.R and its output are in the example download above.
Build 2.0.9008 checks the photographed sector before density transformation and full-sky searches. H07 reproduces the earlier example and gives the corrected outcomes.
