title: 7  Seasonal stellar visibility
text:
7.1 How a date is assigned
Function star.phases() · Package skyscapeR 2.0.9004
At an archaeological site, a star can rise above a ridge while the sky is still too bright to see it. star.phases() asks on which mornings or evenings the terrain, darkness and stellar brightness allow an opportunity to observe it. Its heliacal-rising date is the return of such an opportunity after a season of invisibility.
A seasonal search needs the skyline across the stellar track. See partial photographic horizons before supplying a sector image.

title: 7  Seasonal stellar visibility
text:
Construct the annual cycle. The function fixes the star’s position for the chosen year and samples 365 equally spaced solar longitudes. These steps describe progress through the seasons. Their spacing in elapsed civil time varies. The package maps the longitude of each event back to a representative local Julian-calendar date in the requested year.
Find intervals above the skyline. The stellar track is tested against the altitude of the horizon at the star’s bearing. A full profile can produce more than one interval of clearance. A track which just touches the ridge gives zero time above it. The solver refines terrain crossings separately from the sampling used for solar altitude.
Apply the visibility criteria together. A qualifying interval must last longer than zero, the Sun must be below the adopted solar-altitude threshold, and both a star–Sun altitude separation and an extinction test must be satisfied. If the catalogue magnitude is mm, the required altitude difference is 2.1m+102.1m+10 degrees (Purrington 1988, S74). For a magnitude 1 star this is 12.1°. The package also adds kX(h)kX(h) magnitudes of extinction, where kk is the extinction coefficient and X(h)X(h) is the airmass at stellar altitude hh (Schaefer 1986; Krisciunas and Schaefer 1991, eq. 14). Extinction depends on altitude above the horizontal, even if a ridge is much higher than that.
Classify the day and its transitions. Continuous intervals of visibility give the daily phase codes. A visible ascending or descending interval below alt.rs can qualify as rising or setting. The first transition out of an invisible season defines heliacal rising. Since the year is cyclic, a season that spans the December solstice continues across the end of the table.


7.1.1 What qualifies as a visible interval?
In R/stars.R, the year-specific stellar coordinates are held fixed while the code constructs a reusable diurnal track on a reference day starting at 2000-01-01 00:00 UTC. The seasonal loop changes the solar coordinates. Thus the time nodes of this track have computational meaning; an archaeological observation date comes from mapping the selected solar longitude back to the requested year. For an irregular skyline, the solver locates crossings, combines them with one-minute nodes and the solar grid specified by res, and refines turning points in stellar altitude. It tests each segment midpoint for clearance above the skyline. Multiple unobstructed intervals on the same track remain eligible.
For stellar altitude hh, solar altitude ss, stellar magnitude mm, limiting magnitude LL and extinction coefficient kk, the code uses E(h)=k/[sinh+0.025exp(−11sinh)]E(h)=k/[\sin h+0.025\exp(-11\sin h)] magnitudes. On terrain-clear segments it requires finite, nonnegative extinction, m+E(h)≤Lm+E(h)\leq L, s<𝚜𝚘𝚕𝚊𝚛.𝚊𝚕𝚝s<\texttt{solar.alt} and h−s≥2.1m+10°h-s\geq 2.1m+10°. The angular separation here is a difference in altitudes, even when star and Sun differ substantially in bearing (Purrington 1988; Krisciunas and Schaefer 1991). Threshold margins are interpolated linearly between segment endpoints. An interval survives only when its end is strictly later than its start. Two conditions satisfied at different moments within the same segment do not by themselves establish visibility.



Illustrative dawn track with time tt in minutes, stellar altitude 1+0.15t1+0.15t degrees, solar altitude −16+0.20t-16+0.20t degrees, magnitude 1, k=0.2k=0.2, limiting magnitude 3 and a 4° ridge. Coloured segments satisfy each condition. Only their overlap qualifies as a visible interval.


A second pass restricts eligible intervals to h≤𝚊𝚕𝚝.𝚛𝚜h\leq\texttt{alt.rs} and checks the sign of the stellar altitude change. A rising interval gives R, a descending interval S and both give RS. A day with visibility elsewhere but neither classified passage gives V. With no visible interval it gives I. Thus V can be the appropriate code even for a star which crosses the skyline twice. For a detection close to a threshold, record the adopted res, extinction and solar limit. Coarse solar interpolation and a very brief modelled opportunity have different implications for the assigned date.

title: 7  Seasonal stellar visibility
section: 7.2 Choices that can change the interpretation
text:
7.2 Choices that can change the interpretation







Choice
Consequence for the reader




Supply a terrain profile or a single horizon altitude
A profile allows the skyline to vary along the stellar track. The default solar threshold also depends on the input form. For a fair comparison set solar.alt explicitly to the same value in both runs.


Set extinction, limiting magnitude and refraction
These assumptions change the visibility window. The default extinction coefficient, 0.2 magnitudes per airmass, represents a clear-sky baseline. Local observing conditions may differ.


Use the altitude-difference rule for other kinds of events
Purrington’s empirical relation covers dawn rising and dusk setting on the Sun’s side of the sky, down to about magnitude 3. The package extends the same threshold across relative azimuths. Opposite-horizon events and fainter stars therefore involve extrapolation (Purrington 1988, S74–75).


Count any positive-duration window
A short break above an uneven skyline can qualify. A human observer may need longer to find the star. Moonlight, weather and an observer’s adaptation history also affect detection (Schaefer 1987).


Enter a cluster such as M45
The function applies the cluster’s integrated catalogue magnitude to a single target. Use an individual star to ask about the visibility of a particular Pleiad.

title: 7  Seasonal stellar visibility
section: 7.3 Changes that matter for earlier analyses
text:
7.3 Changes that matter for earlier analyses
The 2.0 development NEWS records changes to handling southern, circumpolar and obstructed tracks. A completely obstructed star now returns an all-invisible result. An always-clear star can still enter different seasonal phases. The separate metadata$horizon.status field lets the analyst distinguish these cases. An earlier analysis involving a star close to the circumpolar limit or a raised skyline is a priority for recalculation.
The output also distinguishes the schematic day of the seasonal cycle from metadata$events$date.julian. Use the latter when passing an event to riseset() for a terrain crossing. The crossing gives a starting time from which to examine the changing dawn sky.
Evidence for the date. The heliacal-rising comparison quantifies agreement for this event under a specified set of observing assumptions. Other phase transitions require their own evidence.
See the event-search chapter for the crossing solver and an example of reoccultation on a rising track.

title: 7  Seasonal stellar visibility
section: 7.4 Comparing the same season across stars and epochs
text:
7.4 Comparing the same season across stars and epochs
plot.skyscapeR.starphases() places a result and any further results on a common seasonal axis beginning at December solstice. A single cycle can be drawn as a ring or a strip. Multiple results occupy concentric rings from the outside inward, or aligned strips in the linear layout. The month divisions are a shared seasonal reference. Use the saved event date for a historical calendar comparison. Ordering results by star or epoch and holding the skyline and visibility thresholds fixed makes it possible to attribute changes in the boundaries to the chosen comparison. The plot reads the classifications already calculated by star.phases(). Adding a ring does not refit the visibility model.

title: 7  Seasonal stellar visibility
text:
7.5 Full package help
The following help page is generated from the archived 2.0.9004 package documentation.


Read the complete star.phases() help page

Model seasonal changes in stellar visibility

Description

Estimate the seasons in which a star's rising or setting could be visible in twilight at
an archaeological site.



Usage

star.phases(
  star,
  year,
  loc,
  alt.hor = 0,
  alt.rs = 10,
  solar.alt = NULL,
  k = skyscapeR.vars()$k,
  limit = 6,
  refraction,
  atm,
  temp,
  res = 1/24/6
)



Arguments





star
Either the star name or a skyscapeR.star object.


year
The year of interest. Historical labels such as "3700 BC" are accepted by astroYear.


loc
Location, either a skyscapeR.horizon or a vector containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.


alt.hor
The altitude of the horizon to consider. Defaults to zero degrees.


alt.rs
The maximum altitude of a star's first or last visibility for it to still be considered to be as rising or setting. Defaults to ten degrees.


solar.alt
Solar altitude threshold in degrees. NULL uses -6 for a horizon, or alt.hor - 6 for coordinate input.


k
Visual extinction in magnitudes per airmass (Schaefer 1986, p. S33). The package adopts 0.2 as a clear-sky baseline. Extinction varies with site and atmospheric conditions (Schaefer 1986, 1993). Defaults to the session value from skyscapeR.vars().


limit
The maximum magnitude of a star that can be visible with the naked eye. Defaults to 6.


refraction
Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in skyscapeR.vars.


atm
Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in skyscapeR.vars.


temp
Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in skyscapeR.vars.


res
Spacing of solar altitude samples in days, greater than zero and at most one. Default 1/144 day (ten minutes). Terrain crossings are refined separately.






Details

Seasonal visibility depends on solar depression, stellar altitude, apparent magnitude
and atmospheric extinction as well as terrain. The model holds the star's position fixed
for the chosen year and samples a 365-day solar cycle with uniformly spaced ecliptic
longitudes. It requires a star-Sun altitude separation of 2.1 times the catalogue
magnitude plus 10 degrees, and compares extinction-adjusted magnitude with the limiting
magnitude. A positive-duration overlap of visibility conditions determines the daily
code. The stellar altitude trend within a visible interval below alt.rs determines
rising or setting. Terrain reappearance of a descending star therefore contributes
a setting phase. Disjoint runs are reported as separate seasons on the circular
model year, including runs spanning the December-solstice reference.

Both constant and varying horizons are evaluated on all 365 model days. A horizon
object supplies the coordinates and piecewise-linear horizon. The profile must
cover all bearings and close at north. Use alt.hor only with coordinate input.
A fixed-coordinate stellar track is shared across model days. The terrain search
uses the same corners, azimuth reversals, interior extrema and 0.01-second root
tolerance as riseset, collecting all crossings during the model day.
Visible windows can lie wholly between minute samples. A touch without clearance
contributes no visible duration. Source terrain resolution and numerical tolerances
limit the shortest resolvable window.

Refraction selects apparent or geometric altitudes for both Sun and star.
A stellar horizon affects obstruction at the star's azimuth. The solar darkness
test uses altitude relative to the astronomical horizon, with default solar.alt
of -6 for a profile and alt.hor - 6 for coordinates. Supply the same solar.alt
to compare a constant profile and a raised scalar horizon. Extinction, the
star-Sun separation and alt.rs use stellar altitude above the astronomical horizon.
Solar altitude is interpolated between res samples. Stellar visibility margins
are interpolated on a grid containing minute samples, solar samples, terrain
crossings and stellar altitude extrema. Decrease res to assess borderline dates.
Any positive-duration opportunity in this threshold model qualifies. Actual
naked-eye detection over a very short interval depends on observing conditions.
The synthetic solar year and solstice calendar mapping
are conventions inherited from the phase model.

Purrington (1988, p. S74, equation 1 and Fig. 2) fitted the altitude-difference
rule to empirical data down to about magnitude 3. It describes rising at dawn and
setting at dusk on the same side of the sky as the Sun. Purrington discusses a
smaller separation for opposite-horizon events (p. S75). This function applies
the same threshold at every relative azimuth. Schaefer (1987, section 4)
examines how sky brightness and observing conditions affect heliacal visibility.
Brady (2015) gives the archaeological context for the phase terminology.

Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing swephRdata; see skyscapeR-package for setup.



Value

A skyscapeR.starphases list. The data table gives each model day and its phase code: I for invisible, V for visible without a classified rise or set, R for rising, S for setting and RS for both. Metadata include the star, year, observer coordinates, phase type, season and event tables, refraction setting and solar altitude threshold. For a named horizon, metadata$site.name retains the site label for comparisons. The logical metadata$horizon records whether a horizon object was supplied. The separate metadata$horizon.status reports "always above", "always below" or "crosses" relative to the supplied skyline. Event rows include solar.longitude in degrees on the synthetic cycle. The date.julian column gives the representative local Julian calendar date at the supplied longitude. Pass this date to riseset with calendar = "J" to time the skyline crossing. For a dawn sketch, advance from that crossing until the star clears the terrain while the sky is still dark enough. The phase date alone does not specify a visible instant.



Extinction and model scope

The implementation uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation,
X(h)=1/(\sin h+0.025\exp(-11\sin h)), multiplying it by k
and adding the result to the fixed catalogue magnitude. Here h is the
stellar altitude selected by refraction, above the astronomical
horizontal. This is distinct from the height above a ridge. The star-Sun
altitude-separation rule uses the catalogue magnitude before extinction.

The model does not calculate scattered moonlight, artificial light pollution,
weather, an observer's adaptation history, or variable-star light curves.
The same separation threshold is used at all relative azimuths. It is therefore
a screening model for seasonal opportunities, not a probability of detection.
Supplying an integrated cluster entry such as M45 treats its total magnitude as
one target; cluster size, surface brightness and resolution into individual
stars do not enter this calculation. It does not predict when each Pleiad is
individually visible.

Horizon status is determined from positive-duration clearance intervals along
the same stellar track used for the phase calculation, with the supplied
skyline and refraction setting. The same calculation applies in both
hemispheres. A track with no clearance returns an ordinary all-I result,
rather than raising an error. An always-clear track still undergoes the
extinction and solar-darkness tests; never setting does not imply visibility.
A star that never sets below a level horizontal can cross a raised ridge.
Isolated tangencies do not count as intervals of clearance or obstruction.
Numerical resolution and the supplied terrain profile limit this status.

The separate metadata$horizon.status field is "always above", "always below"
or "crosses", relative to the supplied skyline. Phase codes R and S describe
the rising or descending part of a visible track below alt.rs; they do not
require a physical skyline crossing that day. An always-clear star may thus
have seasonal R/S codes. The type "circumpolar" is retained for an all-V
result only when the track is always above the skyline; other all-V results
are labelled "visible throughout cycle". Use horizon.status, not type, to
distinguish clearance from seasonal visibility.



Dates and a subsequent sky sketch

Events follow adjacent-sample transitions around the closed cycle, including
the December-solstice boundary. Entering and leaving I mark acronycal setting
and heliacal rising; entering and leaving V mark acronycal rising and heliacal
setting. A season continuing across the boundary creates no event there.
Constant phase sequences have no transition events.

The 365 model samples are equally spaced in solar longitude, not in elapsed
civil time. Printed seasonal labels are anchored to the December solstice.
metadata$events$date.julian instead solves for the event solar longitude
in the requested year and converts it to a local mean-solar Julian-calendar
date using longitude. It is a representative date, not an exact detection
instant, and can differ from the synthetic day label.

Pass the representative date to riseset with
calendar = "J" and an explicit timezone. With UTC or a fixed offset,
inspect neighbouring dates when local mean-solar and civil days differ.
The returned rise is a skyline crossing. Follow it by a short time sequence
with sketchSky and skyStep to inspect terrain
clearance and the changing brightness of the local sky.

A supplied skyscapeR.star is used as given. Recompute it for the requested
year; the phase function does not update an existing object's coordinates.



How precise is a heliacal-rising date?

In 69 of 70 individual comparisons, the estimated first morning of visibility was within a week of the predicted heliacal-rising date.



Reproducing a saved result

Metadata retain the resolved star, year, observer coordinates, extinction,
atmospheric settings and solar-altitude threshold, together with limit,
alt.rs, res and alt.hor. The latter is NA when a terrain
profile replaces the constant horizon. metadata$horizon.profile contains
the numerical az/alt table used, or NULL for a constant horizon.
Landscape images and DEMs are not copied into the result. Existing logical
horizon and skyline fields are retained.

metadata$provenance$packages records the loaded skyscapeR and swephR
versions; an unavailable version is NA, for example when sourcing functions
outside a package namespace. Version strings do not uniquely identify
development builds. Retain the original script, code revision and ephemeris
files as well: the saved metadata do not identify or archive those files.
Earlier saved results do not acquire these fields automatically.



Provenance

Structured results carry a provenance attribute. Read it with
attr(result, "provenance"); its packages entry records the loaded
skyscapeR and swephR versions, with NA when a namespace version is unavailable.
This attribute adds no list entries or table columns. Ordinary subsetting or
transformations may discard attributes; save the original result for reference.
It does not identify ephemeris files, catalogue revisions or a development
commit. Retain those and the analysis script separately for exact reproduction.
The same record remains available in metadata$provenance.



Validation

Seasonal searches require full skyline coverage. H07 checked rejection of a partial photograph and successful calculation with the full profile. See the H07 check in the technical manual.

W02 replayed the Gacrux heliacal-rising date at Skorba West and passed it to the crossing and sky-reconstruction calculations. See the W02 check in the technical manual.



References

Crumey, A. (2014). Human contrast threshold and astronomical
visibility. MNRAS 442, 2600-2619. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1093/mnras/stu992")}.

Purrington, R. D. (1988). Heliacal Rising and Setting: Quantitative Aspects. Journal for the History of Astronomy 19, S72-S84. https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1988JHAS...19...72P.

Schaefer, B. E. (1986). Atmospheric Extinction Effects on Stellar Alignments. Journal for the History of Astronomy 17, S32-S42. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182868601701003")}.

Schaefer, B. E. (1993). Astronomy and the Limits of Vision. Vistas in Astronomy 36, 311-361. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/0083-6656(93)90113-X")}.

Schaefer, B. E. (1987). Heliacal Rise Phenomena. Journal for the History of Astronomy 18, S19-S33. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182868701801103")}.

Brady, B. (2015). Star Phases: the Naked-eye Astronomy of the Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts. In F. Silva and N. Campion (eds), Skyscapes: The Role and Importance of the Sky in Archaeology. Oxbow Books, pp. 76-86.

Krisciunas, K. and Schaefer, B. E. (1991). A model of the brightness
of moonlight. PASP 103, 1033-1039 (equation 14 for extinction airmass).
\Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1086/132921")}.



See Also

plot.skyscapeR.starphases, riseset, sketchSky, skyStep, star



Examples

## Not run: 
if (requireNamespace("swephRdata", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ss1 <- star.phases('Aldebaran',-4000, c(35,-8,200))
  
  # One can then look at the star's phase type:
  ss1$metadata$type
  
  # Date range of seasons:
  ss1$metadata$seasons
  
  # Date range of phase-type events:
  ss1$metadata$events
  
  # And plot them:
  plot(ss1)
  
  # You can play with the parameters and see how predictions change:
  ss1 <- star.phases('Aldebaran',-4000, c(35,-8,200), alt.hor=2, alt.rs=5)
  plot(ss1)
}

title: 8  From a measured orientation to a declination distribution
text:
8.1 What does a measurement PDF represent?
Coverage of bearing densities on partial photographs.
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9011, R/measurement-density.R, R/statistics.R, R/dec-pdf.R, R/mechanics.R and R/misc.R. A doorway admits a range of sightlines; each can meet a different altitude on the skyline. Silva (2020, secs 2–3, figs. 1–5) represents uncertainty in the orientation as a probability density and transforms that density using the local horizon. The worked example follows one doorway from its measured angular opening to three distinct regions in declination.
D01 checks the input densities. D02 compares the propagated density with independent integration and direct simulation on sloping, asymmetric and surveyed skylines. It documents grid-sensitive highest-density regions and the limits of the conditional Gaussian near the celestial pole.
Let AA denote true azimuth, increasing clockwise from north. The density fA(a)f_A(a) expresses how the analyst allocates support across the bearings consistent with the measurement. In Silva’s framework the appropriate density depends on the measurement and the architecture (Silva 2020, sec. 2). A directly observed axis with repeat readings can justify a concentrated density; an opening bounded by two jambs may justify a bounded interval. Assigning equal support throughout a doorway is an archaeological assumption. The PDF does not measure how often an original observer looked in each direction.
crumbs: 8  From a measured orientation to a declination distribution

title: 8  From a measured orientation to a declination distribution
text:
8.1.1 Choosing the measurement model
All six azimuth measurement models express a judgement about the sightline as seen from a particular observing position. Suppose the measured edges of a doorway are 88° and 92°.








Family
What the field evidence supports
Meaning of the arguments




normal
Repeated readings or a calibrated error model support symmetric, approximately Gaussian error around one bearing.
az=90, unc=1 sets a standard deviation of 1°. About 95.45% of the probability then lies between 88° and 92°.


uniform
The edges are firm limits and all sightlines inside are equally plausible.
az=90, unc=2 defines the outer limits 88° and 92°.


epanechnikov
A central axis is preferred and the architecture bounds the view.
az=90, unc=2 gives greatest density at 90° and a parabolic decline to zero at 88° and 92°.


tapered_uniform
The full opening deserves equal weight. Both recorded edges admit a finite margin.
unc=2, taper=0.5 gives a flat 88°–92° core and a half-cosine taper to 87.5° and 92.5°.


triangular
The most plausible axis is identifiable. One side may be less securely reconstructed.
az=90, lower=89, upper=93 gives a linear decline on each side, with a longer tail towards 93°. For a symmetric triangle, supply unc alone.


uniform_normal
The width of an equally weighted opening and an independent, zero-mean Gaussian error in its measured bearing can be estimated separately.
The survey-error SD defaults to 0.5°. An explicit unc=2, survey.sd=0.2 rounds the profile inside and outside 88° and 92°. There is no finite outer cutoff in the underlying Gaussian error.






Six models for azimuth uncertainty on common scales. Vertical lines mark the nominal doorway edges. The detail compares the tapered uniform and the uniform convolved with normal survey error.


For a core half-width ww and a cosine taper of length tt on each side, the plateau has height 1/(2w+t)1/(2w+t) and the two shoulders together contain t/(2w+t)t/(2w+t) of the probability. In this example, 11.1% lies outside the core. For the convolution, write the bearing as the sum of an equally weighted direction through the opening and an independent survey error. If xx is the offset from the centre, the unwrapped density is [Φ((x+w)/s)−Φ((x−w)/s)]/(2w)[\Phi((x+w)/s)-\Phi((x-w)/s)]/(2w), where ss is the error standard deviation. With s=0.2°s=0.2° the probability outside the nominal opening is about 4.0%. The taper stays level to the edge itself. The convolution has already fallen to approximately half its central height there.
Azimuth densities are periodic. A triangular interval from 358° to 3° can therefore have its mode at 0°. The grid samples [0°, 360°) at 0.01° by default. The cutoff of 10−510^{-5} is a density height applied after wrapping. Trimming tails leaves their mass out of the stored curve. Use a spacing fine enough to resolve both the opening and any narrow shoulders.
dec.pdf(). Use this route when the observation and its uncertainty already refer to declination. The physical support ends at ±90°, and the default cutoff is 10−410^{-4}. A normal curve centred near a pole can therefore have less than unit area after clipping. A directly constructed declination density assigns its family in that coordinate. A normal azimuth density passed through terrain can yield a markedly different declination curve (Silva 2020, sec. 3).

title: 8  From a measured orientation to a declination distribution
section: 8.2 Point transformation and the conditional density
text:
8.2 Point transformation and the conditional density
For geometric altitude hh, site latitude ϕ\phi and true bearing AA, the spherical relation is (Silva 2020, eq. 1)
sinδ=sinϕsinh+cosϕcoshcosA.\sin\delta=\sin\phi\sin h+\cos\phi\cos h\cos A.
az2dec() evaluates a single sightline using the inverse Swiss horizontal transformation, shifting the azimuth convention at the interface. With refraction enabled, the code adjusts altitude using observer elevation, pressure and temperature before the inverse transformation. It rounds returned declinations according to the input bearing representation. When reading a value off a measured skyline, distinguish the altitude of the terrain from an angular clearance above it. The inputs, atmosphere and precision must match before using an independent calculation as a comparator (Astrodienst, n.d.).
coordtrans() implements the density transformation developed in Silva (2020). The published idea is to marginalise over the plausible bearings, retaining the dependence of horizon altitude on bearing (Silva 2020, sec. 3, figs. 2–5). In continuous notation,
fδ(d)=∫fA(a)g(d∣a)da.f_\delta(d)=\int f_A(a)\,g(d\mid a)\,da.
For each sampled bearing, 2.0.9004 interpolates the profile height H(a)H(a) and its altitude uncertainty sh(a)s_h(a). It transforms the two endpoint heights H(a)±4sh(a)H(a)\pm4s_h(a) to declinations d−d_- and d+d_+. The conditional density gg is approximated by a normal with mean (d−+d+)/2(d_-+d_+)/2 and standard deviation |d+−d−|/8|d_+-d_-|/8. This preserves endpoint order reversals and allows the width to vary with the skyline. It is an endpoint-based approximation to a nonlinear mapping; the conditional mean need not equal the transform of H(a)H(a). A zero transformed width raises an error because a Gaussian density with zero standard deviation is undefined in this computation. Artificially inflating the reported horizon error changes the model.



Silva’s conditional-density construction applied to the doorway example below. Blue intensity gives the conditional density at each bearing. Integrating with uniform bearing weights produces the three maxima in the recorded package output on the right.


On a steep notch flank, even the geometric central track has a bearing derivative proportional to the skyline slope. Where HH is differentiable, in radians, cosδdδ/dA=(sinϕcosH−cosϕsinHcosA)H′(A)−cosϕcosHsinA\cos\delta\,\mathrm d\delta/\mathrm dA=(\sin\phi\cos H-\cos\phi\sin H\cos A)H'(A)-\cos\phi\cos H\sin A. At a corner the adjacent segments have different slopes. A single error propagated at the centre can consequently miss entire branches sampled by the opening. The numerical mixture accommodates those branches without dividing by a local derivative.
The implementation interpolates the conditional density values and azimuth weights onto an integration grid and sums their products with trapezoidal weights. Distinguish three numerical settings:








Setting
Default
Controls




.prec
0.1°
Azimuth spacing used to integrate the conditional contributions. Bearings spanning north are unwrapped for continuity.


.res
0.1°
Declination spacing at which the mixture is calculated. The upper calculation bound is added explicitly if necessary.


.output.res
0.01°
Spacing of the returned declination curve, obtained by linear interpolation. More output coordinates alone cannot resolve a missed peak.



Version 2.0.9004 uses linear interpolation, avoiding negative overshoot that could occur with a spline. It also explicitly treats distributions split across north. Each individual transformed PDF is normalised by its trapezoidal area on the returned grid. Transforming an already summed SPD does not perform that individual normalisation. In ideal continuous arithmetic, integration and summation commute for a common kernel. Site-specific skylines imply different kernels, while truncation and per-curve normalisation can also change finite-grid results. Supply horizons in observation order. Preserve the original azimuth curves and horizons for any later declination significance test.

title: 8  From a measured orientation to a declination distribution
section: 8.3 Worked example: a doorway across a notch
text:
8.3 Worked example: a doorway across a notch
At a synthetic site at 51° N, give the 88–92° doorway a uniform density. The terrain stands at 6° on either side and falls to 1° between bearings 89.2° and 90.8°, with 0.2°-wide sloping shoulders. Set horizon altitude uncertainty to 0.2° throughout and turn refraction off. A control uses the same doorway and uncertainty with a level 1° skyline. Only the terrain profile changes.
site <- c(51, 0, 100)
notch <- createHor(c(0, 87, 89, 89.2, 90.8, 91, 93, 360),
                   c(6,  6,  6,    1,    1,  6,  6,   6),
                   loc = site, alt.unc = 0.2)
skyscapeR.vars(refraction = FALSE)
door <- az.pdf(90, unc = 2, pdf = "uniform")
d <- coordtrans(door, notch, xrange = c(-4, 9),
                .prec = 0.02, .res = 0.02, .output.res = 0.01)
total <- spd(d, xrange = c(-4, 9), normalise = TRUE)
hpdi(total, mass = 0.68)



The same doorway samples a low notch and two higher flanks. The transformed density has three areas of high concentration.





Skyline
68% highest-density regions in declination




Level at 1°
−0.08° to 1.64°


Notched
0.35° to 1.21°, 3.46° to 3.97°, and 5.37° to 5.83°



The central portion of the doorway faces the low notch. Its two flanks face higher terrain at different bearings, so they have different declinations even at the same terrain altitude. A conversion of only the centre and the two extremes loses this allocation of probability. Halving both calculation spacings from 0.02° to 0.01° gave the same reported interval endpoints to 0.01° in this example. This is a numerical sensitivity check on a constructed case, not field validation.

title: 8  From a measured orientation to a declination distribution
text:
8.4 Summation, highest-density regions and inference
spd() linearly interpolates each retained curve onto a common angular grid, assigns zero outside its support and sums the heights. With an automatically determined range, it zeroes summed heights below the cutoff. An explicit range retains the calculated heights within that range. With normalise = TRUE, it divides by the trapezoidal area over the returned interval. A narrow explicit range therefore conditions the displayed mass on the selected interval. Earlier builds normalised using a sum of sampled heights: on a regular grid with zero endpoint heights, the new heights are the old ones divided by grid spacing. Record normalisation when comparing figure ordinates across versions (see the versioned function help and package NEWS).
hpdi() implements a discrete highest-density region (Hyndman 1996). On an equally spaced grid it sorts density heights and finds the level whose cumulative sum reaches the requested mass fraction, then includes all cells tied at that level. The result can include more than the nominal fraction. Separate connected runs give separate intervals; endpoints are grid coordinates. Gaps representing omitted cells are treated as zero mass, and regions spanning north are returned as two linear intervals. This is a description of concentration under the assumed measurement model. It does not test intentionality or reject a null hypothesis.
A strength of this workflow over a curve assembled by placing the same symmetric kernel at each converted central declination is that the horizon can change the shape of each site’s contribution. Silva’s worked comparison shows why curvigram and kernel-density peaks can shift relative to a terrain-aware SPD (Silva 2020, fig. 5). The price is sensitivity to the skyline, measurement model, endpoint approximation and numerical resolution. At limiting declinations or very small altitude uncertainties, check both grid convergence and the adequacy of the conditional Gaussian. A credible distribution still requires a defensible uncertainty model. The significance chapter shows how these same curves enter simulations.
Download the example scripts, inputs and outputs. The archived package supplies the implementation; the example is reproducible separately from the validation studies.

title: 8  From a measured orientation to a declination distribution
text:
8.5 What the orientation displays calculate
For an opening defined clockwise from left edge ALA_L to right edge ARA_R, compute w=(AR−AL)mod360°w=(A_R-A_L)\bmod360° and centre (AL+w/2)mod360°(A_L+w/2)\bmod360°. An opening from 355° to 5° then has width 10° and centre 0°. Keep a common row order when selecting entrance records and site horizons. Passing w/2w/2 to plotBars() draws symmetric measurement limits. The default geometry is a line interval; explicitly supplying shade selects the bar default unless geometry is also specified. The unit labels the axis. Celestial bands require declination coordinates in this display. On a Cartesian azimuth axis an interval crossing north can extend below 0° or above 360°.
plotAzimuth() draws bearings clockwise from north, with spokes or short rim marks. For each reference declination and target location it computes a diurnal track with orbit(), interpolates altitude as a function of azimuth and solves for the zero-altitude roots on the eastern and western branches where bracketed. A two-epoch group contributes the stored boundary declinations. These compass marks assume a level horizon. The local terrain crossing for the same target can lie elsewhere. Inside/outside controls position the reference lines; labels remain outside. Repeated measured bearings can coincide.
The linked view of plot.skyscapeR.pdf() requires one transformed index, the original azimuth PDF and a matching horizon or ordered horizon list. The panels connect the input distribution, azimuth-to-declination mapping and output density. A mass such as 0.68 can select disjoint intervals. Supplying just one of the source inputs is an error. The legacy show.az switch is ignored with a warning. A plain density plot needs neither source input. subset.skyscapeR.pdf() uses the supplied R index on the list of curves and the name, azimuth, uncertainty and horizon metadata. It leaves other fields as stored. plot.skyscapeR.spd() draws the summed density, optionally with targets. A plotted peak carries no significance level by itself (Silva 2020).

8.5.1 Subsetting a directly constructed declination PDF
Build 2.0.9006 retains the centre vector in the selected order, including empty and repeated selections. The D01 rerun verifies the correction. For a dec.pdf() object, 2.0.9004’s subset.skyscapeR.pdf() selects the requested curves, names and uncertainties but leaves metadata$dec unchanged. Given centres of −10° and +20° named A and B, subset(x, 2) returns B’s curve and uncertainty but retains both centres in the metadata. A reader who pairs the first retained curve with the first stored centre would assign it −10°. To retain a consistent centre vector, apply the selection to the input records and construct their PDF, or explicitly index the original centres with the same selection. The worked check is in object-coverage.R in the photographic horizon examples.

title: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches
text:
9.1 Sampling a diurnal track
A05 tests civil dates, solstitial branches and independent east and west solutions for spatial equinoxes.
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/horizon-events.R, R/mechanics.R, R/events.R and R/misc.R. A point on a track, a terrain crossing, a midpoint bearing, a date and a sampled extreme are five different outputs. Their numerical precision and their archaeological interpretation depend on different assumptions.
Terrain crossing searches assume a complete skyline. A partial photographic profile can yield events outside its observed sector.
The A02 lunar skyline comparison quantifies how ephemeris conventions affect crossing times and azimuths. A04 checks crossing times, bearings and event order against analytic tracks and independent root searches, including JPL solar and lunar centre crossings.
For a fixed declination, orbit() samples right ascension across a full turn, using res in degrees (default 0.25°). It transforms the sampled positions to horizontal coordinates for the supplied observer and atmosphere, retains altitudes above −20° and sorts the output by azimuth. The horizon object supplies the site; the function does not test each point for terrain clearance. Azimuth-sorted points do not give a time ordering or a local rise time. A fixed-declination track is useful for asking which part of the astronomical path could meet a ridge. A moving Solar System body on a particular morning requires its ephemeris.
crumbs: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches

title: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches
text:
9.2 Crossing definition and selection
Let A(t)A(t) and h(t)h(t) be the topocentric bearing and centre altitude of the body, and H(A)H(A) the terrain altitude interpolated at that bearing. The terrain solver seeks sign changes in
C(t)=h(t)−H(A(t)).C(t)=h(t)-H\bigl(A(t)\bigr).
A change from negative to positive marks emergence; positive to negative marks disappearance. Touching the skyline and returning to the same side produces neither event. Select apparent or geometric altitude with refraction, and record the pressure and temperature. The dec setting controls the reported declination. The event geometry remains topocentric.
riseset() has distinct computational routes. For a Solar System body and numeric site coordinates, an explicit scalar alt is passed to the Swiss Ephemeris constant-horizon rise/set routine with the disc-centre convention (Astrodienst, n.d.). For a horizon object, the package interpolates its complete profile; combining this with an explicit alt raises an error. Stellar tracks use the package crossing solver even for a constant altitude. For a dated terrain search, local midnight in the selected calendar and timezone defines the start, and the search runs for 48 hours. The function returns the first upward and first downward crossing separately. Either may be missing, either may be on the next day, and the reported set can occur before the reported rise.
A one-minute base interval is divided into quarters. Azimuth changes are unwrapped locally around north; the solver locates turning points and splits rapid or reversing azimuth motion to bracket passages across terrain vertices. On smooth subintervals whose endpoints have the same clearance sign, the solver checks for an interior extremum that could conceal a short emergence and reoccultation. Bracketed roots are refined to 0.01 s. Skyline altitude must agree at 0° and 360°. The root tolerance describes the numerical refinement; it cannot remove errors in terrain altitude, atmosphere or ancient time conversion. A near-tangency or near-zenith azimuth singularity also limits numerical completeness.

9.3 Worked example: a Sun that sets in the morning
On 20 March 2026, place the observer at 51° N, 0° longitude and 100 m elevation. The synthetic skyline is level until bearing 91.5°, climbs to 8° at 93°, stays there to 94°, and drops to zero at 97°. Use the Gregorian calendar and UTC, with atmospheric refraction off. The ridge is deliberately positioned across the ascending solar track.
ridge <- createHor(c(0, 91.5, 93, 94, 97, 360),
                   c(0,    0,  8,  8,  0,   0), loc = c(51, 0, 100))
events <- riseset(ridge, date = "2026/03/20", obj = "sun",
                  timezone = "UTC", calendar = "G", refraction = FALSE)

That second emergence is evident in the track but is not the first rise, so it has no second row in events$rise. The figure joins minute samples; the tabulated times above are the solver outputs. title: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches
text:
9.4 Spatial midpoint and solar date
Ruggles distinguished the spatial midpoint of the solstitial horizon bearings from definitions based on time or equatorial declination (Ruggles 1997). spatial.equinox() constructs fixed tracks at δ=±ϵ\delta=\pm\epsilon for the epoch’s obliquity. It applies solar parallax before atmospheric refraction, follows each track from lower culmination to lower culmination, and selects first emergence on its rising half and final disappearance on its setting half. This is a different selection rule from the first downward crossing returned by riseset().
For each side let A1,A2A_1,A_2 be the two solstitial bearings. The result uses the midpoint of the shorter circular arc, Am=(A1+wrap180(A2−A1)/2)mod360°A_m=(A_1+\mathrm{wrap}_{180}(A_2-A_1)/2)\bmod 360°. At that bearing the package interpolates the terrain and inverts refraction and mean solar parallax to obtain geocentric declination. A missing required crossing makes that side undefined; opposite bearings have no unique shorter arc. Polar configurations, complete obstruction or a tangency can therefore yield NA. The 2.0 development implementation made epoch and atmosphere explicit and revised the crossing selection; recalculate historical spatial-equinox targets if these conventions matter.
As a separate example, give the same site a 10° northeastern plateau from bearings 35° to 65°, sloping to level ground at 25° and 75°. For 2026, the eastern midpoint is 97.059°, equivalent to declination −4.434°; the western midpoint is 269.996°, equivalent to approximately 0°. The two sides of one site can therefore imply different solar dates. These bearings come from geometric, solar-centre tracks with the package’s default parallax and refraction off.
solar.date() solves a different equation: δ⊙(t)−δtarget=0\delta_{\odot}(t)-\delta_{\mathrm{target}}=0. It samples daily geocentric apparent declinations, uses adjacent samples to bracket turning points, refines the extrema and solves for roots on the monotonic sections. The civil year includes its first midnight UT and excludes the next year’s first instant. Near a solstice, two nearby roots may fall on one civil day; a tangency gives one root. A requested value outside the annual range has no root. The routine returns dates, omitting unavailable targets with a message when verbose, and errors if none are attainable. In 2026, a target of 0° returns 20 March and 23 September in the Gregorian calendar regardless of which terrain profile was used for the midpoint.
crumbs: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches

title: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches
text:
9.5 Sampled planetary extrema
planet.extremes() sets an interval extending three quarters of its planet-specific period on either side of the chosen year and rounds the endpoints to years. The constants in this build are 6.989733 years for Mercury, 8 for Venus, ten times 687/365.25 for Mars, 4331/365.25 for Jupiter and 10747/365.25 for Saturn. These are search-window parameters. The routine samples the ephemeris daily at noon UT from 1 January of the starting year through 1 January of the ending year, taking the range of the returned declinations. Supply a site for local positions and record the declination convention. Without a site the example uses geocentric positions.
For Venus at epoch 2026 the window is 1 January 2020 through 1 January 2032. The geocentric sampled range was −27.32186° to +27.81592° in the archived example. The digits identify the calculation. Sampling at noon can miss an intervening extremum; increasing the printed precision supplies no bound on that error. This routine neither refines continuous extrema nor returns their event times. A comparison with another ephemeris must match the body, frame, site, time interval and sampling cadence before its residuals can be interpreted.
crumbs: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches

title: 9  Terrain crossings and event searches
text:
9.6 Interpretation, limits and reproduction
A terrain solver can resolve multiple skyline encounters on the same ascending track; the constant-altitude solver answers a simpler question. Neither supersedes a field survey of the ridge or an explicit decision about whether the archaeological event concerns a centre, a limb or an observable star. For date and extremum searches, distinguish errors due to the ephemeris from those introduced by the chosen event definition or temporal sampling. Useful future checks include known short crossing pairs, nearly tangent tracks, solstitial targets close to the annual limit and extrema bracketed by daily planetary samples.
Download the scripts, example outputs and ephemeris identifiers. All three event examples were executed with skyscapeR 2.0.9004 and swephR 0.3.2. The paired modern Swiss data files used for these examples identify DE441 in their headers. Their checksums are in the example archive. They illustrate implementation behaviour; the study register retains the independent field and model-comparison evidence.

title: 10  Equinoctial full Moons and crescent crossovers
text:
10.1 Equinoctial full Moons
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/events.R and R/crescent-crossovers.R. Silva & Pimenta (2012, §§2.1–2.2, figs. 3–4) defined families of observable events by comparing where the Moon and Sun rise or set across successive days and lunations. Their Alcyone Ephemeris 2.8 scripts recorded the first qualifying event for each year. skyscapeR implements the searches with Swiss Ephemeris, exposes the observing conventions, and can use a measured skyline (Silva and Pimenta 2012; Astrodienst, n.d.). A crossover is selected by the order of two horizon bearings at their respective events. The bodies need not be on the horizon together.
EFM() searches chronological local civil dates from 60 days before to 65 days after the astronomical March or September equinox. It evaluates the illuminated fraction at the lunar centre crossing and requires at least min.phase (default 0.99). Let D=AMoon−ASunD=A_{\mathrm{Moon}}-A_{\mathrm{Sun}}, using topocentric bearings clockwise from true north. The 2.0.9004 EFM implementation applies the strict comparisons below to the two bearings directly.
The paper starts from a full Moon about two synodic months before the equinox and advances through days. The package makes its temporal bounds explicit in days and tests the phase at the lunar event itself.
On the rising branch, the solar comparator is the first sunrise on the lunar event’s local date. On the setting branch, it is the last sunset preceding moonset among the first solar set events on the current and preceding local dates. A morning moonset will commonly be paired with the previous evening. Missing pairs are skipped. The function returns the first candidate passing both the illumination and bearing tests, and stops with the year and event if none qualifies. Changing the civil timezone can change the pairing. Changing the output declination frame leaves the topocentric selection rule in place.
Worked moonset. At 40° N, longitude 0°, elevation 400 m, the 2026 spring setting event occurred at 05:13:20 UTC on 1 April. The preceding sunset was at 18:21:41 UTC on 31 March. Lunar and solar azimuths were 266.6435° and 276.1790°, giving D=−9.5356°D=-9.5356°. At the reported lunar event the illuminated fraction was 0.991804. Both tests pass. Pairing this moonset with the evening of 1 April would use sunlight from an event that had yet to occur.
The equinox anchors the search; it does not identify the nearest full Moon or require that the event fall after the equinox. The phase cutoff does not model twilight, extinction, atmospheric clarity or the appearance of the upper lunar limb.

title: 10  Equinoctial full Moons and crescent crossovers
text:
10.2 First and last crescents
CC() first locates the relevant solstice and conjunctions. The initial lunation is two conjunctions before the last conjunction at or before the solstice. Its distance from the solstice depends on the Moon’s phase at that solstice. This operationalises a starting window described in synodic months in the paper; a fixed subtraction of two mean synodic months need not start on the same lunation. Successive conjunctions are considered through 150 days after solstice.
For each conjunction the algorithm searches forwards for the first waxing evening or backwards for the last waning morning, up to eight civil days from the conjunction date. It assesses visibility at sunset for waxing crescents and at sunrise for waning crescents. In degrees, the adopted Caldwell–Laney margin is
M=hlower+E/3−11.3,M=h_{\mathrm{lower}}+E/3-11.3,
where EE is the geocentric Sun–Moon angular separation and hlowerh_{\mathrm{lower}} is the topocentric lunar lower-limb altitude. The latter uses centre altitude and an angular radius calculated from instantaneous lunar distance and a physical radius of 1,737.4 km. Refraction affects the altitude when enabled. The rule requires M≥0M\ge0, elongation below 90°, and positive lower-limb clearance at the Moon’s bearing. With a terrain profile, clearance is tested separately; the altitude used in MM remains referenced to the astronomical horizontal (Caldwell and Laney 2001; Silva and Pimenta 2012, sec. 2.2).
The bearing comparison comes after that assessment. For a first crescent, compare sunset with the subsequent moonset; for a last crescent, compare sunrise with the preceding moonrise. The lunar crossing must be on the correct side of the solar event and within half a day. The shortest signed azimuth difference, Moon minus Sun, must be negative for June or positive for December in the package convention. The prose in §2.1 of the original paper describes the summer comparison using a greater-than relation. For reproduction, record the signs implemented here and the azimuth convention; copying the verbal inequality without its reference direction is ambiguous. The previous eligible difference is diagnostic. The current code requires the first eligible event on the specified side; it does not require an additional observed sign reversal from one lunation to the next.
SIM1 tries only the first eligible evening or last eligible morning of each lunation. SIM2 also tries the next evening or preceding morning. The base day takes precedence when both pass. If no lunation qualifies, CC returns missing event fields with a warning. Read diagnostics for the conjunction, assessment time, lower-limb altitude, elongation, margin, azimuth difference, day offset and number of qualifying lunations. Output declinations are geocentric; event selection uses topocentric bearings. The labels “summer” and “winter” retain their June and December meanings at southern sites.

10.3 When a second evening changes the lunation
At the same site, search for the 2022 June first crescent. For the conjunction preceding 1 July, both evenings below passed the visibility criterion. The bearing order determined which evening qualified.









Assessment evening (UTC)
Visibility margin
Moonset minus sunset azimuth
Decision




30 June
+9.09°
+1.92°
Base evening: eligible crescent, wrong side for June.


1 July
+19.85°
−1.73°
Additional evening: right side, eligible in SIM2.






The visibility margin is positive on both evenings. The June bearing condition first becomes negative on the additional evening.


SIM2 therefore returned 1 July, whereas SIM1 returned 28 August, with a margin of +3.98° and azimuth difference −4.49°. The extra evening changed which lunation met the definition. Describing SIM2 simply as a one-day uncertainty on the SIM1 date would miss this effect.
site <- c(40, 0, 400)
CC(2022, site, season = "summer", crescent = "first", simulation = "SIM1")
CC(2022, site, season = "summer", crescent = "first", simulation = "SIM2")

text:
10.4 Comparison with the 2012 simulations
The historical workbooks give annual solar and lunar declinations rather than event timestamps. Their coordinates can identify a likely neighbouring date or lunation, but cannot recover every setting in the original scripts. The comparison below concerns the archival 2.0 development analysis, 1620–2047, with a level horizon, longitude 0°, elevation 400 m, UTC, Gregorian dates, geocentric reported declinations, refraction on, 1013.25 mbar and 15 °C. These are the reproduction settings, not verified meteorological parameters of the original simulations.








Comparison
Archived result
Scope




Spring and autumn EFM moonsets
At 0°, 60° N and 60° S, preceding-sunset pairing increased agreement within 0.02° lunar declination from 2,484 to 2,562 of 2,568.
Five remaining choices were just above the 0.99 illumination boundary and one within about 0.002° of the azimuth boundary.


Four SIM1 crescent series
At the same three latitudes, 5,024 of 5,136 agreed within 0.02°.
No corresponding SIM2 accuracy follows from this count. A similar smoothed distribution can hide a wrong annual selection.


40° N series
Additional systematic coordinate offsets remain.
Exploratory changes to the conversion altitude and timing reduced some residuals. The original settings are unresolved; this latitude is excluded from both counts above.



Two individual records show how to read these comparisons. At the equator in autumn 1913, the archived EFM reconstruction selected a moonset with illumination 0.990003 and lunar declination 4.7246°. The next morning’s declination was 10.4302°, matching the historical table’s 10.43°. The reproduced search accepts the earlier morning by about three millionths in illuminated fraction. The table supports the following-morning interpretation but does not tell us why the earlier date was skipped.
For the winter first crescent labelled 1708 at 60° N, the archived SIM1 run selected 12 January 1709, whereas the source’s pair of declinations matched 13 January. The reconstructed base evening cleared the visibility threshold by only 0.019°. The later date is inferred from both coordinates. Across the wider diagnostic sample, alternative search windows and solar-limb definitions recovered some discrepant cases but also changed previously matching controls. There is no established universal adjustment. Replay materials and archived diagnostics are provided separately: worked examples · historical comparison and source-run records.
The strength of the package implementation is access to the selected event pair, inputs, terrain and diagnostic margins. Agreement with historical simulation tables measures implementation agreement. Estimating the probability of real crescent detection requires observations independent of the rule used to select it.

title: 11  Identifying celestial candidates and limiting declinations
text:
11.1 Construct the search band
Build 2.0.9009 uses annual local solar and lunar limits for dated overlays and compares target ranges before rounding. A08 reproduces the earlier range discrepancy and checks the correction.
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/data-analysis.R, R/events.R, R/horizon.R, R/mechanics.R, R/misc.R and R/stars.R. A field sightline defines a range of possible declinations. The relevant question is which celestial targets enter that band during the archaeological date range, and which could actually have been seen from that viewpoint. The first question can be computed before tackling the second. Silva & Lomsdalen (2025, table 5) illustrate this distinction when screening stellar candidates for the Maltese temples (Silva and Lomsdalen 2025).
For geometric altitude hh above the astronomical horizontal, true bearing AA and latitude ϕ\phi, sinδ=sinϕsinh+cosϕcoshcosA\sin\delta=\sin\phi\sin h+\cos\phi\cos h\cos A (Silva 2020, eq. 1). Use the density chapter when uncertainty across bearings or skyline heights changes the resulting distribution. Decide whether the search interval is an architectural opening, a highest-density region, or a cluster identified in a significance test. These represent different quantities. If several high-density regions are disjoint, search them separately; taking only the smallest and largest endpoints would admit targets in the intervening gaps. A declination band also loses the distinction between the eastern and western branches of a track.
hor2max.dec() searches bearings in a sector of half-width range around north; hor2min.dec() searches around south. In each case the step is 0.01° and the default half-width is 25°. The routines pass the sampled bearings and skyline to az2dec() and return the extreme of the resulting declinations. With a scalar latitude they instead use the supplied constant altitude. On a level horizon at 40° N with refraction off, the meridian extrema are ±50°. The following synthetic horizon keeps the meridians level but puts a ridge at bearings 10–12°.
The wider search picks up the northern ridge. A meridian-only calculation misses more than ten degrees of accessible declination here. These are sampled terrain sightline limits. The default restricted sectors do not guarantee global extrema on every possible skyline.

title: 11  Identifying celestial candidates and limiting declinations
text:
11.2 Solar and lunar reference limits
Let ϵ(y)\epsilon(y) be the true obliquity obtained from Swiss Ephemeris for the year’s January reference instant. With no site supplied, jS() and dS() return +ϵ+\epsilon and −ϵ-\epsilon; eq() returns zero. These are reference declinations. An equinox instant, the Sun’s position at sunrise on the equinox date, and the eastern spatial midpoint of the solstitial bearings at a particular site are three distinct quantities (Ruggles 1997; Astrodienst, n.d.).
The standstill construction adopts i*=5.145°+0.145°i_*=5.145°+0.145°. Before local parallax the northern major and minor limits are ϵ+i*\epsilon+i_* and ϵ−i*\epsilon-i_*; the southern values have the opposite signs. These are the four functions nMjLX(), nmnLX(), sMjLX() and smnLX(). The distinction between a theoretical lunar extreme and an observed Moon is central to archaeological interpretation (Šprajc 2016). The fixed additional term is a skyscapeR implementation choice. The model does not search the lunar ephemeris for an extremum at a particular lunation.
With a site supplied the limit functions subtract the approximate signed correction pcos(h)sin(ϕ)p\cos(h)\sin(\phi), with pp the adopted horizontal parallax (default lunar value 0.952°, solar value 0.00224°). Report the altitude, site and convention when comparing a local limit with a point in a catalogue. The worked 2026 geocentric values are ±23.43813° for the solstices, ±28.72813° for the major lunar extremes and ±18.14813° for the minor ones.
zenith() and antizenith() use ϕ\phi and −ϕ-\phi as the geometrical reference declinations and apply the specified parallax correction. Solar passage eligibility is checked against the solstitial limits using the session’s default epoch; neither function accepts the dating interval of a target search. This matters near the tropical boundary. spatial.equinox() is instead explicitly horizon- and epoch-dependent; the event chapter explains its first-emergence and final-disappearance rule.

title: 11  Identifying celestial candidates and limiting declinations
text:
11.3 Candidate screening by family
findTargets() receives a closed declination band and one year or an inclusive range. For generic candidate bounds [d1,d2][d_1,d_2] and measurement bounds [L,U][L,U], overlap requires d1≤Ud_1\leq U and d2≥Ld_2\geq L. The implementation does not construct or search every family in exactly the same way.



Candidate
Construction and resolution




Sun
Solstitial limits are evaluated by year. Astronomical equinox is a zero-declination entry; equinox and solstice labels use the endpoint years’ apparent solar longitudes. The generic sunrise/set row samples the declination band at 0.01° and solves for solar civil dates in the endpoint years. Those are declination-date windows, not timed local skyline crossings.


Spatial equinox
Requires a horizon. Collect finite eastern and western midpoint declinations at the two endpoint epochs, then take the enclosing range. The envelope can include intermediate declinations that correspond to neither side, and an intermediate epoch can behave differently. Check east and west individually for a specific sightline.


Moon
Test the four analytical standstill ranges across the years. In this build the solar and lunar output limits are rounded to 0.01° before the final overlap filter. Recompute a marginal match near a boundary. EFM and crescent distributions are separate searches in the crossover chapter.


Stars and catalogue objects
Apply the catalogue V-magnitude cutoff (default 2.5), compute declination at noon UT on 1 January Gregorian in every year, and test overlap before rounding. With dates = TRUE, intersect each successive line segment with the band, merge contiguous intersections and round boundaries to whole years. Separate passages remain separate.



Worked screening example. For a hypothetical band of −1.5° to +0.2° in 2020–2026, the magnitude-2.5 search returns the astronomical equinox and a stellar match for Alnilam (ε Ori, catalogue V = 1.69; declination −1.19° to displayed precision). The solar date windows are 16–21 March and 22–26 September. Those alternatives survive the same declination filter. Which branch is visible, at what altitude, during which season and in what light must be assessed separately.
x <- findTargets(c(-1.5, 0.2), year = c(2020, 2026),
                 max.mag = 2.5, dates = TRUE)
x$solar
x$stellar
Prehistoric date window. In a second illustration the input years are 3500–3400 BCE, and the band is −7.65° to −7.55°. Aldebaran’s annual declinations span −7.85° to −7.29° across the full century. The reported overlap is only 3464–3446 BCE. The wide numerical bounds returned for the star describe its whole search-period track, whereas daterange reports when it crosses the narrower input band. This teaching band was deliberately centred on Aldebaran near the middle of the interval. Recovering the star here is no evidence for its selection by ancient observers.



Annual barycentric declinations of Aldebaran over a century, with the narrower input band shaded.


At archaeological timescales the annual grid is convenient for screening. Subannual excursions, catalogue completeness, stellar variability, extinction and local visibility are outside the overlap calculation. An integrated cluster entry can meet the magnitude cutoff even though individual stars have different detectability. Preserve the band, dating evidence, catalogue identifier, magnitude threshold and branch; check the candidate with star.phases(), riseset() and sketchSky() as appropriate. Screening a band selected after inspection remains exploratory.

section: 11.4 Overlays, fixed tracks and version-specific limits
text:
11.4 Overlays, fixed tracks and version-specific limits
skyObject() prepares named targets or numerical declinations for a plot. sky.objects() is its compatibility alias. It can expand “solar extremes” and “lunar extremes”, retain graphic styles and carry different epochs for different groups. The horizon plot supplies the site for its tracks; the compass plot uses the object’s stored location and a level horizon. A declination plot needs no location. A plotted track keeps its declination fixed through a diurnal rotation. For an instant-specific comparison use body.position() in the desired frame and pass its numerical declination to the overlay.
There is a consequential difference between the range algorithms. A stellar overlay takes the range of annual January samples. For a varying solar or lunar limit the 2.0.9004 range helper samples from the first year in 100-year steps, fits a spline and evaluates it across the requested interval. A short interval can therefore have just one source sample. For skyObject("June Solstice", c(2020, 2026)) the returned bounds are both 23.43621°, whereas the direct 2026 geocentric value is 23.43813°. The range helper also defaults to geocentric evaluation for these named limits when called from the two-epoch overlay. This is a reason to compute the underlying limits directly for the required sites and years before using a narrow overlay to classify a borderline match. The choice of a finer plotted grid cannot supply missing input epochs.
The strength of this workflow is traceability from an archaeological band through candidate dates to a site-specific reconstruction. Its output is a set of compatible geometries; it supplies neither a probability of target identity nor a correction for searching many stars, time ranges or subsections of the data. Matched comparisons of range envelopes against direct calculations and independent evidence of observational visibility remain separate tasks. Reproduce the target and crossover examples.
