title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
12.1 Random orientations
Specified-model calibration and Maltese reconstructions.
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/statistics.R and R/model-simulation.R. The procedures below operate on a summed probability density (SPD) of measured orientations. Silva (2020, sec. 4) introduced the random-orientation test. Silva and Lomsdalen (2025, “Methodology” and “Landscape tests”) extended the framework to specified landscape and astronomical hypotheses, including models particular to individual sites. The two functions answer different questions even when they score exactly the same observed curve.
For the construction of the empirical and transformed measurement curves, see the density chapter.
See the independent checks on build 2.0.9005 for results and limitations.
randomTest() asks whether independent draws of structural bearings, with the observed sample size, measurement errors and site geometry, could produce departures at least as large as those observed. Randomness is specified in azimuth. A uniform distribution of bearings generally induces a non-uniform distribution of declinations. Even on a level horizon, the mapping from bearing to declination has turning points; terrain relief changes the mapping further (Silva 2020, secs 3–4).
Each replicate samples one centre per measurement, uniformly with replacement on the source bearing grid in [0°, 360°). Build 2.0.9007 reconstructs each density with its source width, family, grid spacing and cutoff. On the shared-horizon route the observed and simulated azimuth sums use the same .res before transformation. S01 reports false positives, power and the consequences for earlier fits.
The second route constructs one aggregate before transformation. The third preserves the contribution of each site’s skyline and measurement uncertainty through the transformation. Report the route used: with differences in interpolation, truncation and site geometry, the two routes need not return identical curves. Optional normalisation gives each final SPD unit trapezoidal area. It cannot correct a misassigned horizon.

title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
Input
What is compared




Azimuth PDF, no horizon
Sum the reconstructed densities in azimuth. Use this route for a hypothesis about the distribution of bearings around the compass.


Azimuth PDF and one shared horizon
Sum in azimuth, then transform the SPD to declination using the common site. The transformation takes the current atmospheric settings.


Transformed declination PDF, original azimuth PDF and horizon(s)
Start each simulated measurement in azimuth, transform it individually with the matching horizon and the saved atmospheric settings, then sum. The original measurements and horizons must correspond in order.

title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
12.2 Specified orientation models
modelTest() asks whether the observed curve is compatible with a proposed distribution. Silva and Lomsdalen (2025) constructed site-specific slope-aspect models from terrain around the Maltese temples and a shared wind model from reversed wind-direction frequencies. The innovation of that paper was the capacity to test specified alternatives to uniform bearings, including site-specific ones. The general function accepts the resulting distributions; generating and justifying the landscape or astronomical model remains the analyst’s responsibility.
The empirical PDF sets the coordinate system. Supply one table for a common model or one table per observation in matching order. A row gives a candidate angle and a nonnegative weight. Sampling probabilities are proportional to the weights. For a continuous density tabulated on an uneven grid, a cell’s weight should approximate its integrated mass, for example density times represented cell width. Using its ordinate alone can favour a densely sampled sector for purely numerical reasons.
Each replicate draws a centre for each observation. Build 2.0.9008 also reuses the source grid and cutoff for directly constructed densities. Directly constructed PDFs retain any of the six measurement families. Both tests preserve each observation’s taper, Gaussian survey error or triangular asymmetry in simulations. For a direct triangle each candidate is a mode. Overriding unc in modelTest() rescales both sides of the triangle in proportion. For the softened uniform families the taper or survey-error SD remains fixed in degrees. For a declination PDF from coordtrans(), the default instead translates each piecewise-linear measurement curve. If fif_i is the stored density and mi=∫xfi(x)dx/∫fi(x)dxm_i=\int x f_i(x)\,dx/\int f_i(x)\,dx, a candidate cic_i produces the template fi(x−ci+mi)f_i(x-c_i+m_i). Its width, asymmetry and multiple peaks survive translation before grid interpolation. A positive-weight candidate that would push density outside ±90° causes an error. An explicit unc for transformed input selects a normal simulation density. A translated template assumes that the original shape applies at the new mean; a different skyline sector may produce a different shape. This is a modelling choice worth testing when the result depends on it.

title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
12.3 Shared scoring algorithm
Let Y0(x)Y_0(x) be the observed SPD and Y1,…,YBY_1,\ldots,Y_B the simulated SPDs on a common grid. At each xx, all B+1B+1 values define the sample standard deviation s(x)s(x) and quantile bounds. For a two-tailed 95% envelope, the bounds L,UL,U are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. For an upper-tail 95% envelope, use the 95th percentile alone. The implementation calls R’s default sample quantile. Every curve is scored against these same bounds. For a two-tailed test the unsigned contribution is
dj(x)=max(Yj(x)−U(x),0)+max(L(x)−Yj(x),0)s(x).d_j(x)=\frac{\max(Y_j(x)-U(x),0)+\max(L(x)-Y_j(x),0)}{s(x)}.
Set the contribution to zero where all curves agree; omit the lower term in an upper-tail test. Only strict crossings contribute. If the simulations agree but the observation differs, pooling keeps the observed departure eligible and the fit records that angle in constant.departures. The global score is Tj=∑xdj(x)T_j=\sum_x d_j(x). It is a grid sum: keep grid spacing fixed across curves. The defaults are 0.1° for randomTest() and 0.01° for modelTest(). Both default to 1,000 simulations, two tails, 95% pointwise coverage and no final normalisation.
For the global test let bb be the number of simulated scores greater than or equal to T0T_0. The returned value is (b+1)/(B+1)(b+1)/(B+1) (North, Curtis, and Sham 2002; Dufour 2006). At B=1000B=1000, zero exceedances gives 1/10011/1001; complete ties give 1. Exchangeability requires that the observed and simulated datasets be processed comparably under the specified null. More simulations improve rank resolution. They cannot repair a null that ignores dependence among structures.
For a local result, find contiguous crossings of the same bound with at least two grid points spanning at least 0.5°. Sum the departures within each observed cluster. Repeat the cluster search in every simulation and retain its largest cluster score, or zero if none qualifies. Compare each observed cluster with these simulated maxima using the same inclusive rank. A two-tailed search includes both signs. The global test uses all departures, including those too narrow for local reporting. The local correction accounts for searching this grid under the complete null; it does not locate an individual significant endpoint or adjust for comparing many archaeological subsets (Maris and Oostenveld 2007; Sassenhagen and Draschkow 2019). Through 2.0.9005, north-crossing clusters were split at the stored seam. Build 2.0.9006 joins adjacent excesses or deficits across north in both the observations and simulations, and excludes a duplicate north direction from the global score. A reported interval with start greater than end crosses north clockwise. See the fixed-input S03 replay.

title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
12.4 What changed since the publications?








Decision
Published baseline
Version 2.0.9004 and consequence




Reference envelope and global departure
Silva (2020, §4) describes the departure as area. Its accompanying R script already standardises departures using the mean, standard deviation and quantiles of the simulations alone. The Malta application invokes this framework.
The observation enters the pooled bounds and scale exactly once, alongside the simulations. Each excursion is divided by the pooled pointwise standard deviation. A given density excess can therefore contribute differently at a low-variance angle and a high-variance angle.


Monte Carlo tail
Silva (2020, eq. 2) prints a leading complement with rr defined as the number of simulated scores at least as large as the observation. With that definition the printed expression reverses the desired tail. The paper already cites North et al. (2002).
Both routines explicitly count exceedances including ties and return (b+1)/(B+1)(b+1)/(B+1). A large observed departure with few exceedances gives a small p-value. The archived 2020 script instead complements a count of scores strictly below the observation. Algebraically this yields b/(B+1)b/(B+1) before rounding, so zero was possible. The current formula guarantees a positive attainable minimum.


Local selection
Silva (2020, §4) compares the observed region with simulations scored over that same observed interval. Silva & Lomsdalen (2025) report local results within this framework.
Each simulation now undergoes its own interval search. Its maximum cluster supplies the comparator, which accounts for choosing the region after viewing the curve. Earlier and current local p-values answer different questions.


Non-uniform nulls and uncertainty
The 2025 application already used shared and site-specific models, drew an azimuth from the appropriate model, and assigned the structure’s measurement uncertainty.
The reusable interface accepts weighted candidates in either tested coordinate. For transformed declinations it can preserve a measured template, including asymmetry, with an explicit alternative using a specified uncertainty. The template route generalises the published azimuth procedure.



The accompanying 2020 code also permuted the measurement uncertainties in the random draws and excluded observed intervals of width at most five times its declination-grid spacing. Version 2.0.9004 retains the observation-to-uncertainty pairing and applies a fixed angular minimum to both observed and simulated clusters. Standardisation itself was already present in 2020; symmetric pooling and searching each simulated curve are the substantive changes. The source comparison uses the archived 2020 implementation, lines 300–382. These comparisons concern the published algorithms and the archived current source. They do not establish that the conclusions of either paper change. That would require replaying the corresponding data, models and historical implementation. The build’s NEWS instructs users to refit when seeking current local and global inference (Silva 2020; Silva and Lomsdalen 2025).

title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
12.5 Reading a fit
Consider 999 simulations and an observed global score exceeded or tied by 9 simulated curves. The global p-value is 10/1000 = 0.010. For an observed excess over a particular declination interval, suppose 49 simulations have a cluster anywhere on the searched grid at least that large. Its adjusted local p-value is 50/1000 = 0.050. Comparing only at the observed declinations would answer the different question addressed by the original fixed-interval calculation. These counts are illustrative.
For reproducible comparisons set the seed before fitting and specify the same comparison grid and tail across runs. Read metadata$global.pval for the dataset-wide test and metadata$local.pval for the local intervals. Save metadata$inference and metadata$local.inference with the result. In this build they identify the pooled and maximum-cluster algorithms. The returned envelope and constant-simulation departures are retained in data.

title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
12.6 Reading the Ġgantija worked fit
The vignette loads a saved randomTest() fit with 500 simulations, then uses plot.skyscapeR.sigTest() with show.local=TRUE. Its global p-value is 0.004. In the local table the excess from −33.7° to −28.6° has adjusted p = 0.004, the smaller excess near −49° has adjusted p = 0.557, and the deficit row contains no cluster. The plotted excess and deficit rows share the angular axis with the observed curve; show.pval independently controls display of the global value. print.skyscapeR.sigTest() and pval2stars() summarise these stored probabilities. The open circle marks the larger p-value. Overlaying a Gacrux band or selecting the significant positive interval for findTargets() does not recompute the test or assign a probability to Gacrux as the intended target (Silva 2020; Silva and Lomsdalen 2025).



The saved Ġgantija fit over the declination sector containing both upper excursions. Each local p-value uses the largest cluster score in each simulated curve. Crossing the pointwise envelope at −49° gives little evidence once the search across declinations is included.

title: 12  Testing orientation distributions
text:
12.7 Strengths, limits and evidence
For a simple count in predefined angular bins, R’s chisq.test() accepts category counts and hypothesised probabilities (R Core Team, n.d.). Here the objects being compared are whole measurement-density curves. A doorway spanning a range of bearings can contribute across that range, and a declination null can incorporate the site’s skyline. These are methodological advantages for that question. A small global p-value rejects the specified model; it gives neither the identity of a celestial target nor a probability for intentionality.
Neither routine automatically simulates shared construction episodes, uncertainty in fitted model parameters or selection of sites after inspecting the data. If the null is fitted to the same orientations, its fitting step may need to be repeated within simulations. Interpret interval boundaries as descriptions of the observed excursions. Retain the input PDFs, site order, model tables, seed, grid, inference metadata and package revision. Sampling takes place in the caller so that the same seed can be used across worker counts.
The archived package audit checks a saved Ġgantija result and the plotting of local findings. It checks reproducibility of a recorded result, not the family-wise rejection rate over independent datasets. The outstanding validation is to measure rejection rates under known generating models, varying sample size, horizon heterogeneity, the north seam and grid spacing. No historical or new significance fits were run for this manual revision.
Related function entries

Maris, Eric, and Robert Oostenveld. 2007. ‘Nonparametric Statistical Testing of EEG- and MEG-Data’. Journal of Neuroscience Methods. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jneumeth.2007.03.024.

title: 13  Sky reconstruction and visual radiance
text:
13.1 Geometry and state
Implementation. skyscapeR 2.0.9004, R/sketchSky.R, R/light-budget.R and R/galactic.R. A site reconstruction asks two distinct questions: where does a body appear relative to the skyline, and what light reaches the corresponding part of the sky? The plotting stage consumes their results. This distinction matters when a feature remains geometrically above the terrain but fades into the twilight background.
sketchSky() takes a georeferenced horizon and an instant. Record the calendar and timezone when specifying civil time. It resolves astronomical positions at the site using the epoch-appropriate ephemeris and captures the session’s refraction, pressure and temperature settings. The horizontal frame uses true azimuth clockwise from north. The resulting object can be replotted for another sector without moving the sky in time. Recompute the instant with skyStep() for a time sequence. See the ephemeris chapter for file coverage, time scales and the scope of the upstream precision claim.
Natural mode is the default. Stars, the Sun and the Moon are enabled by default; planets require their switch. The Milky Way switch follows the stars unless set explicitly. Turning the Moon off removes its disc and its illumination. A ridge occulting the disc in the plotted scene can still leave scattered moonlight. The constellation geometry section describes the endpoint selection.

title: 13  Sky reconstruction and visual radiance
section: 13.2 Linear radiance and the rendered pixel
text:
13.2 Linear radiance and the rendered pixel
A source of visual magnitude mm has relative flux 10−0.4m10^{-0.4m}. For extinction coefficient kk in magnitudes per airmass, direct flux is attenuated by 10−0.4kX(h)10^{-0.4kX(h)}, with X(h)X(h) the Rozenberg airmass approximation used in the package (Schaefer 1986; Krisciunas and Schaefer 1991, eq. 14). This uses altitude above the horizontal. It is the terrain that determines whether a rendered line of sight is blocked. Near the horizon, actual extinction is particularly sensitive to local conditions.
Stars remain unresolved as the field is enlarged. Planetary and lunar contributions use apparent size and illumination from Swiss Ephemeris. For a cluster with an integrated catalogue magnitude, the renderer subtracts light already assigned to plotted stars inside its projected footprint before distributing the residual glow. This avoids double-counting projected light; membership and individual detectability require different evidence (Crumey 2014). Source sizes and attributions are recorded in the package help and inst/COPYRIGHTS.
For a natural sketch, skyRadiance() samples the unmasked field as magnitude-zero flux per square degree. It returns total, direct-source and Milky Way matrices; subtracting the latter two from the total gives the atmospheric component. Pixel solid angle varies with altitude. For an azimuth width ΔA\Delta A in radians and altitude limits h1,h2h_1,h_2, its solid angle is ΔA(sinh2−sinh1)\Delta A(\sin h_2-\sin h_1) steradians. Convert to square degrees before multiplying the returned surface brightness by area and summing to recover source flux. The Sun’s disc is drawn separately as an overlay.
The natural display combines the components before adapting to background brightness, compressing the brightness range and converting to screen colour. Directly comparing RGB values across zoom levels would mix photometry with pixel area and display mapping. The publication styles instead draw magnitude-scaled symbols. In 2.0 development the natural renderer adopted a shared light budget; historical experiments using the development-only model switch should be replayed with their archived source. The study register identifies the tested build for each result.

title: 13  Sky reconstruction and visual radiance
text:
13.3 Twilight and moonlight
The adopted zenith curve uses Paranal V-band photometry at solar depressions of 5–15°, with tabulated anchors and interpolation outside that interval (Patat, Ugolnikov, and Postylyakov 2006). Directional structure uses Sacramento Peak photometry (Koomen et al. 1952). The implementation interpolates log brightness ratios across viewing altitudes and solar-altitude samples, then blends the solar and antisolar directions with weight (1+cosΔA)/2(1+\cos\Delta A)/2. This yields a continuous azimuthal field that agrees at the zenith. The transition to the daytime gradient is a separate modelling choice. Moonlight uses the phase, altitude and angular scattering dependence in Krisciunas and Schaefer (1991). Twilight colours remain illustrative; local aerosol and atmospheric structure are not reconstructed from the site coordinates (Lee 1994, 2015).

title: 13  Sky reconstruction and visual radiance
section: 13.4 Milky Way boundary, internal structure and calibration
text:
13.4 Milky Way boundary, internal structure and calibration
The outer envelope comes from a tracing of diffuse light in Deep Star Maps 2020 (Wright 2020). Within it the package retains dark patches with at least 10% local contrast and uses brightness tiers at 1.10 and 1.75 times mean band tone after exclusion of dark patches. Retained patches cover at least 10 square degrees. These thresholds classify an image; they are not physiological visibility thresholds. For an alignment defined by the outer boundary, an enclosed dark patch remains inside the band. For visual reconstruction, the internal dark and bright structure matters and is displayed.
The implemented relative intensities are 0 outside the band, 1 for ordinary band, 0 for the dark class, and 1.35 and 2.1 for the two bright classes. These are provisional rendering weights. Atmospheric background can still contribute light in a dark-class pixel. The surface-brightness scale is anchored to a four-degree Carina field at 20.7 V mag arcsec⁻² (Kruit 2024). Normalisation in that field constrains the adopted scale, not every direction around the Galaxy. The direct atmospheric transmission is evaluated separately for the displayed altitude, so a geometrically predicted crossing can be difficult to follow near the skyline. A plotted Galactic equator and an outer Milky Way edge represent different sightlines.

13.4.1 Reading the traced boundary
The tracing starts from the celestial-coordinate diffuse-light image in Deep Star Maps 2020, with bright foreground stars omitted (Wright 2020). On a 0.25° Galactic grid, the tracing script smooths image tone to 1° FWHM. At each longitude it estimates background tone from latitudes 35°–50° on either side of the plane and bright-band tone from the 90th percentile within 12° of the plane. Both longitude series are median-filtered over approximately 5°. For background BB and bright-band tone PP, the selected contour level is B+0.35(P−B)B+0.35(P-B). The algorithm keeps the main connected body across the longitude seam, fills enclosed holes, then smooths the envelope mask at 4° FWHM.



The same Galactic directions appear in each row. The turquoise line traces the deployed outer envelope. The third row shows the five classes assigned by build 2.0.9004. The bottom row renders the intrinsic diffuse component on a common linear grey scale, using the package’s relative intensities 0, 1, 0, 1.35 and 2.1. Atmospheric attenuation and screen adaptation enter later. Dark lanes remain inside the outer edge even where their assigned diffuse flux is zero. Source map: Ernie Wright, NASA/Goddard SVS; ESA/Gaia/DPAC (Wright 2020).


The anticentre band narrows at higher contrast cuts, but the same change also removes much of the extended bulge on the centre side. The adopted 35% cut preserves that structure using one rule around the full circumference. The 45% and 55% candidates below document the trade-off. The source image used to choose the edge cannot independently validate it.


Original centre and anticentre contrast comparisons




Galactic centre. The 35%, 45% and 55% contours are shown on the same source image and exposure.





Galactic anticentre. Compare the contraction of the band at higher cuts with the loss of the extended centre bulge in the preceding figure.





13.4.2 How the Carina field fixes the intensity scale
The implementation in R/light-budget.R samples a circle of radius 2° centred at Galactic (l,b)=(287°,−2°)(l,b)=(287°,-2°) on a 0.1° grid. Let qiq_i be the relative intensity of the class at sample ii. The mean q‾=∑iqicosbi/∑icosbi\bar q=\sum_i q_i\cos b_i/\sum_i\cos b_i accounts for the area represented by each Galactic latitude row. The intrinsic brightness assigned to class jj, in magnitude-zero flux per square degree, is
Bj=qj3600210−0.4(20.7)q‾.B_j=q_j\,\frac{3600^2\,10^{-0.4\,(20.7)}}{\bar q}.
The factor 360023600^2 converts square arcseconds to square degrees. This construction makes the field mean reproduce the adopted Carina brightness (Kruit 2024, table 3). A comparison in the same field therefore checks the normalisation. Independent photometry elsewhere is needed to assess the extrapolation. In the renderer, the Galactic class is looked up along the geometrical direction corresponding to the displayed pixel, and its brightness is multiplied by transmission at the displayed altitude. This explains how the outline can retain the same geometrical extent while a low-altitude section loses visual contrast. The study register distinguishes the traced boundary, measured twilight comparisons, flux recovery and extinction checks.

title: 13  Sky reconstruction and visual radiance
text:
13.5 Constellation selection and planisphere geometry
In sketchSky(), a constellation selection can identify a set, a named figure, a stable identifier such as CHN009, or a table from importConstellations(). Supplying the selection enables constellation lines unless the line switch is explicitly set. A legacy Stellarium FAB row gives one figure identifier, a segment count and two positive HIP identifiers per segment. The importer rejects malformed counts and duplicate figure IDs. It returns a reusable table of connections. The catalogue supplies the stellar positions. A magnitude cut on star symbols does not remove a valid line endpoint. A missing catalogue endpoint limits what can be drawn. The modern and Chinese mansion selections in the vignette can therefore be compared using exactly the same sky. For attribution use the source of the selected sky culture (Stellarium contributors, n.d.).
planisphere() projects those connections on a different surface. With pole sign p=+1p=+1 in the northern hemisphere (including the equator), or −1-1 in the southern hemisphere, radius is 90°−pδ90°-p\delta, plotted angle follows pαp\alpha, and the outer radius is 180°−|ϕ|180°-|\phi|. Between distinct endpoints the code samples the shorter great-circle arc at intervals of at most about 0.2°, then clips the projected line to the accessible sky. Coincident endpoints can denote a single marker. Optional equatorial, ecliptic and Galactic reference curves have distinct geometries. The observer’s terrain profile, timestamp and atmospheric brightness do not enter this chart. Record the epoch, latitude, magnitude cut, figure set and enabled layers when comparing it to a dated sketch.

title: 13  Sky reconstruction and visual radiance
section: 13.6 Display styles, capture and stepping time
text:
13.6 Display styles, capture and stepping time
A natural sketchSky() uses enabled luminous sources and their atmospheric contributions. The publication-colour and publication-mono styles show positions with magnitude-scaled symbols. The catalogue filter max.mag acts before atmospheric dimming and leaves constellation endpoints, the Sun, Moon and planets outside that cut. In a natural sketch, turning the Sun or Moon off also removes its contribution to illumination. The stellar layer sets the default for the Milky Way unless milky.way is explicitly supplied. The ecliptic, celestial and Galactic equators, poles and zenith are independent guides.
stellariumSky() freezes the external application’s clock and captures a full-sphere Cylinder Fill raster. The seam is north, the centre south and the horizontal midline is zero altitude. A 30° crop of a 4096-pixel capture contains approximately 341 source pixels. Zooming into a saved raster cannot add stellar detail. Record Stellarium version, catalogue, selected sky culture and display switches. The capture defaults leave landscape and fog off. Other omitted switches can depend on the existing application state (Stellarium contributors, n.d.).
skyStep() computes JD′=JD+𝚖𝚒𝚗𝚞𝚝𝚎𝚜/1440JD'=JD+\texttt{minutes}/1440. For a native sketch it rebuilds the sky using its stored calendar, style, magnitude limit, extinction coefficient and display selection. It reads refraction, pressure and temperature again from the current session. For a Stellarium sky it requests another screenshot with the saved capture settings. In both cases assign the invisibly returned object before stepping again. Drawing another sector at the same instant only requires replotting. Doorway edge lines added to the graphics device must be redrawn after the new plot.

title: 13  Sky reconstruction and visual radiance
text:
13.7 Comparative strengths and outstanding issues
Stellarium provides an interactive planetarium with navigable sky, exchangeable sky cultures and landscape visualisation (Stellarium contributors, n.d.). For an archaeological analysis, the specific advantage of skyscapeR is the ability to use the same R horizon and instant for the geometry, inspect the separate radiance components, and archive the inputs and calculation alongside the figure. No matched comparison in the register establishes photometric superiority over Stellarium. A screenshot can check gross appearance; validation of angular position, diffuse brightness or human detection requires a reference appropriate to that quantity.
The study register reports the held-out twilight comparisons, the Sirius flux check and the differential extinction calculation. Independent measurements of the outer boundary and of surface brightness away from Carina remain outstanding.

15.1.3 body.position()
A02 validation. In A02, file-backed geocentric directions for ten bodies agreed with their matching JPL parent to within 0.0065 arcseconds across 1,080 comparisons. At the sampled prehistoric epochs the public topocentric convention differed from JPL Horizons by up to 0.70 degrees in local sky direction at a specified instant. Geocentric and local position results.
Function index
An alignment comparison needs an epoch, a reference frame and, for a local sightline, a
site. Character times are converted to UT Julian dates using the selected calendar and
timezone; numeric times are already UT Julian dates. Swiss Ephemeris supplies right
ascension and declination. Without a site the function uses the geocentric frame. With a
site it can use a topocentric position and convert to local azimuth and altitude. A
vector of times is evaluated one instant at a time and returned in input order.

Only the horizon object's location is used; its altitude profile is not used
to determine whether the body is visible above the terrain. With a location,
horizontal altitude is apparent when refraction is TRUE and geometric when
FALSE. Azimuth is measured clockwise from north.

Astrodienst. Swiss Ephemeris programmer's manual. https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm.

Validation on 2.0.9005. Build 2.0.9005 passed all 499 calendar, clock, era, angle and setting checks in A01. The largest discrepancy across 240 absolute Julian dates was 0.000021 seconds. A01 results.
Function index
An instant is specified by its UT Julian date. To label it consistently, choose the
calendar and the offset or civil timezone appropriate to the record. The conversion
rounds to the nearest second, applies the offset at the rounded instant, handles day
rollover and converts the day number with Swiss Ephemeris.

Fixed offsets may be numeric hours east of UTC (for example 5.5), or
strings such as "UTC+05:30", "UTC-02" or "GMT+01".
Offsets must lie between -14 and +14 hours. UTC, GMT and the empty string
mean zero offset; an empty string does not select the system timezone.

Interpretation and limits. For an ancient event near local midnight, retain the UT Julian day alongside the printed date. Round-tripping a civil label tests conversion conventions; it cannot establish the prehistoric difference between terrestrial and rotational time.

Function index
Civil dates require both a calendar and a time convention to specify an instant. The
function parses each supplied date and time, verifies that the calendar date exists by
converting it to a Julian date and back, then applies the chosen offset or civil
timezone to obtain UT. A date without a time uses local midnight. Astronomical year
numbering includes year zero. An era label can also precede the month, for example
"3700 BCE/06/21".

Fixed offsets may be numeric hours east of UTC (for example 5.5), or
strings such as "UTC+05:30", "UTC-02" or "GMT+01".
Offsets must lie between -14 and +14 hours. UTC, GMT and the empty string
mean zero offset; an empty string does not select the system timezone.

15.2 Reducing field observations
The reduced true bearing depends on which direction or solar limb was observed, when it was observed and whether a magnetic correction was supplied. A field reduction and a test of the subsequent skyline have different reference data.

15.2.1 mag.dec()
Function index
Compass reduction depends on when and where the reading was taken. The function
evaluates IGRF-14 through oce at sea level and returns east-positive declination.
Supply a single site for several dates, a single date for several sites, or
one date per site. Results follow input order. Other size combinations raise
an error. The calendar date is converted to a decimal year using the actual
length of that year at midnight UTC. Supported dates run from 1 January 1900
through 1 January 2030 inclusive. Site elevation is ignored by this model call.



Method references

Kelley, D. and Richards, C. oce: magneticField. https://dankelley.github.io/oce/reference/magneticField.html.





Interpretation and limits. An externally supplied magnetic correction and a modelled IGRF value are alternative inputs. Keep the correction’s sign, survey date and origin with the field data. Agreement with a regional magnetic model does not rule out local disturbance at the instrument.

15.2.2 reduct.compass()
W02 checked north-crossing magnetic readings against the supplied corrections before passing true bearings into a skyline analysis. W02 results.
Function index
Magnetic north differs from true north at the time and place of survey. Add the supplied
magnetic declination to each magnetic bearing, or calculate it from the survey
coordinates and date with mag.dec. Corrected bearings are rounded using the input
bearing representation. With an explicit altitude or a measured horizon, the corrected
bearing also enters the conversion to declination.

Supply either a measurement date or a known magnetic declination.
If both are given, the supplied magnetic declination is used and the date is
retained in the output. Explicit altitude values take precedence over a
horizon profile. Otherwise, each measurement's corrected true azimuth is
used to retrieve its horizon altitude; the same altitude is reported and
used to calculate celestial declination. Supply one site and date for the whole
survey or one location row and/or date per bearing, in measurement order.
A supplied correction can likewise be shared or paired with each bearing.

15.3 Terrain horizons and panoramas
Coordinate reference systems, viewpoint, vertical datum and missing terrain affect the computed skyline. Photographic calibration introduces a separate angular reference. Export, colour and image relinking have different effects from changing the numerical horizon.

15.3.1 createHor()
Function index · H01 field validation · H02 skyline comparison
Measured bearings. To evaluate sightlines between measured bearings, the constructor repeats the azimuths
one turn in each direction, removes duplicate azimuth entries and linearly interpolates
altitude and altitude uncertainty onto a 0.01-degree grid from -90 to 450 degrees.
Scalar uncertainty is repeated. Optional smoothing applies a running mean over the
specified number of grid samples to both series, with zero fill at the outer ends.
Latitude, longitude and elevation identify the observer; omitted elevation defaults to
zero. Interpolation cannot recover narrow features between measurements.

Observer and DEM coverage. For a DEM, supply a point with a CRS, projected x and y with loc.crs, or WGS84 latitude and longitude.
The optional third coordinate is ground elevation in metres in the DEM's vertical
datum. Otherwise ground elevation is bilinearly sampled at the site. Observer
elevation in the returned georeference is ground elevation plus eye.height.
A terrain model represents bare earth. A surface model includes the objects
represented in its elevations. Use a single continuous band in metres with a
defined horizontal CRS. Missing samples and terrain beyond the raster edge are skipped. A warning and the incomplete.bearings metadata identify incomplete coverage. Each bearing needs at least one usable sample.

Accuracy, uncertainty and reproducibility.
H01 compared 334 bearings at 31 observing setups.
At the surveyed bearings, createHor() reproduced the observed terrain skyline to within half a degree in 91.9% of cases.
See the H01 field validation in the skyscapeR technical manual for the survey protocol, station results and limitations.

With the same 1 m terrain, createHor() reproduced Horizon’s skylines to a mean absolute difference of 0.004 degrees at each of two English sites. Against field measurements at 344 Irish bearings, createHor() using SRTM had a mean absolute error of 0.328 degrees, lower than either HeyWhatsThat or PeakFinder on that sample. Field accuracy varied by site. See the H02 comparison in the skyscapeR technical manual.

The numerical skyline is a maximum over sampled terrain, not an accuracy
certificate for the DEM. Horizontal and vertical datum differences, observer
height, missing raster values, vegetation and buildings can exceed the sampling
error. DEM elevations and a supplied observer ground elevation must use a
compatible vertical datum. No geoid conversion or vertical-datum correction is
performed automatically. Refine the angular and distance sampling and expand
the radius until the relevant sightlines are stable. Compare with surveyed
bearings and altitudes where available.

alt.unc is supplied by the user and is not estimated from DEM resolution,
control residuals or atmospheric variability. Smoothing a measured profile can
remove narrow notches or peaks. Adaptive panorama sampling and illustrative
lighting concern the image; they do not increase numerical horizon precision.
The terrestrial refraction approximation assumes the supplied atmosphere and
cannot reproduce all near-ground gradients or mirage conditions.

Save the DEM provenance, observer location and datum, constructor arguments,
feature objects, returned horizon and external PNG. Rebuilding from the same
source is distinct from merely replotting the saved horizon.






Method references

Patat, F. (2011). Horizon synthesis for archaeo-astronomical purposes. Astronomische Nachrichten 332, 743-749. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1002/asna.201111570")}.





Interpretation and limits. A feature height is additional relief on the supplied surface. A bank can be visible below the terrain skyline, so inspect the numerical profile and panorama separately. The H01 field residuals quantify agreement at surveyed terrain bearings. Reconstructed features need their own reference measurements.

The default, "adaptive", starts at one local DEM cell and increases radial spacing with distance using the larger of the requested angular acuity and one horizontal PNG pixel. 15.3.2 createHWT()
Function index
A digital horizon supplies estimated angular obstruction around the site. The
optional httr2 package submits one HTTPS request for a panorama. Once the
service returns its identifier, the function waits two minutes before the first readiness check, then polls at intervals
of up to 15 seconds. The polling deadline defaults to 600 seconds. If the wait
expires, use the identifier with downloadHWT once the panorama is ready.
Individual requests have a timeout of at most 30 seconds. The initial submission
and final download are separate from the polling time allowance. Once ready,
the profile is downloaded and assigned the supplied name. Terrain-derived
profiles need field verification where vegetation or structures affect visibility.



Method references

Interpretation and limits. Separate where a provider actually placed its viewpoint from the coordinate in the request. Record the downloaded profile, reference direction and acquisition date. A provider comparison can mix terrain-source and algorithm differences.

An inland depression below that threshold also receives the water tint.

A panorama describes the horizon seen from a particular observer location. The
optional httr2 package retrieves site metadata and 0.125-degree horizon bins over

session. Read-only downloads allow up to three attempts for transient HTTP
failures, with a 30-second limit per request. For each bin, the distance and
angular altitude determine a height difference. The mean angular change for
height offsets of plus and minus 9.73 metres estimates altitude uncertainty.

The export pairs the profile's azimuth and altitude samples in a polygonal horizon file
and records the site, appearance and attribution in a Stellarium configuration. The

object.

DEM and SVG panoramas use a spherical landscape with the PNG rotated -90
degrees for Stellarium's east-origin mapping. A new PeakFinder import also
records the original ZIP location. If native tiles are requested and that archive still matches its checksum
and contains the supported calibrated eight-tile landscape, Stellarium uses
those original textures and their angular settings instead. The export also
includes the skyscapeR numerical profile and SVG-derived PNG.

15.3.8 hor2alt()
In H07, lookup at each edge of a north-crossing panorama returned its measured altitude and lookup beyond either edge returned NA. H07 results.
Function index
For a horizon constructed from measurements or a DEM, cubic splines interpolate altitude and recorded uncertainty at the requested azimuth. Function index
Reconstructions are explicit hypotheses about additional relief above
the supplied terrain. Heights are added to the existing DEM, including any
surviving remains already represented there. Ditch depths are subtracted.

whose opacity reaches alpha.threshold defines the terrain edge. The

15.3.11 importPeakFinder()
Function index
The numerical horizon describes angular obstruction at the observer's
location. A separate vector drawing supplies foreground detail but does not
explicitly record its vertical angular calibration. Both exports are therefore
needed to create a calibrated panorama PNG. Calculations always use the numerical
horizon, never the PNG. Terrain data do not include every tree or building.

In PeakFinder choose Export, Horizon for Stellarium and save the ZIP. For an
image also choose Export, SVG for printing, Silhouettes (Vector SVG), from 0
to 360 degrees, preferably picture format 16:2. Use exactly the same viewpoint
and observer height for both. Contours (Bitmap SVG) is not supported. The PNG
is a white terrain silhouette with dark foreground ridge lines and transparent
sky, without labels or shading. Only PeakFinder's untransformed M/L vector
path format is supported; edited or future formats may require adaptation.

15.4 From bearings to celestial targets
A target search inherits the uncertainty and coordinate conventions of the original sightline. An extreme found within a restricted bearing sector is conditional on the sector searched.

15.4.1 antizenith()
A05 verified the geometric anti-zenith declination and tropical-boundary eligibility at two epochs. A05 results.
Function index
The direction opposite the zenith corresponds geometrically to minus the site latitude.
Build 2.0.9009 tests the site against the obliquity at the requested epoch. At the geometric anti-zenith, parallax vanishes. It
returns NULL outside that band. This is a target declination for comparison with
orientations, not an observable solar transit below ground.

Interpretation and limits. Record the site’s latitude and the epoch and parallax assumptions used for a solar limit. A returned limit is a geometrical target; an observer still needs an independent reason to regard it as culturally significant.

15.4.2 az2dec()
Function index
The same true bearing can indicate different declinations when the observer or horizon
changes. Supply angular altitude directly or interpolate it from one shared horizon or
one horizon per observation. Numeric latitude inputs imply zero longitude and elevation;
a location matrix can include both. When refraction is enabled, the function adjusts the
input altitude using pressure, temperature and elevation, then calls the inverse Swiss
Ephemeris horizontal transformation. Bearings are clockwise from north; the routine
shifts them to the engine convention and rounds the returned declinations using the
input bearing representation.

Interpretation and limits. A target match inherits the skyline, epoch range and sightline uncertainty used to generate it. The number of plausible candidates also depends on catalogue coverage and the search window.

15.4.3 findTargets()
A08 verified closed-band membership, separate stellar passages, sampled contact, magnitude filtering and comparisons before display rounding. A08 results.
Function index
The search tests overlap in declination. Solar and lunar limiting declinations are
sampled across the years of the interval. Site coordinates enable zenith targets
and a horizon enables the spatial equinox. The named equinoxes and solstices use
geocentric apparent solar longitudes of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees. Dates are UT
civil days in the requested calendar. Different dates for the first and last year
appear in endpoint order separated by a slash. Intermediate years can differ.
The sunrise/set date ranges also use the two endpoint years.
For each star passing the catalogue magnitude cut, the search computes its
declination at noon UT on 1 January Gregorian of every astronomical year,
including both endpoints. It tests overlap before rounding and linearly
interpolates between annual samples to estimate entry and exit. Separate
passages are reported separately, with boundaries rounded to the nearest year.
Shorter variations within a sampling year are unresolved. Magnitude describes
catalogue brightness and does not model atmospheric visibility.

Silva and Lomsdalen (2025, table 5) give an example of stellar target screening for the Maltese temples.



Method references

Silva, F. and Lomsdalen, T. (2025). 'No easy way from the earth to the stars': a new statistical approach to the orientation of the Maltese temples. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 17, 96. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1007/s12520-025-02208-4")}.

Return valueA list of candidate solar, lunar and stellar matches. The tables give target names and declination limits in degrees. Stellar matches also carry catalogue identifiers and visual magnitudes. Set dates to TRUE to request stellar date ranges. A category with no matches may be absent.
Candidate selection and visibilityA match is a declination overlap, not evidence that a celestial object was
visible, deliberately observed or associated with the archaeological feature.
The magnitude filter uses fixed catalogue values; it includes integrated
magnitudes for non-stellar entries such as M45. It does not predict naked-eye
visibility through extinction or twilight, or resolve the members of a cluster.
Choose the dating interval and measurement uncertainty from the archaeological
and survey evidence. Then examine candidate stars with star.phases,
riseset and sketchSky. For a statistically selected
local declination band, candidate screening is exploratory; the significance
of that band does not identify its cause. Physical plausibility and independent
archaeological evidence are separate parts of the interpretation.
Spatial equinox epochsWhen a horizon is supplied, the spatial equinox is evaluated at both endpoints
of the requested year range (once for a single year), with the current atmospheric
settings. The candidate interval spans the finite sunrise and sunset declinations
at those endpoints. This is an endpoint envelope, not an exhaustive search for
intermediate changes of terrain crossing over very long periods. Undefined
crossings generate warnings; if all are undefined, the candidate is omitted.

15.4.9 spatial.equinox()
In A05, rising and setting midpoints matched independent track intersections on flat, eastern-ridge and western-ridge skylines; missing polar crossings were identified. A05 results.
H07 checked that partial photographs are rejected and that a full photographic profile can be used. H07 results.
Function index
A spatial midpoint is defined by the local terrain and need not coincide with the
astronomical equinox. The function uses the positive and negative obliquity at
the requested year as the geocentric solstitial declinations. Each fixed track
is followed through one rotation from lower culmination to lower culmination.
Horizontal solar parallax is applied to geometric altitude before atmospheric
refraction. The terrain is interpolated linearly in azimuth.

On the rising half of each track, the first emergence is selected; on the
setting half, the final disappearance is selected. The circular midpoint of
the two solstitial bearings is then found separately for sunrise and sunset.
At each midpoint, refraction and horizontal parallax are inverted to recover
the geocentric declination. Atmospheric settings are identical in both stages.



Method references

Ruggles, C. L. N. (1997). Whose Equinox? Journal for the History of Astronomy 28, S45-S96. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182869702802205")}.

Return valueA list containing azimuth and declination. Each contains rise and set
values in degrees for the supplied horizon. Declinations are geocentric.
An undefined side returns NA for both values, with a warning; the other side
is retained when defined.
Crossing conventions and limitationsBoth rising and setting tracks are considered in either hemisphere. The
search uses the terrain-aware crossing machinery also used by
riseset, including terrain vertices and interior extrema.
Tangencies without a change of visibility are excluded. Multiple terrain
crossings are resolved using the first-emergence/final-disappearance rule;
this need not be the locally preferred observational definition of sunrise
or sunset. Inspect complex skylines before interpretation.
If either solstitial track lacks the required crossing, the corresponding
midpoint is undefined. This includes polar non-rising/non-setting cases and
complete terrain obstruction. Exactly opposite bearings have no unique
circular midpoint and also return NA.
These are fixed-declination solar-centre tracks, not a dated solar ephemeris
or upper-limb calculation. The mean horizontal parallax is fixed, and the
refraction model cannot represent local atmospheric anomalies. Results are
limited by horizon resolution and atmospheric assumptions. Solar semidiameter
is not included. The result is a spatial midpoint, not the Sun's rising or
setting at the astronomical equinox.

text:
15.5 Solar, lunar and planetary events
Distinguish a geocentric extreme from a topocentric crossing on a particular civil date. Numerical precision in the event search does not fix an uncertain horizon or observer position.

15.5.1 CC()
Function index
Crescent crossovers describe a change in the relative horizon positions
of the luminaries across successive lunations. First (waxing) crescents are
compared at sunset and moonset; last (waning) crescents at sunrise and moonrise.
The method follows Silva and Pimenta (2012), sections 2.1–2.2. Seasons use the
paper's northern-hemisphere names: summer means the June-solstice crossover,
winter the December-solstice crossover, also for southern-hemisphere locations.

For each conjunction, days are searched forwards for the first crescent and
backwards for the last crescent. Visibility is evaluated at sunset or sunrise,
respectively, using Caldwell and Laney's criterion: lower-limb lunar altitude
plus one third of the Sun–Moon angular separation must be at least 11.3 degrees.
The lower-limb altitude is topocentric. The arc of light is the geocentric
Sun–Moon separation, as explicitly defined by Caldwell and Laney; it excludes
atmospheric refraction. The lower limb is calculated from the instantaneous lunar distance
and a lunar radius of 1737.4 km. With refraction enabled, the centre altitude is
apparent and the angular radius is subtracted from it. This is an empirical
visibility prediction, not a guarantee under actual weather or extinction.

Comparison with the original simulations.
For SIM1, 5,024 of 5,136 events in the supplied 1620–2047 series at
latitudes 0, 60 N and 60 S agree within 0.02 degrees in lunar declination.
This comparison uses a level horizon, longitude 0, elevation 400 m, UTC,
Gregorian dates, refraction, pressure 1013.25 mbar and temperature 15 degrees
Celsius. The original 40-degree N series has additional systematic offsets.
Of the 112 discrepancies outside that series, inferred matching dates suggest
differences in the lunation search window and first/last crescent selection.
Some lie close to the visibility threshold. Alternative window and solar-limb
conventions improve some cases but disrupt others that already agree, so no
replacement convention has been adopted. The exact original settings remain
unresolved; the paper does not specify all atmospheric inputs. Inspect the
diagnostics before interpreting individual events. Agreement with simulation
tables is not independent observational validation, and these SIM1 counts do
not establish the accuracy of SIM2.






Method references

Silva, F. and Pimenta, F. (2012). The Crossover of the Sun and the
Moon. Journal for the History of Astronomy 43(2), 191–208.
\Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182861204300204")}.

Caldwell, J. and Laney, C. D. (2001). First visibility of the lunar crescent.
African Skies 5, 15–23. The authors' online version defines dalt and arcl:
https://astronomycenter.net/pdf/saao_2001.pdf.





Interpretation and limits. The event-selection rules include ordered conditions across solar and lunar events. Use the recorded diagnostics to identify the first condition that differs when comparing with the Silva and Pimenta simulations. A similar terminal azimuth does not establish identical event selection.

15.5.3 EFM()
Function index
Silva and Pimenta (2012) identify the crossover by the first near-full
Moon on the seasonal side of the Sun. Spring and autumn refer to the March
and September equinoxes. At spring moonrise the lunar azimuth must exceed
the solar azimuth, and at spring moonset it must be smaller. Autumn reverses
both inequalities. Bearings are topocentric, clockwise from north.

The search runs chronologically from 60 days before to 65 days after the
astronomical equinox. Moonrise is paired with the first sunrise on the same
local civil date. Moonset is paired with the most recent sunset before it,
considering the first solar centre crossing on the current and preceding
local civil dates. A candidate without such a sunset is skipped. Local-day
boundaries account for timezone changes, including daylight saving time.
A coordinate vector
specifies a level horizon. A horizon object supplies the horizon for both
bodies. Illumination is tested at the lunar event itself. A date qualifies
as soon as the illumination and strict bearing conditions both hold. A
lower illumination threshold can select an earlier lunation. If no date
qualifies the function reports the year and event and stops.

Comparison with the original simulations.
With the corrected preceding-sunset pairing, 2,562 of 2,568 moonsets in
the supplied 1620–2047 series at latitudes 0, 60 N and 60 S agree within
0.02 degrees in lunar declination. The comparison uses a level horizon,
longitude 0, elevation 400 m, UTC, Gregorian dates, geocentric declinations,
refraction, pressure 1013.25 mbar, temperature 15 degrees Celsius and the
default illumination threshold. Five remaining cases lie just above the
0.99 illumination boundary; one lies about 0.002 degrees beyond the azimuth
crossover boundary. The original series selects the following morning in
each case. Thresholds have not been tuned to reproduce those selections.

The original 40-degree N series retains systematic coordinate differences.
Diagnostic comparisons suggest a different coordinate-conversion or timing
convention, but the original settings have not been established. Agreement
with these simulation tables is not independent observational validation.
The paper does not specify all atmospheric settings; the values above describe
this comparison, not confirmed settings of the original simulations.

Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing swephRdata; see skyscapeR-package for setup.




Scope of the event model.
The illumination fraction is a selection criterion, not a naked-eye detection
model. The calculation does not include weather, sky brightness or extinction.
It uses centre crossings rather than the first appearance of the upper limb.
Only the first qualifying event is returned, so changes in illumination
threshold, civil-day convention or horizon can change the selected lunation.
Remaining differences from the original simulations are described above.
Numerical precision does not establish agreement with a published distribution.
Preserve all inputs when comparing series.






Method references

Silva, F. and Pimenta, F. (2012). The Crossover of the Sun and the Moon. Journal for the History of Astronomy 43. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182861204300204")}.

A02 validation. In A02, all 108 illuminated fractions agreed with the direct Swiss Ephemeris calculation across 54 epochs and two file generations. This checks the R interface. Observed lunar photometry was outside the study. Lunar illumination check.

15.5.7 nMjLX()
Function index
A major standstill defines a limiting lunar declination at the epoch of interest. The
model uses the obliquity plus a fixed 5.145 + 0.145 degrees, then applies the positive
sign for the northern limit. With a location it subtracts the parallax correction for
latitude and altitude. The default lunar parallax is 0.952 degrees. This approximation
defines a target limit; it does not search a time series for an actual lunar event.

Sprajc (2016) describes the limits set by obliquity and the mean lunar
inclination. This package also includes the fixed 0.145-degree term above.

Function index

15.5.10 riseset()
H07 verified that a partial panorama is rejected before searching for solar or stellar crossings on an unobserved skyline. H07 results.
A04 recovered the expected crossing counts and order on synthetic ridges, notches and grazing tracks; solar and lunar centre crossings at the Malta test site agreed with JPL Horizons within 0.85 seconds and 0.0041 degrees. A04 results.
A02 validation. A02 tested sensitivity to ephemeris conventions using a separate solver on airless lunar-centre trajectories. Across 177 prehistoric skyline crossings, default azimuths differed from JPL Horizons by a median of 0.059 degrees and a maximum of 0.322 degrees. Matching delta T reduced the maximum to 0.027 degrees. Lunar crossing results.
Function index
The event is a crossing of the local horizon by the body's centre. A raised ridge can
delay the first visible rise and an uneven horizon can give several appearances or
disappearances. Choose the horizon model, atmosphere, calendar and time convention to
match the observation.

Events refer to the centre of the disc. For a Solar System body with a coordinate vector, alt is
one constant horizon altitude and the Swiss Ephemeris rise/set solver is used.
For stars, the daily track is evaluated against the supplied constant altitude or site skyline. With a horizon object, its profile is linearly interpolated in azimuth and
compared with the body's topocentric altitude; do not supply alt as well.
Refraction TRUE uses apparent altitude; FALSE uses geometric altitude. The
constant-altitude solver likewise disables refraction only when FALSE.
For a profile, search the 48 hours after each requested local midnight and
return the first upward and first downward crossing separately. They need
not enclose one continuous visibility interval or occur on the requested day.
Missing crossings return NA fields. A one-minute base grid, quarter-step samples,
azimuth turning points and recursively subdivided rapid azimuth motion bracket visits
to the profile's corners. Each smooth segment is also searched for an interior altitude
extremum, so short emergence/reoccultation pairs need not straddle time samples.
A pure tangency without a sign change is not a rise or set. Horizon altitudes at
0 and 360 degrees must agree. Root tolerance is 0.01 seconds; interior optimization
uses relative seconds to avoid precision loss from large Julian dates.
These settings are not a physical accuracy guarantee: finite precision, unresolved
terrain and near-zenith azimuth singularities limit numerical completeness. The dec argument
controls returned declination, not the topocentric event search.



Method references

Astrodienst. Swiss Ephemeris programmer's manual. https://www.astro.com/swisseph/swephprg.htm.

15.5.13 solar.date()
The JPL comparison in A05 matched all tested civil-day passages, including paired dates near a solstice. A05 results.
Function index
The Sun can pass the same declination on either side of a solstice. The search
covers the selected civil year from midnight UT, including its first instant and
excluding the start of the next year. Daily geocentric apparent solar declinations
bracket the annual turning points. The function refines each extremum against the
ephemeris and solves separately on either side, then reports the civil day of each
crossing. A tangency gives one date. Two crossings can share a calendar day.
The calculation uses no terrain or solar limb model.

Astronomical positions require Swiss Ephemeris files covering the epoch. We
recommend installing swephRdata; see skyscapeR-package for setup.

15.6 Stellar positions and seasonal visibility
Catalogue epoch, atmosphere, skyline and a threshold-based visibility definition enter at different stages. A representative seasonal date is distinct from the time spent above the ridge on that morning.

15.6.1 plot.skyscapeR.starphases()
W01 checked season boundaries, event positions, quarterly landmarks and star, site and epoch labels in linear and circular layouts. W01 results.
Function index
Read each colour as a daily model classification: visible rising and setting, rising
only, setting only, visible without a qualifying near-horizon passage, or invisible. The
function plots the stored phase sequence on a 365-day scale and can label seasons or
display a legend. A single result defaults to a circular view, advancing clockwise
from December solstice. Further results use concentric rings with one leader per displayed layer;
optional sorting uses the stored apparent magnitude or seasonal onset. Changing the
display does not recalculate the visibility thresholds. Use plot(first, list(second, third)) to compare results.

Interpretation and limits. Track clearance, seasonal visibility and the representative Julian date are different outputs. Month and phase labels organise the cycle; deciding whether a star could be detected requires a time interval above the actual skyline.


Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes




Argument
Formal default
Behaviour in this interface




x
—
A star phase result.


y
—
A second object of skyscapeR.starphases format or a list of skyscapeR.starphases objects for plotting (see Examples).


show.labels
TRUE
Logical. Mark annual events for a single result in either layout. Defaults to TRUE.


show.legend
TRUE
Show a legend for seasons present among the plotted stars (default TRUE). For circular plots FALSE also hides titles, site/epoch text and all layer or event callouts. The seasonal scale stays visible. Linear plots keep their data and event labels.


show.grid
TRUE
Draw monthly dividers through each ring or strip. Defaults to TRUE. Set FALSE to omit the monthly divisions and retain the seasonal axis.


sort.by
—
Optional ordering by catalogue magnitude ("mag"), first R-only sample ("rise") or first S-only sample ("set") on the stored cycle. This is not sorting by the dated heliacal event. Missing classes are placed last; omission retains input order.


pal
—
Five colours in the order RS (rise and set), R (rise only), S (set only), V (curtailed passage) and I (arising and lying hidden). The default uses five colours from the plot style. Monochrome adds textures to distinguish the classes. Supply all five even when only some seasons occur.


...
—
Additional arguments to be passed to plot.


layout
c("auto", "linear", "circular")
"auto" and "circular" draw a single ring or concentric rings in input (or requested sort) order from the outside inward. Leaders connect the layer identifiers to their rings. Select "linear" for strips. Supply this argument by name.


style
"publication-colour"
Analytical display style, either "publication-colour" (default) or "publication-mono". Monochrome uses grayscale and preserves line styles.



Return valueDraws on the active graphics device and returns NULL invisibly.
Seasonal axis and comparisonThe axis is a 365-sample synthetic solar-longitude cycle anchored at December
solstice. Equinoxes and solstices mark quarter-cycle positions. The monthly
dividers mark twelve equal intervals of 30 degrees in solar longitude,
beginning at December solstice. For calendar dates use the underlying result's
metadata$events$date.julian, as described in star.phases.
Objects may represent different stars, epochs, sites or model assumptions.
Shared star, epoch and site appear once. Different epochs of the same star label individual rings or rows. Mixed comparisons identify both star and year. Hold the site,
extinction and other inputs fixed for a controlled epoch comparison, or
state their differences in the figure caption. Names on the supplied list can
override the displayed star names. The legend contains only the union of
season classes present in the plotted objects.
Event annotations use transitions between adjacent samples, including the last
and first samples of the cycle. A season continuing through December solstice
has no event at that boundary. Entry into and exit from I mark acronycal
setting and heliacal rising; entry into and exit from V mark acronycal rising
and heliacal setting. Constant classifications have no transition labels.
A single ring labels each event by name on two lines just outside the rim.
Its short leader meets the ring at the event's model day. A single ring shows the star, epoch and site in its centre
and labels the solstices and equinoxes outside its rim. Both layouts mark the event's model day,
the last sample before entry into I or V, or the first after exit.
The linear seasonal scale sits immediately below the lowest strip. Each quarter
label aligns with its solstice or equinox across every row. Rising-event labels
sit close above a single strip and setting-event labels close below it, leaving
room for the seasonal scale where needed. Both layouts use the same
sequence and colours; the circular layout makes the cycle boundary explicit.
Labels wrap and shrink to fit; crowded comparisons need a larger device.

15.6.2 star()
Function index
A historical comparison requires a stellar coordinate for the epoch under study. The
function resolves a Western common name through star.names or accepts a catalogue
identifier and checks it against Swiss Ephemeris. It evaluates equatorial coordinates at
noon UT on 1 January of each supplied astronomical year in the Gregorian calendar. The
magnitude is a catalogue value. These outputs can feed horizon transformations or
visibility estimates, which additionally require observer and atmosphere information.

The Swiss Ephemeris manual documents fixed-star positions and catalogue magnitudes.

15.6.3 star.phases()
W02 replayed the Gacrux heliacal-rising date at Skorba West and passed it to the crossing and sky-reconstruction calculations. W02 results.
Seasonal searches require full skyline coverage. H07 checked rejection of a partial photograph and successful calculation with the full profile. H07 results.
Function index
Seasonal visibility depends on solar depression, stellar altitude, apparent magnitude
and atmospheric extinction as well as terrain. The model holds the star's position fixed
for the chosen year and samples a 365-day solar cycle with uniformly spaced ecliptic
longitudes. It requires a star-Sun altitude separation of 2.1 times the catalogue
magnitude plus 10 degrees, and compares extinction-adjusted magnitude with the limiting
magnitude. A positive-duration overlap of visibility conditions determines the daily
code. The stellar altitude trend within a visible interval below alt.rs determines
rising or setting. Terrain reappearance of a descending star therefore contributes
a setting phase. Disjoint runs are reported as separate seasons on the circular
model year, including runs spanning the December-solstice reference.

Both constant and varying horizons are evaluated on all 365 model days. A horizon
object supplies the coordinates and piecewise-linear horizon. The profile must
cover all bearings and close at north. Use alt.hor only with coordinate input.
A fixed-coordinate stellar track is shared across model days. The terrain search
uses the same corners, azimuth reversals, interior extrema and 0.01-second root
tolerance as riseset, collecting all crossings during the model day.
Visible windows can lie wholly between minute samples. A touch without clearance
contributes no visible duration. Source terrain resolution and numerical tolerances
limit the shortest resolvable window.



Method references

Crumey, A. (2014). Human contrast threshold and astronomical
visibility. MNRAS 442, 2600-2619. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1093/mnras/stu992")}.

Purrington, R. D. (1988). Heliacal Rising and Setting: Quantitative Aspects. Journal for the History of Astronomy 19, S72-S84. https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1988JHAS...19...72P.

Schaefer, B. E. (1986). Atmospheric Extinction Effects on Stellar Alignments. Journal for the History of Astronomy 17, S32-S42. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182868601701003")}.

Schaefer, B. E. (1993). Astronomy and the Limits of Vision. Vistas in Astronomy 36, 311-361. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/0083-6656(93)90113-X")}.

Schaefer, B. E. (1987). Heliacal Rise Phenomena. Journal for the History of Astronomy 18, S19-S33. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1177/002182868701801103")}.

Brady, B. (2015). Star Phases: the Naked-eye Astronomy of the Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts. In F. Silva and N. Campion (eds), Skyscapes: The Role and Importance of the Sky in Archaeology. Oxbow Books, pp. 76-86.

Krisciunas, K. and Schaefer, B. E. (1991). A model of the brightness
of moonlight. PASP 103, 1033-1039 (equation 14 for extinction airmass).
\Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1086/132921")}.

skyscapeR.vars()$k
Visual extinction in magnitudes per airmass (Schaefer 1986, p. S33). The package adopts 0.2 as a clear-sky baseline. Extinction varies with site and atmospheric conditions (Schaefer 1986, 1993). Defaults to the session value from skyscapeR.vars().

1/24/6

Return valueA skyscapeR.starphases list. The data table gives each model day and its phase code: I for invisible, V for visible without a classified rise or set, R for rising, S for setting and RS for both. Metadata include the star, year, observer coordinates, phase type, season and event tables, refraction setting and solar altitude threshold. For a named horizon, metadata$site.name retains the site label for comparisons. The logical metadata$horizon records whether a horizon object was supplied. The separate metadata$horizon.status reports "always above", "always below" or "crosses" relative to the supplied skyline. Event rows include solar.longitude in degrees on the synthetic cycle. The date.julian column gives the representative local Julian calendar date at the supplied longitude. Pass this date to riseset with calendar = "J" to time the skyline crossing. For a dawn sketch, advance from that crossing until the star clears the terrain while the sky is still dark enough. The phase date alone does not specify a visible instant.
Extinction and model scopeThe implementation uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation,
X(h)=1/(\sin h+0.025\exp(-11\sin h)), multiplying it by k
and adding the result to the fixed catalogue magnitude. Here h is the
stellar altitude selected by refraction, above the astronomical
horizontal. This is distinct from the height above a ridge. The star-Sun
altitude-separation rule uses the catalogue magnitude before extinction.
The model does not calculate scattered moonlight, artificial light pollution,
weather, an observer's adaptation history, or variable-star light curves.
The same separation threshold is used at all relative azimuths. It is therefore
a screening model for seasonal opportunities, not a probability of detection.
Supplying an integrated cluster entry such as M45 treats its total magnitude as
one target; cluster size, surface brightness and resolution into individual
stars do not enter this calculation. It does not predict when each Pleiad is
individually visible.
Horizon status is determined from positive-duration clearance intervals along
the same stellar track used for the phase calculation, with the supplied
skyline and refraction setting. The same calculation applies in both
hemispheres. A track with no clearance returns an ordinary all-I result,
rather than raising an error. An always-clear track still undergoes the
extinction and solar-darkness tests; never setting does not imply visibility.
A star that never sets below a level horizontal can cross a raised ridge.
Isolated tangencies do not count as intervals of clearance or obstruction.
Numerical resolution and the supplied terrain profile limit this status.
The separate metadata$horizon.status field is "always above", "always below"
or "crosses", relative to the supplied skyline. Phase codes R and S describe
the rising or descending part of a visible track below alt.rs; they do not
require a physical skyline crossing that day. An always-clear star may thus
have seasonal R/S codes. The type "circumpolar" is retained for an all-V
result only when the track is always above the skyline; other all-V results
are labelled "visible throughout cycle". Use horizon.status, not type, to
distinguish clearance from seasonal visibility.
Dates and a subsequent sky sketchEvents follow adjacent-sample transitions around the closed cycle, including
the December-solstice boundary. Entering and leaving I mark acronycal setting
and heliacal rising; entering and leaving V mark acronycal rising and heliacal
setting. A season continuing across the boundary creates no event there.
Constant phase sequences have no transition events.
The 365 model samples are equally spaced in solar longitude, not in elapsed
civil time. Printed seasonal labels are anchored to the December solstice.
metadata$events$date.julian instead solves for the event solar longitude
in the requested year and converts it to a local mean-solar Julian-calendar
date using longitude. It is a representative date, not an exact detection
instant, and can differ from the synthetic day label.
Pass the representative date to riseset with
calendar = "J" and an explicit timezone. With UTC or a fixed offset,
inspect neighbouring dates when local mean-solar and civil days differ.
The returned rise is a skyline crossing. Follow it by a short time sequence
with sketchSky and skyStep to inspect terrain
clearance and the changing brightness of the local sky.
A supplied skyscapeR.star is used as given. Recompute it for the requested
year; the phase function does not update an existing object's coordinates.
How precise is a heliacal-rising date?In 69 of 70 individual comparisons, the estimated first morning of visibility was within a week of the predicted heliacal-rising date.
Reproducing a saved resultMetadata retain the resolved star, year, observer coordinates, extinction,
atmospheric settings and solar-altitude threshold, together with limit,
alt.rs, res and alt.hor. The latter is NA when a terrain
profile replaces the constant horizon. metadata$horizon.profile contains
the numerical az/alt table used, or NULL for a constant horizon.
Landscape images and DEMs are not copied into the result. Existing logical
horizon and skyline fields are retained.
metadata$provenance$packages records the loaded skyscapeR and swephR
versions; an unavailable version is NA, for example when sourcing functions
outside a package namespace. Version strings do not uniquely identify
development builds. Retain the original script, code revision and ephemeris
files as well: the saved metadata do not identify or archive those files.
Earlier saved results do not acquire these fields automatically.

15.7 Sky brightness and visualisation
Separate the ephemeris and local geometry, the radiance model, and the mapping of radiance to a display. The natural and publication styles answer different questions about a reconstruction.

15.7.1 importConstellations()
Function index
Each non-comment line contains a unique figure identifier, the number
of segments, then two Hipparcos numbers per segment. Endpoints describe
separate pairs, not one continuous polygon. Blank lines and comments beginning
with a hash are ignored. Non-negative segment counts and positive integer HIP identifiers are validated.
Zero-segment records are retained with an empty HIP field and skipped when drawn.
Repeated endpoints represent a single-star figure, drawn as a small ring.
This supports Stellarium's legacy constellationship.fab format, not the JSON
sky-culture format introduced in Stellarium 25.1. Only lines are imported,
not artwork, labels, boundaries or star positions. Endpoint stars must be in
skyscapeR's stellar catalogue; unavailable stars produce warnings when drawn.
The import does not modify the bundled catalogue or register global names.
Save the returned object with saveRDS(), or load the file in each script.
Respect the source sky culture's attribution and redistribution terms.

Stellarium User Guide, Adding Sky Cultures (legacy editions) and
Sky Cultures (current editions): https://stellarium.org/guide/.
Legacy example: https://github.com/Stellarium/stellarium/blob/v0.22.2/skycultures/western/constellationship.fab.





Interpretation and limits. A drawn figure expresses a chosen connection between catalogue stars. Endpoints, projection and cultural attribution must be documented separately from any claim that the figure was visible together at a particular instant.
