15.7.2 planisphere()
Function index
The default star layer draws individual Pleiades members and omits integrated clusters and other nonstellar entries. The full catalogue remains available for target searches and phase calculations.

The chart compares the accessible part of the celestial sphere with a catalogue sky at
the chosen year. Catalogue stars are filtered by magnitude and by the implemented
declinations that rise above a level geometric horizon. Northern latitudes use
the north celestial pole; southern latitudes use the south celestial pole.
Polar distance sets radius, and right ascension sets angle with opposite
handedness for the two poles. Magnitude controls symbol size, and hour labels
are placed every three hours. The optional ecliptic uses daily solar positions over a
year, using geocentric coordinates without atmospheric refraction. The plot is
not an instantaneous view
through a site's measured horizon. The Milky Way uses the same diffuse-light tracing as sketchSky(), with dark cutouts and two brighter tiers referenced to the whole-band mean. Source: NASA/Goddard SVS and ESA/Gaia/DPAC, Deep Star Maps 2020. It is a fixed sky map rotated to the requested epoch with Swiss Ephemeris precession and nutation. Its width is illustrative. It does not predict visibility or reconstruct the Galaxy’s internal evolution.

Deep Star Maps 2020. https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4851/.

Astrodienst. Swiss Ephemeris programmer's manual.

Return valueDraws the polar chart on the active graphics device and invisibly returns the saved xpd, mar and pty graphics settings.
Constellation patternsConstellation segments follow the shorter great-circle arc between catalogue
endpoints at the requested epoch. They use the same polar projection as the
stars and are clipped to the chart's accessible sky. Faint endpoints remain
available for line drawing even when no star symbol is shown. Missing catalogue
endpoints generate a warning and their segments are omitted. These are line
figures; repeated endpoints mark single-star figures with small rings. They
are not constellation boundaries or lunar-mansion sectors. See
constellations for sources, licences and historical limitations.
Projection and visibility limitsThis is a polar azimuthal equidistant chart. For latitude at or above zero,
radius is 90 minus declination and right ascension increases clockwise from
the top. For negative latitude, radius is 90 plus declination and right
ascension increases anticlockwise. The chart radius is 180 minus absolute
latitude; a non-round cutoff is retained exactly. All layers use this same
projection. At the equator the north-polar convention is used.
Stars are included when their upper culmination is strictly above a level
geometric horizon; stars that only touch it are excluded. This is potential
annual access to that part of the sky, not visibility at any particular time.
There is no date/time of night, local terrain, atmospheric extinction,
moonlight or twilight detection model. Magnitudes are fixed catalogue values,
and point size is a graphical brightness indicator. For a particular site and
instant use sketchSky with a georeferenced horizon.

Sun, Moon and stars default to TRUE; other switches default to FALSE, except that the Milky Way follows stars unless explicitly set. The additional constellations entry accepts names or an imported data frame, rather than a logical value. See Constellations below. A named logical vector is sufficient when supplying only switches.

One of "natural", "publication-colour" or "publication-mono". Publication styles have a white background and dark guides. Colour uses muted stellar and planetary colours and a warm solar disc; mono uses black and white. Neither publication style predicts visibility.


max.mag

skyscapeR.vars()$k

This clear-sky baseline is an assumption, not an estimate of the site's weather. Zero removes extinction and the modelled lunar scattering. Publication styles do not apply extinction to symbols.



Return valueAn object of classes skyscapeR.sketch and skyscapeR.sky.
It stores jd, loc, style, display, settings
(calendar, magnitude cutoff and extinction), and atmosphere.
stars and coords contain azimuth, altitude and symbol size;
star.opacity retains an earlier symbol-opacity diagnostic; natural
sketches draw from light.budget. bodies, diameters,
planet.size and lunar describe selected Solar System bodies.
clusters holds supported cluster footprints and opacity when applicable;
guides, light, background and twilight fields support drawing.
Components can be empty when a layer is disabled. No image file is written.
Reading a natural sketchThe sky is calculated for the specified instant. Stars, clusters, planets and
the Moon contribute light on a common visual (V-band) magnitude scale.
Diffuse Milky Way light and atmospheric background are measured per unit
sky area. Their light is added before brightness is compressed for display.
To inspect the values underlying a view, use skyRadiance.
Stars remain unresolved as the field is enlarged. Mercury, Venus, Mars,
Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon use apparent disc sizes and illuminated
fractions from Swiss Ephemeris. A close view can therefore show the phase
of Venus. Star colours follow catalogue spectral classes; the diffuse band
has a neutral tint. Colour and projection influence the screen appearance.
Publication styles use magnitude-scaled star and planet symbols on white.
Azimuth increases clockwise from true north. Refraction, pressure and
temperature come from skyscapeR.vars when the sky is calculated.
The Sun and Moon switches control their contributions to sky illumination as
well as their discs. Use display = list(moon = FALSE) for a moonless
comparison. The terrain masks the drawn sky; a local ridge hiding the Moon
can still leave scattered moonlight in the sky.
ConstellationsUse display = list(constellations = "Orion") to select and enable line
figures. "modern" selects all 88 Western figures, "chinese" the
full Chinese set, and "chinese_mansions" the 28 lunar-mansion figures.
Names and abbreviations are case-sensitive; for example c("Ori", "Tau").
Alternatively, supply a data frame from importConstellations.
See constellations for sources and identifiers.
Supplying a selection enables lines unless constellation.lines = FALSE
is also supplied. Setting constellation.lines = TRUE without a selection
uses modern figures. Endpoint coordinates are calculated independently of the
star-symbol magnitude cut. Lines therefore remain when their stars are faint,
extincted, or switched off. A single-star figure is drawn as a ring. Normal
plot clipping and the horizon foreground still apply. These are reference
figures; their visibility is not an observing prediction.
Twilight and extinctionAt twilight the sky brightens differently towards and away from the Sun.
Zenith brightness uses the Paranal V-band observations of Patat et al.
(2006) at solar depressions of 5 to 15 degrees. Sacramento Peak measurements
supply earlier twilight levels and the directional variation (Koomen et al.
1952). These clear-sky estimates depend on site conditions. Moonlight uses
the scattering model of Krisciunas and Schaefer (1991), with its dependence
on lunar phase, altitude and angular separation.
Direct light fades towards the horizon as its path through the atmosphere
lengthens. The coefficient k sets the loss per airmass. The model
uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation (Krisciunas and Schaefer 1991);
uncertainty is greatest close to the skyline. The twilight colours are
illustrative (Lee 1994, 2015).
Milky Way and clustersThe Milky Way is traced from the diffuse light in Deep Star Maps 2020.
Within the smoothed envelope, retained dark patches have at least 10 percent
local contrast; two bright tiers begin at 1.10 and 1.75 times the mean band
tone after the dark patches are excluded. Retained patches cover at least
10 square degrees. Natural sketches anchor the mean surface brightness
of a four-degree field in Carina to 20.7 V magnitudes per square arcsecond
(van der Kruit 2024). Brightness elsewhere is approximate. Atmospheric
extinction can make the band difficult to follow down to its calculated
horizon crossing. The Galactic equator is an optional geometric guide.
A supported cluster contributes its catalogue light across its angular
extent. Light already assigned to plotted stars within that footprint is
subtracted before the remaining glow is drawn. This accounts for projected
overlap; it does not establish membership. Integrated cluster magnitude
alone is insufficient to predict first detection (Crumey 2014).
Using a sketch with a stellar phase dateIn 69 of 70 individual comparisons, the estimated first morning of visibility was within a week of the predicted heliacal-rising date.
Use riseset to locate the skyline crossing on each morning,
then skyStep to follow the star as it climbs through a
brightening sky. A plotted pixel does not establish naked-eye visibility.
A quantitative test needs a point-source threshold and an assumed observer
limit (Crumey 2014). See also star.phases.
Record site, horizon, epoch, calendar, timezone, extinction
and display switches when reporting a reconstruction.

Function index
Direct light includes stars, residual cluster light, planetary discs
and the illuminated lunar disc. The Milky Way uses the accepted tracing and
a provisional Carina surface-brightness calibration. Stars remain unresolved
as the view is enlarged. See sketchSky for sources, assumptions
and interpretation.

15.7.5 skyStep()
Function index
Add the signed increment in minutes divided by 1440 to the saved Julian date. A native sketch is recalculated locally using the saved display selection, style, extinction and magnitude limit, and the current session atmosphere. A Stellarium capture is repeated using its saved external capture settings. The function plots the new view and invisibly returns its sky object. Assign that return value to continue the sequence from the new instant. The remote connection is needed only for the capture branch.
Interpretation and limits. Preserve the sky object or captured image and the settings of the system that produced it. Stepping through several instants is informative near a terrain crossing; a screen capture alone carries no per-pixel naked-eye detection threshold.

and display selections. Refraction, pressure and temperature are read again

for a time-only comparison, including when resuming a saved sketch in another

the external application's atmospheric settings.

15.7.6 stellariumSky()
Function index
Enable Remote Control under Configuration > Plugins in Stellarium Desktop, select Load at startup and restart if needed. Enable the server in the plugin settings. Use the local server without a password and install the R packages httr2 and png. Close dialogs and use a normal rectangular viewport. Point screenshot.dir at the directory configured in Stellarium.

The script freezes time and takes one full-sphere Cylinder Fill screenshot. The centre is south, the seam is north, and the horizon is halfway up. Choose width for more pixels per degree. R keeps the native pixels for each plotted sector. For a 30-degree sector a width of 8192 supplies about 683 source pixels. The physical plot size and graphics device determine the displayed resolution. If the script times out, check the screenshot path and that your Stellarium version offers Cylinder Fill.

15.8 Uncertainty and orientation distributions
Record the density family, sampling interval, cutoff, coordinate transformation and any unit-area normalisation. Interpolating an SPD onto a finer grid does not improve a bearing measurement.

15.8.1 az.pdf()
Verified on 2.0.9006. Periodic azimuth densities passed the fine-grid and wide-width D01 checks. D01 rerun.
Validation on 2.0.9005. The analytic density checks in D01 found a folding error near north at 0.005-degree spacing and omitted periodic tails in the two 100-degree-width cases. D01 results.
Function index
Azimuth is circular. Curves wrap across north before the density-height
cutoff is applied. For an asymmetric triangle, the clockwise arc from lower
to upper must include az and be shorter than a full turn.
For example, limits 358 and 3 enclose a mode of 0. For the four new families,
the field interval (including both cosine tapers, if used) spans at most one
turn. An aperture convolved with Gaussian survey error can still have tails
across the full circle. The grid starts at zero and ends before 360. Each
measurement is retained separately. Trimming does not renormalise the stored
ordinates. Choose a grid fine enough to resolve the narrowest shoulder.

Field examples and comparison of all six profiles.


Method references

Silva, F (2020) A probabilistic framework and significance test for the analysis of structural orientations
in skyscape archaeology Journal of Archaeological Science 118, 105138. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jas.2020.105138")}





Interpretation and limits. A reported uncertainty enters differently as the standard deviation of a normal density and as the half-width of a uniform density. Record which interpretation the measurement supports before combining sites.

One measurement family per call. See 'Choosing a measurement model' for all six names. The default is "normal". The historical abbreviations "n" and "u" are accepted and names are case-insensitive.

15.8.2 coordtrans()
For a partial photograph the stored positive bearing density must lie within its photographed sector. H07 verified agreement with a complete skyline on the covered north-crossing cases and rejection of uncovered densities. H07 results.
In D02, declination quantiles agreed with direct propagation within 0.008 degrees across nine terrain and observer cases. Near the celestial pole the discrepancy reached 0.17 degrees on the fine grid; at the pole a zero conditional width prevented calculation. D02 results.
The integration uses the full bearing density from any of the six measurement families. Measurement families.
Function index
A sightline has a distribution of possible bearings, and each bearing samples a
potentially different part of the horizon. For every sampled bearing the function
interpolates horizon altitude and uncertainty, maps an altitude range to declination and
approximates the conditional declination distribution by a Gaussian. It weights that
distribution by the azimuth density and integrates the product by the trapezoidal rule.
A shared horizon can serve several observations, or a supplied list can represent their
individual sites.

Density values are calculated at declination spacing .res, then
linearly interpolated onto a grid with spacing .output.res. The upper
calculation bound is evaluated explicitly if the step does not land on it,
avoiding extrapolation at the tail. Linear interpolation preserves
nonnegative calculated densities and avoids cubic-spline overshoot.
Individual PDF outputs retain their existing area normalisation; SPD outputs
retain their existing unnormalised transformation behaviour. Coarse
calculation spacing can still miss narrow peaks; interpolation does not
replace a resolution-convergence check. Azimuth integration uses a separate
grid from -90 to 450 degrees with step .prec. For a distribution split across north, integration uses contiguous bearings around zero at the same spacing. The output grid starts
at the lower bound and ends at the last full step within the upper bound.
Refine the calculation grid to check that narrow features are resolved.
Set atmospheric refraction, pressure and temperature with skyscapeR.vars before transforming. The values used are recorded in the returned PDF or SPD.
All three spacings are stored in metadata$param.

15.8.9 spd()
For two bearings on a shared slope, the D02 comparison of summing before and after transformation gave an integrated absolute density difference of 0.00159 after normalisation. D02 results.
Verified on 2.0.9006. Broad azimuth SPDs were continuous at north and correctly interpolated across the final grid segment. D01 rerun.

Function index
A summed probability density gives each input measurement one density curve. The
function linearly interpolates these curves onto one angular grid, assigns zero outside
each curve's sampled support and adds their heights point by point. With an
automatically chosen range it zeroes summed heights below the cutoff. With an explicit
range it retains the calculated heights across that range.

Normalisation takes place after interpolation and any cutoff, over
the returned grid. An explicit restricted xrange therefore normalises
the retained portion only. Zero-area, nonfinite or negative densities and
grids with fewer than two points cannot be normalised and produce an error.
Earlier versions divided by the sum of sampled heights. Normalised outputs
now have a different scale; on a regular grid with zero endpoint densities,
new heights equal old heights divided by .res. Existing saved objects
are not converted. Changing resolution can still affect interpolation and
truncation accuracy, but the returned trapezoidal area is one.

15.9 Null models and significance
The reference distribution, score, Monte Carlo rank and any search across intervals all affect the inferential claim. A display symbol summarises an already-calculated p-value.

15.9.1 bernoulli.trial()
Validation on 2.0.9005. Exact and upper-tail probabilities agreed with independent binomial calculations for the tested counts up to 1,000, including zero hits. S03 results.
Function index
Define a hit and the per-structure chance of a hit before counting the orientations. A
single-count probability answers how often exactly that count arises; the upper tail
answers how often a count at least that large arises.

The binomial model assumes independent structures with the same
target probability p. The upper-tail probability is a one-sided
p-value under this model. Calculations use stats::dbinom and
stats::pbinom, avoiding factorial overflow and subtraction from 1.
At least zero hits has probability 1. With zero structures, zero hits has
probability 1 for either type. Inputs are scalar; invalid inputs error.



Method references

Ruggles, C (1999) Astronomy in Prehistoric Britain and Ireland. Yale University Press.





Interpretation and limits. The binomial formulation requires a defensible success probability and trial structure. Repeated structures at the same location may not act as independent trials. Delimit the target window before counting successes.

15.9.2 modelTest()
In S02, identical candidate bearings produced identical directly constructed observed and simulated densities on build 2.0.9008. Global rejection at the 5 percent level ranged from 4.35 to 5.50 percent under the six matched null designs. S02 results.
Verified on 2.0.9006. The observed and simulated azimuth curves use the same circular cluster search. The original test matrix gave one interval from 346° to 15°. S03 rerun.
Validation on 2.0.9005. Independent scoring reproduced the stored linear-grid probabilities. A north-crossing azimuth excess can split into two clusters; including both 0 and 360 degrees can also affect the global rank. S03 results.
A directly measured triangular density follows the sampled mode, retaining its left/right proportions. Both softened uniform families preserve their second width in degrees. Measurement families.
Function index
A proposed topographical or astronomical explanation can predict some orientations more
frequently than others. Testing that explanation requires simulating its predicted
distribution at the sites under study.

Silva and Lomsdalen (2025) extended the random-orientation framework of Silva (2020)
to test specific hypotheses about temple orientations in Malta, including topographical and
astronomical explanations. Here the hypothesis specifies the relative probability of each
candidate orientation. A small global p-value is evidence against that particular model.

Model weights and interpretation.
Weights are discrete sampling probabilities up to proportionality. If a
continuous model is evaluated on an uneven coordinate grid, density heights
alone do not represent probability mass; construct weights that account for
the bin widths before calling the function. Put site-specific model tables in
the same order as the observed measurements.

A large p-value does not prove the proposed explanation or measure its
probability. The test asks whether the specified model is incompatible with
the observed departure statistic. Alternative models can remain compatible.
The simulations do not automatically represent dependence between sites,
selection after viewing the data, or uncertainty in fitted model parameters.
See randomTest for study-design and Monte Carlo limitations.






Method references

Silva, F. (2020). A probabilistic framework and significance test for the analysis of structural orientations in skyscape archaeology. Journal of Archaeological Science, 118, 105138. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jas.2020.105138")}.

Silva, F. and Lomsdalen, T. (2025). ‘No easy way from the earth to the stars’: a new statistical approach to the orientation of the Maltese temples. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 17, 96. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1007/s12520-025-02208-4")}.

Maris, E. and Oostenveld, R. (2007). Nonparametric statistical testing of EEG- and MEG-data. Journal of Neuroscience Methods. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jneumeth.2007.03.024")}.

Sassenhagen, J. and Draschkow, D. (2019). Cluster-based permutation tests of MEG/EEG data do not establish significance of effect latency or location. Psychophysiology. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1111/psyp.13335")}.

Dufour, J.-M. (2006). Monte Carlo tests with nuisance parameters: A general approach to finite-sample inference and nonstandard asymptotics. Journal of Econometrics, 133, 443-477. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1016/j.jeconom.2005.06.007")}.

North, B. V., Curtis, D. and Sham, P. C. (2002). A note on the calculation of empirical P values from Monte Carlo procedures. American Journal of Human Genetics, 71, 439-441. \Sexpr[results=rd]{tools:::Rd_expr_doi("10.1086/341527")}.

The null draw relocates each observation’s full measurement model, including triangular asymmetry, taper and independent survey error. Measurement families.
Function index
Following Silva (2020), the test combines the observed measurement densities into a summed probability density (SPD).
For each simulated dataset, the function draws one azimuth per measurement with replacement
from the uniform grid from 0 to 360 degrees at the source azimuth spacing. It applies the
source density family and measurement uncertainties and constructs a comparable SPD.
For a declination test, random azimuths are transformed using the site geometry; the
resulting null distribution in declination depends on latitude and horizon.

A new transformation takes its atmosphere from skyscapeR.vars. A saved declination PDF supplies its original settings. The fit records these in metadata$atmosphere for declination tests.

Study design and numerical checks.
The simulated null describes independently sampled orientations with the
specified site geometry and measurement model. It does not automatically model
shared construction episodes, correlated measurement errors, geographical
clustering or selection of sites after inspecting their orientations. Such
structure needs a justified sampling model or separate sensitivity analysis.

The pointwise envelope is not a simultaneous confidence band. A significant
global result rejects the specified random-orientation model; it does not
identify a celestial target. Refine the comparison grid and increase
nsims to assess borderline results, preserving the seed and inputs.
More simulations improve Monte Carlo resolution, not the validity of the
archaeological sampling design. Repeated searches over alternative subsets or
models are not included in the within-fit local-cluster adjustment.

title: 16  Following the package vignette
text:
16.1 Field data
W02 records the intermediate tables from the archived and 2.0.9009 Malta workflows, plus independent synthetic field controls.
Use this guide alongside skyscapeR: from field measurements to skyscape analysis, the vignette in the 2.0.9012 source. Each entry follows a decision in that workflow to its technical explanation. In R, open the installed vignette with vignette("skyscapeR", package="skyscapeR") when vignettes are installed. The source is vignettes/skyscapeR.Rmd inside the package download in the function methods catalogue.
The opening setup checks for spreadsheet and ephemeris dependencies. Conditional examples may be skipped when the vignette is built without those inputs. The ephemeris chapter identifies the backend and data required for reproducing ancient positions.

title: 16  Following the package vignette
text:
16.1.1 Import your observations
Read the Compass worksheet with readxl. Keep the original bearing, date, site identifier, latitude, longitude, elevation and measured skyline altitude in the same row. A spreadsheet import is an external R operation. Its column order and units determine what the reduction receives.
Technical explanation.


16.1.2 Reduce compass readings to true azimuth
Pass the location matrix and observation dates in worksheet order. Preserve the raw magnetic readings alongside the declination correction and the returned true bearings.
Technical explanation. reduct.compass(), mag.dec().


16.1.3 Reduce a theodolite survey with a solar sight
The solar limb, local clock and unchanged instrument circle setting identify the reference for the structural bearings. Pair the reduced bearings with their measured horizon altitudes.
Technical explanation. reduct.theodolite(), ten(), sunAz().


16.1.4 Convert each sightline to celestial declination
The measured horizon altitude belongs to the same true bearing and observer latitude. The direct transform gives one declination per row. Uncertainty propagation requires an orientation distribution.
Technical explanation. az2dec().


16.1.5 Which targets fit the measurement?
Screen the two-degree interval around the example measurement over the stated dating interval. The two degrees are a choice in the vignette. The search does not estimate this uncertainty.
Technical explanation. findTargets().

title: 16  Following the package vignette
text:
16.2 One site

16.2.1 The doorway at Mnajdra South
The bundled malta_entrances table contains 32 entrances. Its unnamed companion list malta_horizons contains the corresponding profiles generated by Tore Lomsdalen with Andrew Smith’s Horizon software from the Heritage Malta 5 m DEM. Check the stored site metadata after any reordering. Select a named entrance before extracting its edges. The vignette can average these two edge bearings because its opening does not cross north. For a north-crossing opening, take the clockwise width modulo 360° before computing its midpoint.
Technical explanation.


16.2.2 Importing site horizons
Measured profiles, transparent photographs, HeyWhatsThat, PeakFinder and a DEM provide different evidence about the same direction. The bundled Mnajdra skyline is selected by the entrance row index. Read each edge altitude from that profile before transforming the edge.
Technical explanation. createHor(), importPanorama(), createHWT(), importPeakFinder(), exportStellarium(), hor2alt(), az2dec(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().


16.2.3 Which objects fit the doorway?
Use the declinations of both doorway edges and the monument’s date range. If the skyline has a notch or ridge inside the opening, also inspect the interior, since the extremal declination need not occur at either edge.
Technical explanation. findTargets().


16.2.4 Equinoctial sunrise
A zero-declination reference track and the Sun at its terrain crossing are different astronomical quantities. The equinox occurs at an instant, which can be hours after local sunrise. Retain the returned crossing declination for the dated track.
Technical explanation. riseset(), sketchSky(), skyObject(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().


16.2.5 The heliacal rising of the Pleiades
Take the event’s local Julian calendar date, compute the terrain crossing on that date, then advance the time to allow the centre to clear the ridge. Integrated M45 and the individual Alcyone use different magnitudes and can receive different phase dates.
Technical explanation. star.phases(), riseset(), time2jd(), sketchSky(), plot.skyscapeR.starphases(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().


16.2.6 Watch the cluster rise later in the season
Adding 60 days to the earlier JD selects a later date for a new rise calculation. Adding five minutes to a particular crossing, or stepping a reconstructed sky ten minutes, instead changes the displayed instant. Keep the doorway edges and sector fixed across frames.
Technical explanation. riseset(), sketchSky(), skyStep(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().

title: 16  Following the package vignette
text:
16.3 Multiple sites

16.3.1 Start with the Ġgantija entrance bearings
Use the same indices for the entrances and their horizons. Plot centre bearings on the compass and half-widths on the interval plot. A compass solstice mark uses the level-horizon crossing at the supplied site.
Technical explanation. plotAzimuth(), plotBars(), skyObject().


16.3.2 Give each opening a distribution
A uniform azimuth PDF treats the directions between doorway edges as equally probable. Transform each opening across its own skyline before summation. The linked single-site view can show several disjoint intervals at the requested density mass.
Technical explanation. az.pdf(), coordtrans(), spd(), plot.skyscapeR.pdf(), plot.skyscapeR.spd().


16.3.3 Test random orientations
The vignette reads a saved 500-simulation fit. Its lower panel displays separately adjusted excess and deficit clusters. Reading the bundled fit does not run 500 new simulations. Retain the seed, observations and matching skylines to reproduce the fit.
Technical explanation. randomTest(), plot.skyscapeR.sigTest().


16.3.4 Exploring celestial candidates
Filter the positive clusters by adjusted p-value before searching their declination intervals. A compatible Gacrux band is a candidate. Checking its phase and the view from Skorba West asks a separate site-specific question.
Technical explanation. findTargets(), skyObject(), star.phases(), riseset(), time2jd(), sketchSky(), modelTest(), plot.skyscapeR.sigTest(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().

title: 16  Following the package vignette
text:
16.4 Other tools

16.4.1 Compare the three sky styles
Recompute the same horizon and instant in each style. The natural rendering maps a light budget to the display. The two publication styles use symbols to show geometry, even when natural visual contrast is weak.
Technical explanation. sketchSky(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().


16.4.2 Compare stellar seasons
Pass the first result as x and further results in the second argument. Compare one star across epochs, several stars at one epoch, or a list ordered by star and year. A shared seasonal reference aligns the rows.
Technical explanation. star.phases(), plot.skyscapeR.starphases().


16.4.3 Compare constellation patterns
Keep site, epoch and field fixed while changing modern figures, Chinese mansion asterisms or selected figure identifiers. The bundled constellations table has 88 modern rows, 318 Chinese rows and a separate 28-row mansion selection. Each pair of HIP identifiers is an independent segment. The star.names lookup maps Western names to catalogue identifiers; it does not define the line patterns. The same catalogue star can participate in a different line pattern. Imported legacy HIP pairs specify connectivity.
Technical explanation. sketchSky(), importConstellations(), skyStep(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().


16.4.4 Explore the Milky Way and reference circles
The traced band, its dark and bright structure, and the Galactic equator have different geometrical meanings. A sketch and a planisphere expose these as separate layer choices.
Technical explanation. sketchSky(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().


16.4.5 Capture a sky from Stellarium
A captured image reflects the external application’s state. Replotting a sector uses the existing raster, while stepping time requests a fresh capture. Record the external settings and the screenshot width.
Technical explanation. stellariumSky(), skyStep(), plot.skyscapeR.horizon().


16.4.6 Equinoctial full Moons and solstitial crescent crossovers
EFM pairs lunar and solar events. CC additionally applies the selected crescent and simulation gates. Inspect the diagnostics and the visibility margin when explaining why a particular day was selected.
Technical explanation. EFM(), CC().


16.4.7 A planisphere for the site’s latitude
The chart clips the epoch’s celestial sphere to the declinations that can rise at the specified latitude. Its geometric boundary and catalogue magnitude limit answer different questions from local detectability behind an actual skyline.
Technical explanation. planisphere().

title: 17  Studies by question and package build
text:
17.1 H01. Horizon altitude at surveyed bearings
A result belongs to the build, inputs and settings that produced it. The tables give the latest verified run for the stated question and sample in these archives. The function chapters describe build 2.0.9004. An older build in the table means that the reported result has not been established here for the newer implementation.
Research question. How accurately does createHor() predict the angular altitude of the visible terrain skyline from a DEM at an independently surveyed azimuth?
Outcome. Across 334 distinct bearings at 31 observing setups, the median absolute difference from the field measurement was 0.036°, the mean absolute difference was 0.169°, and 91.9% of predictions fell within ±0.5°. Mean signed error was +0.048° (predicted minus measured). Thus the DEM-derived skyline usually agreed with the observed terrain horizon to within half a degree at these bearings. Individual errors reached 7.26°. The 0.5° figure is an observed proportion for this sample and cannot serve as an uncertainty bound for an individual sightline.
Each residual combines the effects of the terrain model, observer position and height, numerical skyline calculation and field measurement. The surveys sample particular directions at each setup. Accuracy between those directions, including narrow peaks or notches, remains unmeasured. The station and terrain summaries below show how far the pooled result transfers across the tested conditions.
The horizon methods chapter describes the ray geometry, curvature and terrestrial refraction used by the tested build, 2.0.9004. The screened field dataset contains 775 distinct bearings from 36 observing setups in six countries. Digitised measurements from Artegna form an additional comparison.
Field and numerical protocol. Each observation retains the survey, observing position, target description, original table or figure, true azimuth and measured altitude. The analysis counts an exact repeated angular pair once within a setup. Where two distinct altitude readings have the same published bearing at the same setup, their mean contributes one residual. Coordinate provenance distinguishes an instrument fix, an adopted site coordinate and a shared coordinate for nearby setups. The run manifests record any assumed instrument height. No location or height was selected by minimising the field residuals.
For each terrain product, the function traces the horizon at 0.25° azimuth spacing and the specified radial step. The validation script interpolates the numerical profile linearly at the recorded bearing. A sight is eligible at the stated radius when both bracketing rays have finite terrain samples to that distance. A signed residual is the predicted altitude minus the field altitude, in degrees. Positive values place the modelled horizon above the measured one. The pooled summary weights each distinct station–bearing combination equally. Several bearings can describe the same ridge, and the number of bearings per station varies.
Results by terrain selection. The table compares the two tested search distances in Wales and Tenerife under both Irish terrain selections. Other regions keep their original settings. Each 50 km sample is a subset of the corresponding 15 km sample.
The longer-radius working sample includes 29 setups, compared with 31 at the shorter radius. Extending those two regions to 50 km leaves 28 of the original 126 Welsh bearings and 16 of the original 37 Tenerife bearings with continuous terrain. The archive preserves both editions’ results. In Ireland the 25 m EU-DEM supplies 117 complete bearings at 65 km, while SRTM supplies all 510. On the 117 bearings shared by both products, the mean absolute errors are 0.167° for EU-DEM and 0.120° for SRTM. The wider SRTM result changes both the terrain input and the distribution of sampled directions.
Station and range effects. West Kennet gives a mean absolute error of 0.032° over 12 bearings. Rectory Farm S2 gives 0.823° over 11 bearings with the same 1 m Environment Agency terrain product and 5 km radius. Several discrepant Rectory Farm profiles reach their apparent maximum only 245–289 m from the instrument. The 15 and 50 km Welsh runs have 28 common bearings. Each prediction changes by less than 0.001°. In Tenerife, 16 bearings have complete terrain samples at both 15 and 50 km. Each changes by less than 0.001°. At Chaco the four setups give identical predictions at 25 and 50 km. At the Argentine stations a 30 to 70 km extension changes one prediction by 4.24°, while extension from 70 to 120 km changes predictions by at most 0.00073°. Those Argentine runs use a 30 m surface model and are reported separately.
Interpretation and outstanding checks. Welsh results depend on complete native LiDAR coverage along the extended sightlines. Coastal gaps preclude native-resolution scoring at the two Maltese setups and along the Maeshowe sightlines under this rule. The report identifies the coarser product used at those stations. Tenerife retains the authors’ GPS locations and their refraction-corrected altitudes. A finer Spanish ground model is published regionally, but numerical tiles must be verified along the survey bearings before those statistics can be assigned to that resolution. At La Nariz the paper’s sanctuary coordinate and Murcia’s officially designated centre are 21.64 km apart. The predictions at both positions remain diagnostic. The test describes field agreement for these sites, inputs and settings. H02 compares the computed skylines. Spanish terrain product status · Murcia site designation
Records and reproduction. The report gives the signed residual distribution, error statistics and histograms for the pooled sample, each DEM source and resolution, and each observing setup. The archive contains the original row locators, coverage decisions, per-bearing predictions, R code, download recipes and terrain checksums. Detailed H01 validation report · Download the H01 study and code
Field sources include Wilson’s horizon surveys, Humble’s Rectory Farm tables, Reijs’s Orkney survey, Esteban and Delgado Cabrera’s Tenerife measurements, Ocharan Ibarra and Esteban’s La Nariz tables, Lomsdalen’s Maltese total-station readings, Munro’s Chaco field sheets, and Leibowicz and colleagues’ Cachi survey. The image-derived Italian comparison uses Patat’s Figure 3.

title: 17  Studies by question and package build
section: 17.2 H02. How well does createHor() reproduce terrain skylines?
text:
17.2 H02. How well does createHor() reproduce terrain skylines?
Research question. How closely does createHor() reproduce a skyline calculated independently from the same terrain, and how accurately does it predict horizon altitude at surveyed bearings?
Outcome. On the same 1 m terrain, createHor() reproduced Horizon’s skylines with a mean absolute difference of 0.004° at each of the two English control sites. On the covered directions at 30 Maltese viewpoints, its mean absolute difference from Horizon was 0.062°.
Against field measurements, createHor() using SRTM had a mean absolute error of 0.328° across 344 bearings at eight Irish setups, lower than either HeyWhatsThat or PeakFinder on those bearings. Its accuracy varied by site. Using the same 1 m terrain product in England, createHor() had a mean absolute error of 0.032° at West Kennet and 0.823° at Rectory Farm. It was closest to the observations at West Kennet. Both online services were closer at Rectory Farm.
The Maltese figure covers 20,059 directions with continuous 5 km terrain coverage. Xemxija is held out because its archived viewpoint is disputed. At Kunċizzjoni, the Horizon comparison uses the archived Horizon position for both programs. Only predictions made at the field position enter the field comparison. The Irish service comparison uses each provider’s delivered profile and terrain. H02 comparison report · Data and code archive

title: 17  Studies by question and package build
text:
17.6 Sky rendering
A plausible image can conceal errors in its outline, brightness or response to altitude. Each row concerns one quantity. A change to the outline can require repeating one study while leaving a recorded twilight comparison relevant.







Question
Evidence, tested implementation and scope




Milky Way shape. Where are the outer boundary and internal lanes?
The 2.0 development archive retains the diffuse-light source map, candidate thresholds, traced boundaries and bright and dark masks. These document how the depiction was derived and how sensitive its shape was to the tracing choices. The later photometric field comparisons concern brightness in selected patches. They do not independently establish the position of an outer edge. For alignment work the outer outline includes the enclosed dark regions. If a later release revises the anticentre outline, its boundary comparison needs a new run.


Twilight. Does the sky brighten by the observed amount in different directions?
In 2.0.9003 the study compared the calibrated curve with Koomen’s Maryland observations held outside the fit. Across 22 directions/solar-altitude combinations the mean absolute difference, expressed in magnitudes, was 0.48 for the revised curve and 2.28 for the earlier curve on the same observations. This checks the observed configurations at solar altitudes −3° and −6°.


Flux. Does a point source retain its integrated light when the field of view changes?
The 2.0.9004 release check recovered the modelled Sirius flux at 90°, 45° and 5° field widths (reported ratio 1 at each width). Additional checks compare Sirius, the cluster and a Carina field. Recovery of the input flux verifies the calculation. It does not by itself calibrate the absolute brightness of the night sky.


Extinction. Does the Milky Way dim by the specified altitude-dependent factor?
The 2.0.9002 test compared the same skies with the band extinction coefficient set to 0 and 0.2. The script checked the band radiance against the expected multiplier. Model transmission at 0.2 was 0.149 at 5° altitude and 0.832 at 90°. This verifies application of the extinction law. It is not a set of atmospheric transmission measurements.

The heliacal-rising comparison draws on the rendering model for a separate question about the timing of an event.

section: 17.8 When a test changes the package
text:
17.8 When a test changes the package







What changed?
How the manual reports it




Implementation changes, but the question, data, settings and metric stay the same
Add a run to the same study. Show the latest tested build first, with the old and new values, the reason for the code change, and links to both records. Until a rerun exists, identify the last build actually tested.


A new station, dataset, phenomenon or accuracy claim is introduced
Add a linked study alongside the existing one. If extending a cohort, retain results for the original common sample and give the expanded sample its own denominator.


An error in the reference data, selection or scoring invalidates a result
Mark the affected result as superseded and explain why. Put the corrected result in the main text. Retain the original record and the correction together in the history.


A discrepancy was used to tune the model
Label the repeated comparison as calibration or a regression check. Report an independent validation separately when observations unused in tuning are available.



Each study should have a stable link. Each run should identify the exact source revision or package archive checksum, the data and protocol versions, settings, metric, sample and dated outputs. The main text carries the conclusion a reader can use for the documented release. Earlier runs remain accessible in that study’s history.

title: 18  A02 · Ephemeris accuracy and lunar skyline crossings
text:
18.1 Geocentric positions and the R interface
Research question. How closely do skyscapeR’s planetary and lunar positions reproduce their reference ephemerides, and how much does the choice of convention change a prehistoric lunar alignment?
Outcome. In build 2.0.9004 the largest geocentric angular separation from the matching JPL parent was 0.0065″ across 1,080 positions. For 177 prehistoric lunar skyline crossings, default skyscapeR azimuths differed from JPL Horizons by a median 0.059°, with a maximum of 0.322°. Matching ΔT reduced that maximum to 0.027°. With the clocks and apparent-position conventions matched, the remaining difference chiefly affected the crossing time, by up to 3.03 minutes. These are differences between reconstructions over the sampled dates. Observations of the prehistoric sky would be needed to establish absolute accuracy.
The run used R 4.3.3, skyscapeR 2.0.9004, swephR 0.3.2 and Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03. We evaluated the Sun, Moon and eight planets from Mercury through Pluto (excluding Earth) at 54 dynamical-time arguments. Eight instants in each of 3500, 2500 and 1000 BCE and 1900, 2000 and 2025 CE sampled different orbital configurations. Six further instants fell on either side of, or exactly at, two 600-year file boundaries. The archive identifies each Swiss file’s parent generation and SHA-256 hash.
For each of DE431 and DE441, we independently evaluated JPL’s ASCII Chebyshev coefficients, deriving the Earth’s position from the Earth–Moon barycentre and the geocentric Moon. We compared geometric geocentric Cartesian directions in equatorial J2000 ICRS at the same numerical dynamical-time argument. Separation was computed by the two-argument arctangent of the cross-product magnitude and dot product of the unit vectors. The evaluator reproduced 46 JPL test components per generation within 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ AU for position or AU/day for velocity. The archive also retains signed right ascension, declination and range residuals (Astrodienst, n.d.b; Jet Propulsion Laboratory, n.d.).
The supplier’s quoted compression precision is 0.001″. The observed geocentric separations exceed this value in 52 of 1,080 cases. At the R interface, all 4,320 body.position() calls agreed with direct swephR calculations to within 10⁻¹² degrees in azimuth, altitude, right ascension and declination. The matrix crossed both file generations, both geocentric and topocentric modes, and both refraction settings. All 108 moonphase() illuminated fractions matched the direct Swiss call. This last check establishes agreement with the backend and supplies no independent photometric calibration.
A valid planetary and lunar file pair succeeded. Empty, planet-only, Moon-only, out-of-block, just-before-block and corrupt-planet installations each raised skyscapeR_ephemeris_error. The planet-only case matters because the native Sun call returned the Swiss backend flag even though the lunar file was absent.

section: 18.2 Local direction at a specified time
text:
18.2 Local direction at a specified time
We compared 216 airless topocentric directions for the Sun, Moon and Venus at Atacama, Malta and Wiltshire, four instants in each of the six sampled years. Dates before 1962 use UT1. For later dates we converted Horizons UTC to UT1 with its reported DUT1. The package’s topocentric true-position convention differs from the apparent direction reported by Horizons. A control used apparent positions and supplied Horizons TDB−UT1 as an approximation to TT−UT1. We compare total angular separation so that azimuth near the zenith does not dominate the metric (Jet Propulsion Laboratory, n.d.; Astrodienst, n.d.a).

The 0.719° case was the Moon at Atacama (24.63° S, 70.40° W, elevation 2,600 m), JD 443077.0, 1 January 3500 BCE at 12:00 UT1 on the proleptic Gregorian calendar. Horizons placed the Moon at azimuth 295.354°, altitude 43.341°. Swiss gave 294.797° and 42.748°. Their equatorial directions differed by just 44.9″. Reprojecting the Swiss apparent equatorial direction with Horizons’ local apparent sidereal time reduced the separation to 0.0125°. The sidereal times differed by 2 min 50 s. Horizons documents an IAU 1976-based sidereal-time model, while Swiss uses a long-term prescription outside 1850–2050 (Jet Propulsion Laboratory, n.d.; Astrodienst, n.d.b).

title: 18  A02 · Ephemeris accuracy and lunar skyline crossings
text:
18.3 Lunar bearings at the skyline
Across six 72-hour windows beginning on 1 January at noon, we independently solved for zero clearance of the airless lunar centre above each specified skyline. A change from negative to positive clearance denotes a rise and the reverse a set. At Atacama, Malta and Wiltshire we used level horizons of 0° and 5° and an undulating skyline of altitude 4°+3°sin(2A+30°)4°+3°\sin(2A+30°), with azimuth AA measured clockwise from north. A fourth series used Tore Lomsdalen’s archived Kunċizzjoni panorama (malta_horizons[[27]]) at its recorded viewpoint of 35.90085° N, 14.34014° E, elevation 158.3 m. This comparison does not use the field measurements from the nearby viewpoint.
All 351 crossings paired one to one by date, viewpoint, skyline and rise or set. Rows below summarize the 177 prehistoric crossings. Multiple profiles sample the same lunar passage. Absolute differences are shown here; the archive retains signed model-minus-Horizons residuals.

The Atacama Moon crossed the next 0° skyline 70.5 s earlier and 0.192° lower in azimuth with the public default. At the following rise it crossed 108.5 s earlier and 0.188° higher in azimuth. The largest prehistoric azimuth difference (0.322°) occurred at a Wiltshire moonset on the undulating skyline in 3500 BCE. At Kunċizzjoni the maximum was 0.227°, falling to 0.0182° with matched ΔT and apparent positions. Across the 174 historical and modern crossings, the public default maximum was 0.00018° in azimuth and 0.11 s in time.



Maximum differences in lunar crossing azimuth and time by prehistoric epoch. Each point is the largest absolute difference across the sampled sites and skylines.


Numerical checks and limits. We interpolated east–north–up direction vectors on a 10-minute grid. Repeating the analysis on a 20-minute grid recovered the same events and changed paired residuals by at most 0.00086 s and 0.000005°. Fresh Horizons evaluations at 60 computed crossings gave at most 0.005″ absolute skyline clearance. The solver tested crossings of the lunar centre from body.position() trajectories. A04 tests the event solver, including grazing tracks, refracted stellar crossings and modern solar and lunar centres. A02 addresses prehistoric ephemeris sensitivity. Neither study measures optical limb contact.
Implication for archaeological inference. Keep the Swiss default and record the assumed ΔT when an interpretation depends on a few tenths of a degree in prehistoric lunar bearing. For these observations ΔT accounted for most of the change in crossing azimuth. After matching ΔT, the choice of sidereal-time convention chiefly changed the time assigned to the crossing. The sample spans selected three-day windows and supplies no universal tolerance for other epochs or skylines.

title: 19  Calendar, density and significance checks
text:
19.1 A01 · Calendar, clock and angular conventions
A01, D01 and S03 tested the unmodified skyscapeR 2.0.9005 source archive, SHA-256 0446c0a57afe16274e7ef033113ac8d9f251b4f812b1a2d2ea22eac145bb3bbe. Download the exact tested package. D01 and S03 were subsequently rerun on build 2.0.9006, SHA-256 0a97b65385bb253b75b287f160b6e79da63a0ddae29b6be31c5ad6902c6cd6d2. Each study uses a numerical reference independent of the implementation under test. Each archive contains the scripts, expected and observed quantities and reproduction instructions. The previous chapters identify the builds used for their own examples.
Question. Can a civil date or historical era label be placed on the correct UT Julian date and converted back with the intended clock, calendar and sign?
Outcome. All 499 assertions passed. The test compared 240 absolute Julian dates and independently checked 240 returned civil strings. The maximum difference in the Julian-date comparisons was 0.000021 seconds, below the 0.0001-second tolerance. The remaining 19 assertions covered era parsing and formatting, angular signs, clock changes, invalid inputs, midnight rounding and session settings.
We computed the Julian day number by integer Gregorian or Julian calendar arithmetic, with the day starting at noon, then applied the stated clock offset. Reference anchors included J2000 noon (JD 2451545.0), the Unix epoch at midnight (JD 2440587.5) and the Julian epoch at noon (JD 0). Ten dates from astronomical year −4712 to CE 2024, four times of day, both proleptic calendars and three fixed offsets (−03:30, UTC and +05:45) formed the crossed grid. The inverse checks supplied reference JDs directly to the package. The JPL J2000 definition supplies an external anchor.
The London checks included the missing and repeated 01:30 local times on the 2024 clock-change dates; both produced errors, as documented. Year zero, Julian leap-year behaviour, a negative sub-degree angle, a date rounded across midnight, argument overrides and restoration of session timezone were also exercised. These checks cover civil-time conversion; they provide no constraint on prehistoric ΔT or the accuracy of every historical timezone database entry.
Download A01 code, fixtures and all 499 results. Calendar and angle methods · Validation programme.

title: 19  Calendar, density and significance checks
section: 19.2 D01 · Measurement densities, sums and highest-density regions
text:
19.2 D01 · Measurement densities, sums and highest-density regions
Question. Do sampled measurement densities retain the expected shape, mass and circular support, and do summaries and subsets retain the intended observation?
Extension · 2.0.9011. Checks of the six measurement families compare sampled ordinates with analytic values, integrate the four new doorway examples, check an asymmetric triangle across north, and compare a broad wrapped convolution with a periodic reference. A deterministic model at the observed bearings or declinations reproduces the empirical SPD for each new family after subsetting and reordering. All 173 original D01 assertions and 13 supplemental assertions also passed on this build. Download the family checks and the repeated D01 results.
Earlier outcome · 2.0.9006. All 173 original assertions passed, including the 18 previous discrepancies. Thirteen further checks verified broad wrapped Gaussians, the closing segment of interpolated azimuth sums and equivalent input bearings. A 0.005° grid now retains 359.995° at its own bearing. Gaussian contributions and all copies of a uniform support interval are combined at each bearing before applying the density cutoff. Declination subsets now carry centres in the selected order, including repeated and empty selections. Download the corrected D01 run.
Previous run · 2.0.9005. Of 173 assertions, 155 passed and 18 showed differences. Of 144 ordinary-width sampled-density comparisons, 132 agreed. All 12 differences occurred at the north seam on the 0.005° grid. The two additional broad-width cases and four declination-centre metadata checks also differed. The archive retains all residuals, including failures.
For each coordinate we evaluated Gaussian and uniform densities directly from their analytic definitions. Azimuth distances were taken around the circle, while declination was confined to [−90°, 90°]. The matrix comprised four azimuth centres and five declination centres, uncertainty 2°, four grid spacings and two density cutoffs. We compared every retained value, total grid mass and the first two moments about the centre. An independent numerical integral checked the retained Gaussian mass at three spacings. The summed and unit-area normalised SPDs agreed in the tested cases. Known highest-density regions, including disconnected supports and ties at threshold, returned the expected endpoints and reached the requested mass. For equal-height modes, retaining the full tied set can exceed the target mass. These are discrete-grid checks of the PDFs in the framework of Silva (2020).







Finding on build 2.0.9005
Consequence




On the 0.005° azimuth grid, the implementation folds samples above 359.99° across north. Twelve narrow-density cases centred at 359°, 0° or 1° differed from the periodic reference.
Density can be displaced across the seam. For the 0° Gaussian, the maximum pointwise discrepancy was 0.19947 per degree even though the integrated mass was nearly unchanged.


A 100° uniform half-width and a Gaussian standard deviation of 100° both exceeded the effective 90° margin used for folding.
The resulting curves omit part of the periodic density. A grid-spacing change alone cannot recover those tails.


Selecting the second declination PDF, reversing the order, repeating a selection or selecting no rows retained the original declination-centre vector.
The selected curves and names followed the requested order. Reading metadata$dec as the centres of the selected curves can misidentify an observation.

title: 19  Calendar, density and significance checks
section: 19.3 S03 · Monte Carlo ranks, local clusters and reported probabilities
text:
19.3 S03 · Monte Carlo ranks, local clusters and reported probabilities
Question. Given the same observed and simulated curves, do the two significance tests report the expected global rank, local clusters and adjusted probabilities?
Current outcome · 2.0.9006. The independent scorer agreed on global ranks, local endpoints and adjusted probabilities in all 19 comparisons. These include the two original public simulation matrices replayed unchanged. All 88 binomial, print, symbol and plot assertions passed. The count fell from 92 because the two example fits now each report one cluster across north. Twelve additional checks confirmed invariance of the ranks to rotation of the angular origin and agreement between memory and disk scoring. Download the corrected S03 run.
On the original randomTest() curves, the corrected global probability is 0.4375 and the 349.5°–10° excess has adjusted p = 0.1875. On the original modelTest() curves the corrected excess spans 346°–15°, with global and adjusted local p = 0.0625. A start bearing greater than the end bearing denotes a single interval running clockwise through north. The uniform-bearing null samples north once; the global score counts each direction once, and the observed curve and every simulated curve undergo the same circular cluster search. The repeated endpoint may still appear in the display. Declination ranges remain linear. Stored fits from previous builds retain their original probabilities; refit the original input data to obtain current inference.
Previous run · 2.0.9005. Independent enumeration reproduced every global probability, local interval and adjusted local probability in 17 linear-grid cases. These included fixed fixtures and seeded calls through both public functions. All 92 separate assertions on binomial probabilities, symbol thresholds, printed results and plotted cluster marks passed. A circular reference exposed a seam effect on the local results and, in one seeded fit, on the global p-value.
The Python reference pooled the observed and simulated values at each coordinate, computed sample standard deviations and interpolated quantiles, and ranked the sum of standardised excursions. One-tail tests used upper excursions and two-tail tests also included lower excursions. For each simulated curve the reference selected its own largest qualifying cluster before ranking the observed local score. The discrete reference included ties, all-identical curves, an isolated excursion, clusters on both sides, and spans at and just below 0.5°. For public calls, the R harness recorded the actual simulation matrix passed to inference; Python then scored it independently. This isolates the scoring stage from the null-generation and power studies scheduled under S01 and S02.
What changed since the published algorithms? Silva (2020) used simulation-only bounds and scored simulations over the observed local interval. Silva & Lomsdalen (2025) extended testing to shared and site-specific null models. The present functions pool the observation with simulations, include tied exceedances, use the positive rank floor and search for the largest cluster in every simulation (Silva 2020; Silva and Lomsdalen 2025). On a fixed set of 16 curves, a reconstruction of the archived 2020 scoring equations gave global p = 0 and local p = 0 for the excess over 2–9°. Build 2.0.9005 gave 0.125 for both with the same curves. In a separate eight-simulation example with zero exceedances, the positive floor was 1/9. This comparison concerns scoring on controlled inputs. The original archaeological datasets were not reanalysed. Historical implementation and methodological comparison.
North seam on 2.0.9005. The earlier build searches the azimuth grid as a line, splitting a north-crossing excess into separate intervals. A circular diagnostic joined the first and last runs and counted the duplicated 0°/360° direction once. In the seeded 15-simulation randomTest() example, the package gave global p = 0.375 and separate intervals 349.5–360° (adjusted p = 0.750) and 0–10° (p = 0.9375). The circular comparison gave global p = 0.4375 and one 349.5–10° interval (p = 0.1875). The small number of simulations makes the arithmetic transparent. These values illustrate sensitivity to the seam and supply no estimate of false-positive frequency. Declination has physical endpoints and uses the linear comparison.

The prescribed track exercised the internal crossing solver. The named-star cases exercised riseset() on 1 January 2000 UTC. Mintaka’s reference used its noon declination from the same ephemeris and an independent spherical calculation. Polaris returned missing rise and set records on the eastern-ridge profile. All 14 event checks passed on 2.0.9006. The maximum absolute azimuth discrepancy was below 0.000001° for the prescribed track and below 0.000022° for Mintaka, against a tolerance of 0.001°. The extended study added 137 assertions, all of which passed.
At latitudes 50° N and 35° S, we compared event counts, direction, order, times and bearings with a one-second scan and independently bisected roots on flat, uniformly raised, notched, ridge and step-like skylines. All 28 reference crossings were recovered with no extras. The maximum timing discrepancy was 0.00038 s against a tolerance of 0.02 s. Flat and raised times also agreed with the closed-form hour-angle solution. A constructed touch without a sign change produced no event; a two-second emergence produced both roots.
On 2 January 2000, a ridge at 50° N, 100° E produced rise, set and re-emergence for Mintaka. The public function selected the first rise and first set independently with refraction both on and off. Independent five-second ephemeris scans located the same events within the 1.1 s allowance for whole-second output. Polaris returned no events at either 50° N (always above) or 50° S (always below). A lunar rise after the next local midnight returned the following date in UTC−02:30.
At 35.90083° N, 14.34° E, we compared geometric centre crossings for the Sun and Moon with JPL Horizons. The reference interpolates airless topocentric direction vectors and solves for clearance above the skyline. We tested both scalar and profile representations of a flat skyline and an asymmetric profile. The largest discrepancies were 0.842 s and 0.00410°, within the 3 s and 0.015° comparison tolerances. Doubling the reference sampling interval from 10 to 20 minutes moved the reference times by less than 0.001 s. The tolerances allow for whole-second timestamps and differing ephemeris conventions. These are tests of centre crossings. First limb contact and naked-eye visibility require different definitions.

section: 19.5 D02 · Bearing uncertainty on flat and irregular skylines
text:
19.5 D02 · Bearing uncertainty on flat and irregular skylines
We tested coordtrans() at 50° N with a constant 2° skyline and refraction disabled. Bearings had a Gaussian standard deviation of 2° about centres of 90°, 359° and 0°. Independent Gaussian altitude errors had a standard deviation of 0.5°. For each centre, we transformed one million paired draws through the spherical altitude equation and compared the median and both endpoints of the equal-tailed 95% interval with the package density. We used the same seeded draws at each centre.
At calculation and azimuth integration spacings of 0.1° and 0.05°, all 18 quantile comparisons fell within the specified 0.02° tolerance. The largest absolute discrepancy was 0.00505°, at the upper endpoint for a bearing centred on north on the coarser grid. All six returned densities integrated to one within 0.000001. The discrepancy includes Monte Carlo sampling variation. The extended study varied each numerical spacing separately. Ten configurations returned densities on five grids, and an eleventh tested the documented zero-width limit. The references were (1) direct spherical propagation of 524,288 scrambled Sobol draws and (2) independent quadrature over 8,192 bearing strata using the package’s endpoint-Gaussian implementation of the conditional-density method (Silva 2020). The refracted case shared the Swiss altitude correction to isolate propagation. The archive reports mass error, maximum CDF distance, quantiles, prominent modes and 80% highest-density regions.

The Canrooska input linearly interpolates surveyed bearings and altitudes at the stone row. The Kunċizzjoni input uses Tore Lomsdalen’s archived Horizon terrain model. Across nine configurations away from the celestial-pole limit, all three quantiles on all five grids agreed with direct propagation within 0.008°. The maximum CDF distance was 0.00411. For the summed-density check, transforming a normalised sum of two bearing PDFs gave area 0.99999947. The integrated absolute difference from summing the two individually transformed PDFs was 0.00159 after normalisation.
Grid sensitivity. The ridge had three prominent modes near −0.77°, 3.87° and 9.89°. On the default grid, the 80% highest-density region split the middle band and returned four intervals. Reducing the calculation and azimuth integration steps to 0.05° and the output step to 0.005° recovered the three reference intervals. For this ridge, refining only the integration spacing reduced the largest quantile discrepancy from 0.00645° to 0.00245°. Refining only the calculation spacing reduced it to 0.00485°; refining only the output spacing gave 0.00642°.
Celestial-pole limit. At latitude 50° N with a 47° northern skyline, the fine-grid result differed from direct propagation by up to 0.1715° in quantiles and 0.0589 in cumulative probability. Agreement with independent integration of the conditional Gaussian was within 0.00070° in quantiles. The discrepancy is therefore primarily in that approximation. At a 50° northern skyline, the transformed endpoints coincide for the central bearing. The function raised its documented zero-width error on every grid even though direct propagation had a central 95% interval of 87.071°–89.819°. These cases distinguish the celestial-pole geometry from a geographic-pole observer, for which a density was recovered.

section: 19.6 S01 · Calibration of the uniform-orientation test
text:
19.6 S01 · Calibration of the uniform-orientation test
How frequently does randomTest() reject when orientations have been independently drawn from its stated uniform-bearing model? How frequently does it detect a cluster of known strength and width? We fixed the survey geometry, measurement widths, sample size and bearing support before drawing each dataset.
Implementation check. In 2.0.9006 the simulated PDFs used the constructor’s default spacing and cutoff. The shared-horizon simulation also summed the bearings at the default SPD spacing, whereas the observed sum used the requested spacing. With identical centres of 30° and 120°, widths of 22° and 32°, a 30° source grid, a 0.0001 source cutoff and a 2° test spacing, maximum absolute observed–simulated density differences were 0.00203 for azimuth, 0.02020 for the shared skyline and 0.17537 for site-paired declinations. On 2.0.9007 all three differences were zero. The correction can affect probabilities calculated with non-default source settings and the shared-horizon route whenever its selected SPD spacing differed from the simulation default. Refit affected analyses from their original inputs. The 2.0.9007 socket worker setup also resolves the parent library path on each worker. In a two-library installation, the corrected serial and two-worker results agreed exactly on all three routes.
Design. We ran 2,000 independent outer datasets in each of 13 null settings and four cluster alternatives. Every outer dataset had fresh Monte Carlo reference draws. Normal and uniform measurement families, sample sizes of 2 to 24, one and two tails, different grid widths and 9, 19, 39 or 99 simulations were represented. For each outer fit we recorded the global probability and the smallest maximum-cluster-adjusted probability across the reported intervals, assigning one when there was no interval. The preselected thresholds were 1%, 5% and 10%. Finite ranks have spacing 1/(B+1)1/(B+1), with inclusive ranking for ties.
To make repeated calculations feasible we reused deterministic package-generated densities for each permitted bearing, width and site. For the shared route we tabulated the entire transform for every ordered input pair. A separate implementation scored the pooled observed and simulated curves. In 16 public-interface replays, all reconstructed curves agreed within 8×10−158\times10^{-15} in density and all global and minimum local probabilities agreed exactly. The shared-route design uses two observations and six or twelve possible directions. Its calibration applies to those designs.
Null results. Entries give the rejection percentage at the nominal 5% level, with pointwise 95% Wilson intervals over datasets. A local rejection means at least one adjusted interval crossed the threshold.

19.7 S02 · Specified and site-specific null models
Can modelTest() recover the expected false-positive rate when the proposed model gives different weights to candidate directions at different sites? The study used five unequally spaced candidate directions, weights interpreted as probability masses, eight observations and 39 fresh reference draws per fit. We tested azimuth densities, directly constructed declination densities and asymmetric templates shifted to candidate means.
Same-input comparison. In 2.0.9007, simulated azimuth and declination PDFs used constructor defaults even when the input PDF had been constructed on a different grid or with a different cutoff. With a 0.5° source grid and 0.002 cutoff the largest observed–simulated density discrepancy was 0.0015831 in both fixtures. The same draws on 2.0.9008 gave zero discrepancy. Public fits agreed with independent assembly of their observed and simulated curves and with independently scored global and local ranks. An independent first-moment calculation also checked asymmetric template shifting, explicit replacement uncertainties and the pole-boundary error. Two actual horizon-transformed PDFs agreed with independent shifts to within floating-point precision.

section: 19.8 H07 · Coverage of partial photographic skylines
text:
19.8 H07 · Coverage of partial photographic skylines
A photograph covering 330° through north to 30° supplies no terrain height at 180°. In the archived manual example, 2.0.9007 returned a finite declination distribution spanning −39.302° to −35.032° for a uniform bearing of 180° ± 1°, and a sunrise at 92.481° on 20 March 2026. Direct altitude lookup already returned a missing value at 180°. The shifted profile rows intended to support interpolation at north also allowed other consumers to interpolate across the missing sector.
Build 2.0.9008 checks coverage at the point of use. In the archived example both the unsupported transformation and the sunrise search now give explicit coverage errors. The complete test suite also supplied an independent level mask with known edges.







Operation
Verified behaviour




hor2alt()
Both edges and bearings inside the photographed arc return finite values. Outside bearings return missing values.


coordtrans()
Inside and north-wrapping densities agree with the complete level skyline. Positive density crossing an edge, or lying wholly outside, raises an error. Zero SPD tails outside coverage were accepted in the tested case.


riseset(), star.phases(), spatial.equinox()
Full-sky searches reject a partial photograph. The corresponding full-profile controls run successfully.

Partial photographs are rejected for both textured and numerical landscape export. Both modes accept the full photograph.

section: 19.10 A05 · Solar dates and limiting declinations
text:
19.10 A05 · Solar dates and limiting declinations
A05 distinguishes the civil day on which the Sun reaches a declination, the instant of a named season, and the direction of a crossing at a particular site. We tested each quantity against its own reference. All 121 assertions passed on 2.0.9009.



Quantity
Reference and result




Solar civil dates
A six-hour JPL Horizons geocentric apparent-of-date table supplied 12 crossings at six declinations in 2000. solar.date() matched every UT civil day. As a separate diagnostic, solving against the package’s underlying solar ephemeris gave differences of at most 2.65 seconds from the interpolated JPL roots. The largest occurred close to the June turning point.


Calendar branches
Independent bracketing on a quarter-day grid checked 2000 CE and 3250 BCE in Gregorian and Julian calendars. At the maximum declination a tangency gave one passage, an immediately lower target gave two, and an unreachable target gave none. A civil-year boundary fixture gave three passages.


Named seasons
The four named season dates matched the US Naval Observatory 2000 record. Underlying apparent-longitude roots differed by at most 26 seconds from the minute-rounded reference. The public labels report civil days.


Northern and southern terrain limits
The direct spherical reference searched a dense grid throughout each specified sector. An interior crest gave a maximum of 48.5884° and an interior trough gave a minimum of −47.7023°. Both functions agreed within 0.00028°. The tests also covered level terrain at four latitudes.


Spatial equinox
An independent hour-angle track and sign-bracketed roots checked northern and southern sites, a flat horizon and separate east and west ridges. Rising and setting midpoints and derived declinations agreed within 0.000003°. The high-latitude case correctly lacked the pair of crossings needed for a midpoint. These checks disabled refraction and parallax to isolate geometry.


Zenith and anti-zenith
At geometric overhead and underfoot the parallax correction vanishes. Build 2.0.9009 uses the obliquity of the supplied year for tropical eligibility. The fixtures include both tropical boundaries, modern and prehistoric epochs, and an unreachable polar site.



The prehistoric date checks use an independent root search with the same Swiss ephemeris. The JPL and USNO comparisons apply to the modern cases tested. Download the A05 scripts, reference data and results.

title: 19  Calendar, density and significance checks
section: 19.11 A08 · Target screening and dated bands
text:
19.11 A08 · Target screening and dated bands
A measured band can intersect a target briefly, more than once, or exactly at a turning point. We compared findTargets() with independent annual stellar samples and a separate line-segment intersection calculation. For solar and lunar limits, the reference evaluates January obliquity and the local parallax term for every integer year. All 129 assertions passed on 2.0.9009.
Stellar membership. In a 30–42 CE search, a narrow band around a turning point for Sirius returned 35–35 CE and 38–39 CE after rounding the interpolated boundaries to years. The exact annual maximum gave one contact in 36 CE. The study also tested magnitude inclusion and exclusion, one-year searches, catalogue identifiers and aliases, and the pairing of colours and styles with their targets. The implementation treats stellar differences within 0.0000001° of an edge as a contact. The reference shares the stellar ephemeris. This study validates selection and aggregation; stellar positions at subannual extrema remain outside this model.
Solar and lunar bounds. Earlier builds could collapse a short overlay range to one sampled value and lose the observing site’s parallax when calculating a dated envelope. At 50° N over astronomical years −3400 to −3100 the old southern major lunar overlay gave approximately −29.34° to −29.32°. The annual local limits were −30.08° to −30.05°. The largest endpoint error in the fixtures was 0.7334°. Build 2.0.9009 reproduced the annual local bounds, including both endpoints, for one-year, short, modern and prehistoric ranges. Spherical inversion of the returned orbit coordinates recovered their input declinations.
Candidate selection now uses unrounded declinations. The two-decimal limits are display values. Solar zenith/anti-zenith screening uses the archaeological period and requires a reachable passage. The spatial-equinox candidate uses the rising and setting solutions from the endpoint epochs; this particular candidate does not claim to enclose every intermediate year’s terrain midpoint.
